CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Today

Agents, environments, sensors, and actuators
Percepts and percept sequences
Agent functions and agent programs
Vacuum-cleaner world as a running example
Performance measures and failure modes
Rationality, omniscience, and autonomy




Agent



Percepts



Vacuum world



Performance

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Agents and Environments
An agent is defined by how it receives information and how it acts on the world.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is an Agent?



An agent is a software or hardware system that interacts with an environment through sensors and actuators.


Sensors: perceive the state of the environment.
Actuators: change or affect the environment.


An agent is not just a program; it is a program situated in an environment.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example: Robot Vacuum Cleaner



Sensors:

detect obstacles
detect dirt
detect edges

Actuators:

move the vacuum
adjust suction
send signals



What should the vacuum do when the room is clean but the next room may not be?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Percepts
Agents do not directly receive “the world”; they receive sensor inputs.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Percept



A percept is the input an agent receives at a specific moment through its sensors.

Example:

A self-driving car detects a red traffic light.


Percepts are momentary; they describe what the agent receives now.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Percept Sequence

A percept sequence is the complete history of all percepts received by the agent.

Example:

At t_1: detects a red light
At t_2: detects a pedestrian crossing
At t_3: detects a green light


Agent decisions can depend on both the current percept and the percept history.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Agents Interact with Environments



(Fig. 2.1 of AIMA)



The agent sees only what its sensors report.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Agent Functions and Programs
The same behavior can be described abstractly as a function or concretely as a program.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Agent Function

The agent function maps a percept sequence to an action.

Mathematical representation:

f: \text{PerceptSequence} \rightarrow \text{Action}


Defines the behavior of the agent.
Can be simple rule-based logic.
Can be complex learned behavior using AI algorithms.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Agent Program

The agent program is the implementation of the agent function.
It runs on the agent’s hardware to produce actions from percepts.




Agent Function
Agent Program




Abstract mathematical mapping
Practical implementation


Independent of hardware
Executes on hardware


Defines ideal behavior
Uses algorithms and code

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vacuum-Cleaner World
A tiny world is enough to expose the core ideas: percepts, actions, goals, and rationality.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vacuum-Cleaner World


Environment

Room A
Room B
Dirt

Vacuum Agent

Sensors: room sensor, dirt sensor
Actuators: motor, vacuum



(Fig. 2.2 of AIMA)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vacuum-Cleaner Agent Function







Percept Sequence
Action




You are in Room A. Room A is dirty.
Suck


You are in Room A. Room A is clean.
Go right


You are in Room A. Room A is clean. You are in Room B. Room B is dirty.
Suck




The action is chosen from the percept sequence, not from the true world state directly.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Performance Measures
To evaluate an agent, we must say what counts as success.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Performance Measures



A performance measure defines how success is evaluated for an agent.

For a vacuum-cleaner agent, possible measures include:

amount of dirt cleaned
energy efficiency
minimizing unnecessary movement


What behavior does your scoring rule reward?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Failure Example
Poorly Defined Performance Measure

“Score 1 point for every pile of dirt sucked up.”

The agent may:

suck up dirt
dump the dirt back out
repeat forever to maximize score


Poorly designed objectives can produce unintended behavior.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Better Performance Measure
Improved Objective

“Score 1 point for each clean room every minute.”

Lessons:

Focus on desired outcomes.
Avoid rewarding undesirable shortcuts.
Align the measure with the true task objective.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rational Agents
Rationality is about choosing well under the information available.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rational Agent



A rational agent chooses actions expected to maximize its performance measure.

Factors considered:

performance measure
prior knowledge
percept sequence
available actions

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Definition of a Rational Agent
For each possible percept sequence, a rational agent should:

Select the action expected to maximize performance.
Base decisions on:

evidence from percepts
built-in knowledge



Rationality does not require perfect knowledge. It requires good action selection from available evidence.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rationality vs. Omniscience







Rationality
Omniscience




Best decision with limited information
Perfect foresight


Realistic
Unrealistic


Evaluated by expected performance
Requires knowing actual outcomes in advance




If an agent makes the best decision from limited evidence but the outcome is bad, was it irrational?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autonomous Agents
Autonomous agents can reduce their dependence on fixed prior knowledge.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autonomous Agents
Some agents can:

recognize what they do not know
gather information through sensing and exploration
learn from observations
update their own behavior over time

Examples

self-driving cars
reinforcement learning agents
adaptive robots


Autonomy lets agents improve through experience and remain useful in changing environments.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways



Agents interact with environments through sensors and actuators.
A percept sequence is the agent’s history of observations.
An agent function maps percept sequences to actions.
Performance measures shape behavior, sometimes badly.
Rational agents maximize expected performance from available evidence.




Asset credits

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Classical AI


AI = Representation + Search

Describe the problem.
Choose a useful abstraction for partial solutions.
Define operations that change the representation.
Search through those changes until a solution is found.


Representation defines the world the agent can think in; search decides how it moves through that world.





Puzzle pieces as a visual metaphor for representation and search

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is Search?

Search is the process of finding a solution or path in a problem space.
It is useful when an agent must reason through possible future states before acting.






Navigation example


Pathfinding




Chessboard example


Game playing




Puzzle example


Puzzle solving

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Search Problems



Component
Question




Initial state
Where do we start?


Actions
What can we do from the current state?


Transition model
What state follows an action?


Goal test
How do we know we are done?


Path cost
What rewards or penalties accumulate along the way?




The same real-world task can become easy or hard depending on how these five pieces are defined.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example: Vacuum-Cleaner World





Vacuum-cleaner world




State count: 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8.
Vacuum location: Room A or Room B.
Room A: clean or dirty.
Room B: clean or dirty.
Actions: L, R, S.
Goal: both rooms are clean.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vacuum State Space

Vacuum-cleaner state space
Fig. 3.2 of AIMA: states are nodes; actions are edges.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example: 8 Puzzle



A sliding puzzle with 8 numbered tiles and one empty space.
Objective: arrange the tiles in a target order.
States: all tile configurations.
Actions: slide a neighboring tile into the empty space.





8-puzzle board



Fig. 3.3 of AIMA.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example: Eight Queens



Place 8 queens on an 8 \times 8 chessboard.
No two queens may share a row, column, or diagonal.
A search formulation must decide what counts as a state and what counts as an action.





Eight queens puzzle


Wikipedia: Eight Queens Puzzle

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Eight Queens: Naive vs. Better


Naive Formulation

States: any board with 0 to 8 queens.
Initial: empty board.
Actions: place a queen on any empty square.
Goal: 8 queens, none attacking.
State space: \sim 10^{15} states.


Better Formulation

States: one queen per column, filled left to right.
Actions: place a queen in the leftmost empty column without attacks.
Goal: 8 queens, none attacking.
State space: \sim 2000 states.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example: Navigation



States: current city.
Initial: starting city.
Actions: drive to a neighboring city.
Transition: arrive at the neighboring city.
Goal: destination city.





Car navigation illustration

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Overview: Uninformed Search







Algorithm
Idea




BFS
Explore all nodes at the current depth before going deeper.


DFS
Explore as far as possible along one branch before backtracking.


UCS
Expand the least-cost node first.


DLS
Run DFS with a depth limit.


IDS
Combine the memory profile of DFS with the completeness of BFS.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Overview: Informed and Specialized Search


Informed Search

Greedy Best-First Search
A* Search

Uses heuristic information to guide expansion.

Other Search Families

Bidirectional Search
Local Search
Adversarial Search

Use structure from the task to reduce work or model competition.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Tradeoffs



Criterion
Meaning




Soundness
Returned value is always a solution.


Completeness
If a solution exists, it will be found.


Optimality
The returned solution is the best possible one.


Time complexity
Time required to find a solution.


Space complexity
Memory required to find a solution.




“Satisficing” means a solution may not be optimal, but is usually good enough. Learn more on Wikipedia.

Asset credits

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Uniform-Cost Search



UCS is an uninformed search algorithm.
It expands the path with the lowest cumulative cost so far.
It is BFS-like when all edge costs are equal.
It is equivalent to Dijkstra’s algorithm when we stop at a single goal.


UCS is not looking for the fewest actions. It is looking for the cheapest path.





Navigation illustration for path cost search

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why BFS Is Not Enough


Unweighted



BFS is optimal when every edge has the same cost.

Weighted



UCS is needed when edge costs differ.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Priority Queue Intuition



Frontier item
Path cost




Start -> C
2


Start -> B
4


Start -> C -> D
5


Start -> B -> D
9




The next expanded path is always the cheapest frontier path, not necessarily the shallowest one.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
UCS Guarantees


Works Well When

edge costs are non-negative
path costs are meaningful
the cheapest solution matters


Watch For

high memory use
many nearly equal-cost paths
no optimality guarantee with negative edge costs

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Dijkstra’s Algorithm
Dijkstra(G, s):
    set d[v] = infinity for every node v
    set d[s] = 0
    insert (0, s) into priority queue Q

    while Q is not empty:
        remove node u with the smallest d[u]

        for each neighbor v of u with edge cost w(u, v):
            if d[u] + w(u, v) < d[v]:
                d[v] = d[u] + w(u, v)
                insert (d[v], v) into Q

    return all distances d[v]

UCS stops at a goal. Dijkstra keeps going to compute shortest paths to all nodes.

Bidirectional Search




Run a forward search from the start.
Run a backward search from the goal.
Stop when the two frontiers meet.


Instead of roughly O(b^d) nodes, bidirectional search can explore about O(b^{d/2}) nodes from each side.

Big-O Notation
Big-O ignores constant factors and lower-order terms as input size grows.



A function f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n_0 such that

0\le f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)

for every n\ge n_0.





For n\ge1, 3n^2+5n+7\le15n^2. Choose c=15 and n_0=1 to show O(n^2).


State whether a bound describes the worst case, average case, or another case. Big-O alone does not specify which.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
KD-Tree Nearest Neighbor
Task: among stored points P, find a point closest to a query q. In two dimensions, use Euclidean distance:
d(q,p)=\sqrt{(q_x-p_x)^2+(q_y-p_y)^2}.


Search idea

Search the side containing q first.
Keep the nearest candidate p and its distance r.
Backtrack if the other side could contain a closer point.


Complexity intuition

Balanced tree height: O(\log n).
A nearest-neighbor query may visit many leaves.
Worst-case query: O(n).



A region’s distance bound can rule out every point inside it. Tree balance alone does not guarantee effective pruning.


Here n is the number of stored points and r=d(q,p). Efficient pruning often makes low-dimensional queries fast, but there is no universal logarithmic worst-case query bound. High dimensions and unfavorable point/query distributions can force nearly a full scan. Points kept at internal nodes must also be tested while traversing. Sources: Carl Kingsford’s kd-tree lecture, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ckingsf/bioinfo-lectures/kdtrees.pdf, and the SciPy KDTree documentation, https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.KDTree.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Graph Representation Matters
Let V be the number of vertices and E the number of edges in a finite graph.



Representation
Stored graph
Full BFS/DFS traversal




Adjacency list
O(V+E)
O(V+E)


Adjacency matrix
O(V^2)
O(V^2)





For A, a list stores just (C,2) and (G,9).
A matrix row checks all five possible destinations, including absent edges.
For a sparse graph, most matrix entries describe no edge.




Bounds describe a traversal covering all vertices, starting additional traversals for disconnected components if necessary. In a single-source search, only reached vertices need their neighbors scanned. Absent matrix edges need a sentinel distinct from legitimate zero-cost edges. The graph’s adjacency lists contain 6 total entries. A 5 by 5 matrix has 25 entries. Graph storage is separate from additional search records.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
BFS Complexity
Mark each state reached on insertion, so each vertex enters the queue at most once.


Time

Expands each reached vertex and scans its adjacency list.
O(V+E) with adjacency lists.
O(V^2) with adjacency matrices.


Additional search space

Queue, reached set, and parents use O(V).
The queue can contain parts of two adjacent layers.
A wide last layer can dominate memory.



A complete tree with branching factor b>1 and maximum depth d has b^d leaves. BFS may need O(b^d) frontier space on that tree.


These are worst-case traversal bounds and exclude the stored graph from additional search space. Here d is the maximum depth of a finite complete tree, not the solution-depth convention in an unbounded search tree. Goal testing on removal in an implicit tree can generate the next layer before stopping, so state that convention when comparing textbook b-to-the-d formulas. Reference: AIMA Chapter 3 and https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/search/uninformed.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
DFS Complexity
Mark a vertex when entering it and skip already visited vertices.


Time

Expands each reached vertex and scans its adjacency list.
O(V+E) with adjacency lists.
O(V^2) with adjacency matrices.


Stack versus visited set

A chain can require O(V) active calls.
A balanced tree needs O(\log V) active calls.
A graph-search visited set still uses O(V).



Recursive DFS uses O(V) additional space in a general graph. A shallow call stack alone does not make the entire search use O(\log V) space.


The recursion-stack bound assumes adjacency-list iterators or equivalent DFS frames, so each level records its next neighbor rather than copying all remaining neighbors. A tree traversal needs no visited set when parent/child direction already prevents cycles. A node-stack implementation with repeated pending entries can have a different memory bound. Keep implementation assumptions explicit.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
UCS, Greedy, and A*
For a finite explicit graph, let V be vertices and E be edges.



Algorithm
Priority
Assumption for the usual bound




UCS
g
Nonnegative edge costs


Greedy
h
Expand each state at most once


A*
g+h
Consistent heuristic, no re-expansion



With adjacency lists and a binary heap holding one entry per frontier state:
\text{Time}=O((V+E)\log V),\qquad \text{storage}=O(V+E).
Decrease-key lowers an existing entry’s priority and restores heap order in O(\log V), using an index to locate that entry.

Storage includes the graph. Reopening states or retaining stale heap entries requires extra accounting.


With an indexed binary heap, insert, pop, and decrease-key cost O(log V). Up to V state removals and E examined edges give O((V+E)log V) time with constant-time edge/heuristic evaluation. The total O(V+E) space includes the graph; the heap, parent, and best arrays use O(V). A lazy heap can hold O(E) entries and gives O((V+E)log(V+E)) directly; on a simple graph this has the usual O((V+E)log V) form because E is at most V squared. A* with inconsistent heuristics can re-expand states, so those assumptions no longer suffice. Greedy’s bound here assumes duplicate control, not optimality.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A* Best and Worst Cases


Weak Heuristic

If h(n) gives little useful guidance, A* behaves much like UCS.
It may expand many nodes.


Strong Heuristic

If h(n) is very accurate, A* can move almost directly toward the goal.
Even an exact heuristic may leave many tied optimal paths to explore.

title: AC-3 Constraint Propagation
text:
Download notebook (.ipynb)

A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) consists of variables, their possible values, and constraints. AC-3, Arc Consistency Algorithm 3, removes values that have no supporting value in a neighboring domain.
The variables here are a, b, c, and d, each initially a digit from 0 through 9. Propagation reduces domains; it does not necessarily choose one complete assignment. Run the cells in order; only Python’s standard library is needed.

title: AC-3 Constraint Propagation
text:
Complete AC-3 Walkthrough
The code below defines domains, constraints, the revise operation, and the AC-3 loop. The printed domains show how consistency narrows the search space before any backtracking is needed.

# a + b = 3
# b + c = 4
# c + d = 2
# d + a = 1

# using AC-3 to solve it
# the domains of a, b, c, d are all 0~9 digits
# the constraints are the four equations above

from collections import deque
from typing import List, Tuple

def print_domains(domains: dict):
    print("a: {}".format(domains['a']))
    print("b: {}".format(domains['b']))
    print("c: {}".format(domains['c']))
    print("d: {}".format(domains['d']))

def ac3(constraints: List[Tuple[str, str, int]], domains: dict):
    queue = deque(constraints)
    while queue:
        (xi, xj, value) = queue.popleft()
        if revise(domains, xi, xj, value):
            print(f'queue: {queue}')
            print_domains(domains)            
            if not domains[xi]:
                return False
            for xk, xl, this_value in constraints:
                if xl == xi and xk != xj:
                    # print the constraints that will be added to the queue
                    print(f'adding {xk}+{xl}={this_value}')
                    queue.append((xk, xi, this_value))
    return True

def revise(domains: dict, xi: str, xj: str, value: int):
    revised = False
    print(f'revising {xi}+{xj}={value}')
    del_x = []
    for x in domains[xi]:
        if not any(x + y == value for y in domains[xj]):
            del_x.append(x)
            revised = True
    for x in del_x:
        domains[xi].remove(x)
    return revised

def solve(constraints: List[Tuple[str, str, int]]):
    domains = {x: list(range(10)) for x in set(x for x, _, _ in constraints)}
    if ac3(constraints, domains):
        return domains
    return None

constraints = [
    ('a', 'b', 3),
    ('b', 'c', 4),
    ('c', 'd', 2),
    ('d', 'a', 1),
]


domains = solve(constraints)
if domains:
    print('final result of domains:')
    print_domains(domains)
else:
    print('No solution')

title: K-Nearest Neighbors on MNIST
text:
Download notebook (.ipynb)
  Download page (.html)
K-nearest neighbors (KNN) predicts a label by finding similar labeled examples and taking a vote. Unlike a neural network, it does not learn weights during fitting.
MNIST, the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology dataset, contains 28-by-28 grayscale images of handwritten digits. Run the cells in order with PyTorch, torchvision, NumPy, and Matplotlib installed. The first run downloads the data and needs an internet connection.

title: K-Nearest Neighbors on MNIST
text:
Load Data and Define KNN
This cell prepares MNIST tensors, defines the distance-based prediction rule, and evaluates the classifier.

import torch
import torchvision
import torchvision.transforms as transforms
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter

# set random seed for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)

# Set device
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print(f"Using device: {device}")

# -------------------------------
# 1. Load and Preprocess MNIST
# -------------------------------
# Define transformations: Convert to tensor & normalize
transform = transforms.Compose([transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))])

# Load MNIST dataset
batch_size = 10000  # Load a large batch since KNN requires all data
train_dataset = torchvision.datasets.MNIST(root='~/temp_data', train=True, transform=transform, download=True)
test_dataset = torchvision.datasets.MNIST(root='~/temp_data', train=False, transform=transform, download=True)

# Convert dataset to DataLoader
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset=train_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset=test_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)

# Extract data from DataLoader
train_data, train_labels = next(iter(train_loader))
test_data, test_labels = next(iter(test_loader))

# Flatten images (28x28 → 784)
train_data = train_data.view(train_data.size(0), -1).numpy()
test_data = test_data.view(test_data.size(0), -1).numpy()

# Convert labels to numpy
train_labels = train_labels.numpy()
test_labels = test_labels.numpy()

print(f"Train data shape: {train_data.shape}, Train labels shape: {train_labels.shape}")
print(f"Test data shape: {test_data.shape}, Test labels shape: {test_labels.shape}")

# -------------------------------
# 2. Implement Custom KNN
# -------------------------------
class CustomKNN:
    def __init__(self, k=3):
        self.k = k
        self.train_data = None
        self.train_labels = None

    def fit(self, X, y):
        """Stores training data and labels"""
        self.train_data = X
        self.train_labels = y

    def predict(self, X):
        """Predict labels for given test data"""
        predictions = []
        for test_sample in X:
            # Compute distances (Euclidean)
            distances = np.linalg.norm(self.train_data - test_sample, axis=1)
            
            # Find k nearest neighbors
            k_indices = np.argsort(distances)[:self.k]
            k_nearest_labels = self.train_labels[k_indices]
            
            # Get most common label among neighbors
            most_common = Counter(k_nearest_labels).most_common(1)[0][0]
            predictions.append(most_common)
        
        return np.array(predictions)

# -------------------------------
# 3. Train & Evaluate the Model
# -------------------------------
k = 3  # Set k
knn = CustomKNN(k)
print("\nTraining KNN model...")
knn.fit(train_data, train_labels)

print("\nEvaluating model...")
test_predictions = knn.predict(test_data)
accuracy = np.mean(test_predictions == test_labels)  # Accuracy calculation
print(f"KNN Classification Accuracy: {accuracy * 100:.2f}%")

# -------------------------------
# 4. Visualize Some Predictions
# -------------------------------
def visualize_predictions(n=5):
    indices = np.random.choice(len(test_data), n, replace=False)
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    for i, idx in enumerate(indices):
        image = test_data[idx].reshape(28, 28)
        true_label = test_labels[idx]
        predicted_label = test_predictions[idx]

        plt.subplot(1, n, i + 1)
        plt.imshow(image, cmap='gray')
        plt.title(f"True: {true_label}\nPred: {predicted_label}", color="green" if true_label == predicted_label else "red")
        plt.axis('off')
    
    plt.show()

visualize_predictions(5)

text:

Simulated annealing minimizes an objective while sometimes accepting a worse candidate. Temperature controls how willing the search is to do this: high temperature encourages exploration, while low temperature favors improvement.
Run the cells in order with NumPy and Matplotlib installed. This small example uses a one-dimensional objective so both the landscape and the search history are visible.

title: Simulated Annealing
text:
Objective Landscape
First we define and plot the objective so the optimization path has visual context.

# simulated annealing demo
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def objective(x):
    return -(x + np.sin(x)) * np.exp(-x**2.0)

# draw the landscape of objective function
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 1000)
y = objective(x)
plt.plot(x, y)
# print the minimum value and its location
index = np.argmin(y)
print('x= {:.2f}'.format(x[index]))
print('minimum f(x)= {:.2f}'.format(y[index]))
# plot the minimum point
plt.plot(x[index], y[index], 'ro')
plt.show()

x= 0.68
minimum f(x)= -0.82

title: Simulated Annealing
text:
Annealing Loop
The algorithm proposes random moves, accepts improvements, and occasionally accepts worse moves according to the current temperature.

# simulated annealing algorithm
# the objective is to find the value of x that minimizes the objective function

# set the seed
# np.random.seed(1)

# define the total iterations
n_iter = 1000
# initial guess
x = np.random.uniform(-5, 5)
# run the algorithm
scores = list()
for i in range(n_iter):
    T = 1.0 - (i / float(n_iter)) # temperature schedule
    # take a step
    x_new = np.random.uniform(-5, 5)
    # evaluate the objective function
    f_new = objective(x_new)
    f_old = objective(x)
    if f_new < f_old:
        x = x_new
    else:
        p = np.exp((f_old - f_new) / T)
        if np.random.rand() < p:
            x = x_new
    # keep track of scores
    scores.append(f_old)
# print the best result
print('Done!')
print('Best x: {:.2f}'.format(x))
print('Best score: {:.2f}'.format(objective(x)))
# plot scores
plt.plot(scores)
plt.show()

title: Genetic Algorithm for N-Queens
text:
Download notebook (.ipynb)

A genetic algorithm evolves a population of candidate boards using selection, crossover, and mutation. The file name refers to eight queens, but the supplied experiment uses 30 queens.
Run the cells in order. Only Matplotlib needs installation; random is part of Python. The default population and generation limits can be computationally expensive; a smaller board is useful for quick experiments.

title: Genetic Algorithm for N-Queens
text:
Evolutionary Search
This cell defines the board representation, fitness score, genetic operators, and the main evolution loop.

import random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Parameters
default_board_size = 30
population_size = 1000
generations = 1000
mutation_rate = 0.3

# print target fitness
print("Target Fitness:", (default_board_size * (default_board_size - 1)) // 2)

random.seed(0)
# random.seed(1)
# random.seed(2)

# Fitness function: Counts non-attacking pairs
def fitness(board):
    non_attacking = 0
    n = len(board)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if board[i] != board[j] and abs(board[i] - board[j]) != j - i:
                non_attacking += 1
    return non_attacking

# Generate an individual (random permutation of row positions)
def generate_individual(n=default_board_size):
    return random.sample(range(n), n)

# Create initial population
def generate_population(size, n=default_board_size):
    return [generate_individual(n) for _ in range(size)]

# Selection: Tournament selection
def selection(population):
    return max(random.sample(population, 10), key=fitness)

# Crossover: Order Crossover (OX)
def crossover(parent1, parent2):
    n = len(parent1)
    start, end = sorted(random.sample(range(n), 2))
    child = [-1] * n
    child[start:end] = parent1[start:end]
    fill_values = [x for x in parent2 if x not in child]
    child = [fill_values.pop(0) if x == -1 else x for x in child]
    return child

# Mutation: Swap mutation
def mutate(individual):
    if random.random() < mutation_rate:
        i, j = random.sample(range(len(individual)), 2)
        individual[i], individual[j] = individual[j], individual[i]
    return individual

# Genetic Algorithm main loop
def genetic_algorithm():
    population = generate_population(population_size)
    for generation in range(generations):
        population = sorted(population, key=fitness, reverse=True)
        # print the average fitness of the population
        print("Generation:", generation, "Average Fitness:", sum(fitness(x) for x in population) / len(population))
        if fitness(population[0]) == (default_board_size * (default_board_size - 1)) // 2:
            return population[0]
        next_gen = [population[0]]  # Elitism: Carry best individual forward
        while len(next_gen) < population_size:
            p1, p2 = selection(population), selection(population)
            child = mutate(crossover(p1, p2))
            next_gen.append(child)
        population = next_gen
    return None

# Run the algorithm
solution = genetic_algorithm()
print("Solution:", solution)
print("Fitness:", fitness(solution))

A* ranks a candidate by the cost already paid plus an estimate of the remaining cost: f(n) = g(n) + h(n). This example uses unit-cost moves in four directions and Manhattan distance.
Run the cells in order with NumPy and Matplotlib installed. The map helpers mirror the BFS/DFS notebook, so the main change is how the frontier chooses its next path.

title: A* Search on a Grid
Uniform-Cost Search and Dijkstra’s Algorithm

A route with fewer edges is not necessarily cheaper. Uniform-cost search (UCS) expands the frontier entry with the lowest accumulated cost, rather than the smallest depth.
This notebook builds a weighted graph, traces a least-cost route, and then finds routes to every reachable node from the same source. Run the cells from top to bottom. The external packages are NetworkX, Matplotlib, and NumPy; the other imports belong to Python’s standard library.

title: Uniform-Cost Search and Dijkstra’s Algorithm
text:
Weighted Graph Setup
This cell builds and visualizes a random weighted graph.

# generate random weighted graphs and show it
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import random
import numpy as np

def generate_random_graph(n, m, seed):
    # n: number of nodes
    # m: number of edges
    # seed: random seed
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    G = nx.Graph()
    for i in range(n):
        G.add_node(i)
    for i in range(m):
        # get an edge that is not in the graph
        while True:
            u = random.randint(0, n-1)
            v = random.randint(0, n-1)
            if u == v:
                continue # no self loop
            if not G.has_edge(u, v):
                break
        w = random.randint(1, 10)
        G.add_edge(u, v, weight=w)
    return G

def show_graph(G):
    pos = nx.spring_layout(G)
    nx.draw(G, pos, with_labels=True)
    labels = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'weight')
    nx.draw_networkx_edge_labels(G, pos, edge_labels=labels)
    plt.show()
    return pos


G = generate_random_graph(8, 12, 0)
pos = show_graph(G)

title: Uniform-Cost Search and Dijkstra’s Algorithm
text:
Uniform-Cost Search
The loop removes a cheapest entry, skips an already finalized node, and records its parent. A node becomes visited when it is removed, not when first discovered: a cheaper route may be found while it is still in the frontier.
With nonnegative weights, the first removal of a node finalizes its shortest-path cost. The goal test therefore belongs after removal. On reaching the target, parent links are followed backward and the list is reversed into source-to-target order.
Neighbor entries may duplicate a node already in the heap. The visited check discards those stale alternatives. If the heap empties first, the function returns None.

def uniform_cost_search(G, source, target):
    visited = set()
    queue = [(0, source, [])]
    all_parents = {}
    heapq.heapify(queue)
    while len(queue) > 0:
        print(queue)
        cost, node, parent = heapq.heappop(queue)
        # draw a picture of the search process
        nx.draw(G, pos, with_labels=True)
        labels = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'weight')
        nx.draw_networkx_edge_labels(G, pos, edge_labels=labels)
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, nodelist=visited, node_color='r') # visited nodes
        nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, nodelist=[node], node_color='g') # current node
        plt.show()
        
        if node in visited:
            continue
        visited.add(node)
        all_parents[node] = parent
        if node == target:
            path = [node]
            while node != source:
                node = all_parents[node]
                path.append(node)
            path.reverse()
            return path
        for neighbor in G.neighbors(node):
            if neighbor in visited:
                continue
            weight = G[node][neighbor]['weight']
            heapq.heappush(queue, (cost + weight, neighbor, node))
    return None

title: Uniform-Cost Search and Dijkstra’s Algorithm
text:
Dijkstra for All Targets
Dijkstra keeps going after one target, producing shortest paths from the source to every reachable node.

# dijkstra's algorithm for every pair shortest path
def dijkstra(G, source):
    visited = set()
    queue = [(0, source, [])]
    shortest_paths = {}
    heapq.heapify(queue)
    while len(queue) > 0:
        cost, node, path = heapq.heappop(queue)
        if node in visited:
            continue
        visited.add(node)
        path = path + [node]
        shortest_paths[node] = (cost, path)
        for neighbor in G.neighbors(node):
            if neighbor in visited:
                continue
            weight = G[node][neighbor]['weight']
            heapq.heappush(queue, (cost + weight, neighbor, path))
    return shortest_paths

shortest_paths = dijkstra(G, source)
for node, (cost, path) in shortest_paths.items():
    print(f'{node}: {path}')

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Reward Hacking

Reward hacking, often called specification gaming, occurs when an agent exploits a scoring rule to earn a high reward without achieving the intended goal.




 Our vacuum example


Goal: keep rooms clean.
Score: count dirt picked up.
Shortcut: dump and re-collect dirt.



 Today’s coding agents


Goal: fix the software bug.
Score: count passing tests.
Shortcut: change tests to pass while leaving the bug.



Optimizing the score is not the same as achieving the goal.


A long-standing problem, still studied today: DeepMind (2020); Anthropic (2026).


Connect this to the previous slide: repeated dirt collection earns points without keeping rooms clean. The score is a proxy, a measurable stand-in for what we actually want. This is not a newly invented problem; specification gaming is a closely related term. Reward hacking does not require human-like malicious intent.
In reinforcement learning, a reward signal provides feedback used for learning; our performance measure describes what counts as success. Those need not be identical, and a poorly chosen reward can fail to reflect the intended measure. We will study reinforcement learning later.
The coding example summarizes a type of behavior studied in controlled evaluations, not a claim that every coding agent does this. The March 2026 Anthropic study audited debugging tasks with deliberately impossible tests and explicit instructions not to modify them. When a test conflicts with the specification, the appropriate response is to flag the conflict, not silently weaken the evaluation. Broader safeguards include protected tests and independent checks of actual outcomes; no single metric guarantees success.
[Sources]

Google DeepMind, “Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity,” April 21, 2020. https://deepmind.google/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/
Kissane, MacDiarmid, and Roger, “Measuring and improving coding audit realism with deployment resources,” March 23, 2026. https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/coding-audit-realism/

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Specify the Task with PEAS
PEAS = Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.







Component
Our two-room vacuum




Performance measure
Keep rooms clean; avoid unnecessary actions.


Environment
Rooms A and B, dirt, and the vacuum’s location.


Actuators
Move left, move right, suck dirt, or do nothing.


Sensors
Current location and dirt in the current room only.




Describe success and available information before choosing an algorithm.


PEAS is a task specification, not an agent algorithm. The evaluator may know more than the agent’s sensors reveal. Ask why seeing the current room is not the same as seeing the whole world.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 2, task environments. https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/4th-ed/slides-pdf/chapter02.pdf

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
One World, Explicit Assumptions



Two connected rooms: A on the left, B on the right.
A move or a cleaning action takes one step.
Sensors are accurate; actions always succeed.
Dirt does not reappear in the baseline world.
NoOp means “no operation”: stay idle for one step.





Which assumption makes “I cleaned this room earlier” useful now?


The assumptions define the teaching simulator, not all real vacuums. No new dirt plus deterministic cleaning lets the agent infer that a previously cleaned room remains clean. We will deliberately break the no-new-dirt assumption later.

title:

(Intro to) AI
section: Four Ways to Choose an Action
text:
Four Ways to Choose an Action







Agent design
Central question




Simple reflex
What rule matches my current percept?


Model-based reflex
What is the state, given my history and model?


Goal-based
What actions can reach a desired state?


Utility-based
Which outcome is preferable, including tradeoffs?




These describe decision mechanisms, not a ranking of intelligence.


Memory and models also appear in goal-based and utility-based agents. Learning is not a fifth rung that replaces the other designs: it can improve their components. Preview the distinctions here and use the next slides to unpack them.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, structure of agents. https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/4th-ed/slides-pdf/chapter02.pdf

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Simple Reflex: Match a Rule
Current percept only. No stored history and no look-ahead.


   CurrentperceptCondition-actionrulesAction



If the current room is dirty: Suck.
Otherwise: move to the other room.


A simple rule can work well when the current percept is enough.


Rules can be supplied by a designer or learned; simple reflex describes what information is used for action selection. Here the second rule deliberately does not know whether the other room is already clean.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, simple reflex agents. Original course diagram.

section: A Reflex Agent Can Keep Moving
text:
A Reflex Agent Can Keep Moving
Suppose both rooms are already clean. The same rule keeps firing.


   A: cleanB: cleanA: cleanB: cleanRightLeftRightCleanliness stays the same; action costs accumulate.



Can the agent safely stop based only on “my current room is clean”?


No, not with this sensor and without additional information: the other room might still be dirty. The issue is not that every reflex policy oscillates, but that this particular policy does, and current-room cleanliness does not establish the global goal.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Model-Based: Maintain Internal State
A model describes how actions and the environment change the world.


   Previous state+ previous action+ world modelCurrent perceptUpdate internalstateApply rules;choose action



Internal state is an estimate of the world, not direct access to hidden facts.


For this vacuum, the internal state records whether A and B are known to be clean, dirty, or still unknown. The model says Suck succeeds and dirt does not reappear. Other model-based agents may track probabilities rather than a single estimated state.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, model-based reflex agents. Original course diagram.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Goal-Based: Consider Future States
Goal: both rooms are clean. Start in A with both rooms dirty.


   Both roomsdirtySuck, Right, SuckRight, Suck, Left, SuckBoth roomsclean



A goal test says whether a state is acceptable.
Search or planning can find actions that reach it.


These are illustrative candidate plans, not a full search tree. A goal-based agent uses a model to consider future consequences. A goal test accepts both outcomes; a search algorithm may additionally minimize path cost. Goal-based does not mean oblivious to cost. This introduces the need for search without teaching BFS early.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, goal-based agents. Original course example and diagram.

text:
Utility-Based: Compare Acceptable Outcomes
A utility function assigns a numerical preference to outcomes.








Plan from A
Reaches the goal?
Non-idle actions




Suck, Right, Suck
Yes

If each action uses energy, prefer the first plan, all else equal.
With uncertainty, compare expected utility.
Tradeoffs can include cleanliness, energy, time, and risk.


Reaching a goal and choosing a preferable outcome are different questions.


Utility represents preferences, not the agent literally feeling happiness. There is no need to introduce expectation notation yet. A goal plus path cost already expresses a simple preference; utility is a more general way to compare outcomes and uncertainty.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, utility-based agents. Plan lengths are derived from the course example.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Learning Can Improve Any Design



Learn better rules from experience.
Learn a better model of action outcomes.
Learn to predict utility more accurately.
Use feedback to update the decision-making components.





Remembering a room’s condition is not, by itself, learning better rules.


Our memory-based Python agent will update state but will not change its rules or learn a model. In the classic learning-agent decomposition, the performance element chooses actions, the critic supplies feedback, the learning element improves components, and the problem generator encourages informative experience. Mention these verbally if students ask; formal learning algorithms come later.
[Sources]

Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 2, learning agents.

Which Component Is Missing?







Situation
Needed addition




The vacuum forgets rooms it has already cleaned.
Internal state


It needs an action sequence that cleans both rooms.
Goal-directed planning


Two plans work, but one uses much less energy.
A preference / cost criterion


It should improve its rules after repeated mistakes.
Learning




Can a single agent use all four additions?


Reveal one answer at a time. Yes: the categories describe components and mechanisms that can be combined. This is a quick check before translating the ideas into Python.

Python Demo: One Fair Experiment

Both agents start in A, with both rooms dirty.
Run each for 8 steps, including idle steps.
After each action, award 1 point per clean room.
Subtract 0.25 points per non-idle action.


S = \text{clean-room time} - 0.25 \times \text{non-idle actions}


Same environment, sensors, starting state, and scoring rule.

Demo and experiments | Download Python

Use this slide to open the runnable demo, then step through the implementation slides. Clean-room time is the sum of the number of clean rooms after each action, not only the number clean at the end. NoOp still advances time and earns cleanliness points, but has no action penalty. The coefficient is a classroom choice, not a universal measure of vacuum quality. No extra Python packages are required.

The Simulator Owns the World
class VacuumWorld:
    def __init__(self, start="A", dirt=None):
        self.position = start
        self.dirt = {"A": True, "B": True} if dirt is None else dict(dirt)

    def perceive(self):
        room = self.position
        return room, self.dirt[room]

True means dirty; False means clean.
The simulator stores both rooms’ conditions.
The agent receives only (current_room, current_dirt).


World state belongs to the simulator. Percepts are the agent’s input.

Agent 1: A Simple Reflex Rule
class ReflexAgent:
    def act(self, percept):
        room, dirty = percept
        if dirty:
            return "Suck"
        return "Right" if room == "A" else "Left"

Dirty here? Clean here.
Otherwise, go to the other room.
No record of what happened before.


What will it do after it has cleaned both rooms?

text:
Connect Sensing, Acting, and Scoring
Start with a fresh world, an empty trace, and score = 0.0.
for step in range(1, steps + 1):
    percept = world.perceive()
    action = agent.act(percept)
    world.apply(action)
    clean = sum(not value for value in world.dirt.values())
    effort = int(action != "NoOp")
    score += clean - 0.25 * effort
    trace.append((step, percept, action, clean, effort))

The evaluator can inspect both rooms. The agent cannot.


This is the baseline loop in run_agent, without the optional new-dirt event used later. No score or complete world-state dictionary is passed into act. The demo keeps running after NoOp so both agents are evaluated for the same horizon. Highlight input, action, evaluation, then logging.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Design Exercise: A Battery-Limited Vacuum


  Acharging dockBCD


Battery capacity: 6 units. Each move or Suck costs 1 unit. Recharge at A restores all 6 in one step; NoOp costs no energy. Dirt can reappear. Sensors report location, current-room dirt, and battery level.

Specify PEAS, including recharging at A.
What should the agent remember?
Which decision mechanisms should it combine?
Find a case where “clean whenever dirty” fails.


Allow small groups to work, then compare designs. Assume the layout is known, NoOp costs no battery, and Recharge is available only at A and restores capacity in one step. One example: starting full at A, the agent reaches dirty D with 3 units left. Cleaning costs 1, leaving only 2 units for the 3 moves back to the dock. No code or optimal-policy derivation is required.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One Possible Design

PEAS: sustained cleanliness without getting stranded; four rooms and a dock; move, Suck, NoOp, Recharge; local dirt, location, and battery sensors.
Internal state: room map, last observations, observation ages, and battery level.
Goal and planning: complete useful cleaning trips and return to the dock.
Preference: compare cleanliness gains, energy costs, and stale information.


At D with 3 units left, cleaning would leave too little energy to return to A.


An explicit safety check can reserve enough energy for a return trip before committing to an action. With deterministic one-unit moves, distance to the dock gives the needed reserve; uncertainty would need additional margin or a different model. Treat avoiding stranding as a constraint, not merely a tiny penalty that could be outweighed. Learning could improve estimates of how often rooms become dirty, but is not required for an initial design.

Takeaways



PEAS specifies the task before implementation.
Rules, state, goals, and utility answer different questions.
Learning can improve the components of an agent.
Evaluate agents under the same conditions.
Recheck the design when its assumptions change.




Asset credits

from vacuum_agents_demo import MemoryAgent, ReflexAgent, run_agent

)

Questions to investigate

What happens when both rooms start clean? How does the memory agent establish that fact?
Why must the stopping test use value is False, rather than not value? What happens to an unknown room represented by None?
How do the scores change if the action penalty is zero?
Can periodically checking the other room help when dirt reappears? What extra cost does it introduce?
What would need to change if cleaning sometimes failed?

text:
Takeaways



Atoms: give each symbol one stable meaning.
Connectives: distinguish OR, XOR, implication, and biconditional.
Translation: check “only if” and negation scope.
Evaluation: a truth table checks every assignment.
Equivalence: preserve all truth values when rewriting.





A formula’s truth conditions may permit more than its author intended. Look for an unwanted assignment that still satisfies the written rules.

Next: what conclusions follow from a collection of facts and rules?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformers, Continued
Today: multi-head attention, decoding, causal training, positional encodings, transformer blocks, and transformers beyond language.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Recall: Scaled Dot-Product Attention

\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
V\cdot \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{K^TQ}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)




Term
Meaning




K^TQ
similarity scores


\operatorname{softmax}
converts scores into weights


V
content being mixed


\sqrt{d_k}
stabilizing scale

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Multi-Head Attention
Instead of one attention head, use many heads with different projections.




Different heads can attend to different relationships in the same sequence.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Multi-Head Formula

\operatorname{MultiHead}(\mathcal{W},X,X_Q)
=
W_O
\begin{bmatrix}
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,1},W_{Q,1},W_{V,1},X,X_Q)\\
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,2},W_{Q,2},W_{V,2},X,X_Q)\\
\vdots\\
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,m},W_{Q,m},W_{V,m},X,X_Q)
\end{bmatrix}

The output projection W_O brings the concatenated heads back to the desired embedding dimension.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Self-Attention
Self-attention means the sequence attends to itself:

X_Q=X

In autoregressive language modeling:

Each position builds a latent representation.
It should use previous context.
It should not see future tokens.


That last condition is why we need causal masking.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Inference: Next Token
Given a hidden representation h:

h=\operatorname{MultiHead}(\mathcal{W},X,x_n)

Predict the next-token distribution:

\operatorname{softmax}(B^Th)

where B contains token embeddings for the vocabulary.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Temperature Sampling
Logits \ell_i become probabilities through a temperature-scaled softmax:

p_i=
\frac{\exp(\ell_i/T)}
{\sum_j \exp(\ell_j/T)}




Temperature
Effect




low T
sharper, more deterministic


T=1
ordinary softmax


high T
flatter, more diverse




Temperature changes only the sampling distribution, not the model weights.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Top-K Sampling
Full-vocabulary sampling includes a long tail of tiny probabilities.
Top-K keeps only the K most likely tokens:

\tilde{s}_i=
\begin{cases}
s_i, & \text{if } i \text{ is among the top-}K \text{ logits},\\
-\infty, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}


Temperature controls sharpness; top-K controls which candidate tokens are even allowed.

CS 463G & CS 663

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Causal Masking
Rather than slicing every prefix separately, train all positions at once with a mask.


scores = KTQ / sqrt(d_k)


for each query position i


for each key position j


if j > i: scores[j, i] = -infinity


weights = softmax(scores)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Causal Mask Matrix
Future positions receive -\infty before softmax.




Each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Layer Normalization
Layer normalization stabilizes training.
For embedding x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_e}:

y=
\frac{x-\mathbb{E}[x]}
{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[x]+\epsilon}}
\gamma+\beta

where \gamma and \beta are trainable scale and shift parameters.

Normalization keeps intermediate activations in a better numerical range.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Attention Is Permutation-Invariant
For any permutation matrix P:

\operatorname{Attn}(W_K,W_Q,W_V,XP,X_Q)
=
\operatorname{Attn}(W_K,W_Q,W_V,X,X_Q)

Meaning: attention over a set of key/value tokens has no built-in notion of order.

five minus two and two minus five contain similar words, but order changes the meaning.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Positional Encoding
Add a position-dependent vector to each token embedding:

\text{embedding}(x_i,i)
=
\text{token encoding}(x_i)
+
\text{positional encoding}(i)

Sinusoidal positional encoding:

[\operatorname{PE}(t)]_j=
\begin{cases}
\sin\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2k/d_e}}\right),&\text{if } j=2k,\\
\cos\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2k/d_e}}\right),&\text{if } j=2k+1.
\end{cases}

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Sinusoidal Intuition
A sine wave has frequency and phase:

x(t)=a\sin(2\pi ft+\phi)




Different dimensions use different frequencies, so the model receives both local and long-range position signals.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)
RoPE applies position information inside attention by rotating query and key vectors.

R_\theta(i)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(i\theta)&-\sin(i\theta)\\
\sin(i\theta)&\cos(i\theta)
\end{bmatrix}


\tilde{q}_i=R_\theta(i)q_i,\qquad
\tilde{k}_j=R_\theta(j)k_j


Many modern LLMs use RoPE because attention scores can encode relative position differences.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
RoPE Relative Position
Using rotation identities:

\langle \tilde{q}_i,\tilde{k}_j\rangle
=
\langle q_i,R_\theta(j-i)k_j\rangle

Result:

The dot product depends on the offset (j-i).
Relative position enters the attention score directly.
This helps long-context extrapolation and relative reasoning.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformer Block Overview
A transformer block combines:

Multi-head self-attention (MHSA).
Feed-forward network (FFN).
Residual connections.
Layer normalization.


Residuals let each layer learn a refinement instead of relearning the entire representation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text: Transformer Block Diagram

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Pre-LN vs. Post-LN
Pre-LN (common in modern deep transformers)

x+\operatorname{MHSA}(\operatorname{LN}(x))
\rightarrow
x+\operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(x))

Post-LN (original Transformer style)

\operatorname{LN}(x+\operatorname{MHSA}(x))
\rightarrow
\operatorname{LN}(x+\operatorname{FFN}(x))


Pre-LN is usually easier to optimize for very deep models.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Key-Value (KV) Cache
During autoregressive generation, tokens are produced one at a time.
Without caching, the model recomputes keys and values for all previous tokens at every step.




KV cache is one reason deployed LLM inference can be fast enough for interactive use.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Prompt Engineering
Prompt engineering is the practice of designing inputs to guide LLM outputs.
Useful habits:

Be explicit about the task.
Provide structure or templates.
Include examples when format matters.
Restrict ambiguity.
Iterate and refine.


Instead of Explain Transformers, try Explain Transformers in 3 bullet points suitable for a first-year CS student.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Types of Prompting







Type
Idea




zero-shot
no examples, only an instruction


few-shot
show input-output examples


chain-of-thought style
ask for step-by-step reasoning when appropriate


system/instruction design
set high-level behavior, role, or constraints


structured output
require JSON, tables, bullets, or schemas

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Evaluating Language Models
Perplexity measures how well a model predicts a ground-truth sequence:

\operatorname{Perplexity}
=
\exp\left(
-\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
\log p(w_i\mid w_{<i})
\right)

Other common text metrics:

BLEU: precision-oriented n-gram overlap, common in translation.
ROUGE: recall-oriented overlap, common in summarization.


Metrics are useful, but they rarely capture everything humans care about.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformers Beyond Language
Transformers are not just for text.
They can be applied whenever data can be represented as a sequence of tokens:

image patches,
audio frames,
video tokens,
graph or trajectory tokens,
multimodal inputs.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vision Transformers (ViT)
Vision Transformer (ViT) treats an image as a sequence of patches.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Linear Patch Encoding
For an image x\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}:

Split into N fixed-size patches.
Flatten each patch:


\operatorname{patch}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{P^2C}


Project to the embedding space:


z_i=W\operatorname{patch}_i+b,\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P^2C}

The resulting patch embeddings act like tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Diffusion Transformers (DiT)
Diffusion Transformers replace the convolutional denoising backbone with a transformer over latent image patches.
Paper: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers, Peebles and Xie, 2022.
Key idea:

patchify the noisy latent,
add timestep/class conditioning,
process tokens with DiT blocks,
reshape outputs back to latent noise predictions.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
U-Net vs. DiT








Backbone
Main structure
Strength




U-Net
encoder-decoder with skip connections
strong spatial inductive bias


DiT
transformer over latent patches
scalable global token mixing

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
DiT Architecture


DiT applies transformer blocks to noisy latent patches and uses timestep/class conditioning inside the block.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Latent Diffusion Models
Instead of running diffusion in pixel space, diffuse in a compressed latent space.

z=E(x)

Forward noising:

z_t=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}z+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon

A U-Net or DiT predicts the noise in latent space, then a decoder reconstructs:

\hat{x}=D(z_0)


Latent diffusion lowers memory cost and makes high-resolution generation more practical.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Multi-head attention lets different heads learn different relations.
Sampling controls such as temperature and top-K affect generation behavior.
Causal masking prevents future-token leakage during parallel training.
Positional encodings and RoPE give transformers order information.
Transformer blocks combine attention, FFNs, residuals, and normalization.
ViT and DiT show how transformer tokens can represent image patches.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autoregressive Models
Autoregressive models generate structured data one piece at a time, conditioning on what they already generated.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is a Modality?
A modality is a type or form of data.



Modality
Examples




Text
sentences, documents


Image
photographs, medical scans


Audio
speech, music


Video
image sequences over time


Multimodal
image plus text, video plus audio

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Text vs. Images



Text
Images




Sequential
Spatial

2D pixels, often 3D with channels

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Means Autoregressive?
“Auto” means the model uses its own previous outputs.
For a sequence:

p(x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})


Generation becomes repeated conditional prediction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Next-Token Prediction
Example:

p(\text{blue}\mid \text{The sky is})


The sky is ? blue

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autoregressive Generation Loop


function Generate(prompt, model)


sequence = prompt


while not finished


distribution = model(sequence)


next = sample(distribution)


append(sequence, next)


return sequence

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Types of Autoregressive Models



Model
Core mechanism




RNN
Hidden state updated step by step


LSTM
RNN with gates and cell state for long dependencies


GRU
Simpler gated recurrent unit


Transformer decoder
Self-attention over previous tokens


PixelCNN
Masked convolution over previous pixels

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Recurrent Neural Network
An RNN maps:

f_\theta:(x_t,h_{t-1})\mapsto(y_t,h_t)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Stacked Recurrent Networks
Stacking adds depth at each time step.




Depth helps learn more abstract sequence representations.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
LSTM
LSTMs add gates and a cell state.



Component
Role




Input gate i_t
Controls new information


Forget gate f_t
Controls what to erase


Candidate g_t
Proposed new content


Output gate o_t
Controls exposed hidden state


Cell state c_t
Long-term memory path

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
LSTM Updates

i_t=\sigma(W_{ii}x_t+b_{ii}+W_{hi}h_{t-1}+b_{hi})


f_t=\sigma(W_{if}x_t+b_{if}+W_{hf}h_{t-1}+b_{hf})


g_t=\tanh(W_{ig}x_t+b_{ig}+W_{hg}h_{t-1}+b_{hg})


c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot g_t,\qquad
h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRU
GRU is a simpler gated recurrent unit.







Gate
Purpose




Update gate
Controls how much previous state is kept


Reset gate
Controls how much previous state is used in candidate update




GRUs often train faster than LSTMs while keeping much of the benefit of gated memory.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PixelCNN
PixelCNN generates images pixel by pixel in raster order.



Masked filters prevent the model from looking at future pixels.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Pixel Mask Intuition



seen
seen
seen


seen
current
future


future
future
future




Autoregressive image generation imposes an ordering on pixels, just like text imposes an ordering on tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Autoregressive models factor a joint distribution into sequential conditionals.
Generation repeats prediction and sampling.
RNNs summarize history with hidden states.
LSTMs and GRUs improve recurrent memory with gates.
PixelCNN applies autoregression to images using masks.
Transformers will modernize this idea with self-attention.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO and GRPO
Policy-gradient methods are powerful, but naive policy updates can be unstable.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Where We Are
From policy gradients, the basic update is:

\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)

The problem:

A gradient step can make the new policy very different from the old one.
A once-good policy can collapse after one overly aggressive update.
We want improvement, but not destructive policy movement.


PPO is built around a simple control knob: keep the new policy close to the policy that collected the data.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Trust Region Intuition
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) directly constrains policy change:

\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_t
\left[
\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}
A_t
\right]
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\,\|\,\pi_\theta)\leq\delta



TRPO

Hard trust-region constraint
More complex optimization
Requires second-order information


PPO

Soft constraint through clipping
Easier first-order optimization
Widely used in practice

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Probability Ratio
PPO compares the new policy to the old policy with:

r_t(\theta)
=
\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}

Interpretation:







Ratio
Meaning




r_t(\theta)=1
New policy gives the sampled action the same probability


r_t(\theta)>1
New policy makes the sampled action more likely


r_t(\theta)<1
New policy makes the sampled action less likely

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO Clipped Objective
PPO maximizes:

L^{\text{PPO}}(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_t
\left[
\min\left(
r_t(\theta)A_t,\;
\operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_t
\right)
\right]


If the policy update tries to move too far, clipping removes the extra incentive.

\epsilon is usually small, often around 0.1 to 0.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why the Min Matters


Positive advantage
If A_t>0, PPO wants to increase the probability of a_t.
Clipping prevents increasing it too much.

Negative advantage
If A_t<0, PPO wants to decrease the probability of a_t.
Clipping prevents decreasing it too much.


The objective is conservative on purpose: accept useful improvement, reject excessive movement.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO Training Loop


theta, phi = initial policy and value parameters


for iteration = 1, 2, …:


D = collectTrajectories(pi_theta)


R_hat, A = estimateReturnsAndAdvantages(D, V_phi)


theta_old = theta


for epoch in 1 … K:


for batch in minibatches(D):


ratio = pi_theta(a|s) / pi_theta_old(a|s)


actorLoss = -mean(min(ratio  A, clip(ratio)  A))


criticLoss = mean((R_hat - V_phi(s))2)


theta, phi = optimizerStep(actorLoss, criticLoss)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why PPO Works Well

Stable enough for long training runs.
Simple enough to implement with standard gradient descent.
Reuses collected trajectories for several epochs.
Works with large neural policies.

Common use cases:

Robotics and continuous control
Game playing
RLHF-style language-model training


PPO became popular because it is a practical compromise: not the most theoretically exact, but robust and implementable.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
From PPO to GRPO
PPO usually uses both:

A policy model, the actor.
A value model, the critic.

For large language models, the critic can be expensive:

It adds memory cost.
It adds training complexity.
It can be hard to fit accurately for long reasoning traces.


Can we estimate advantages without training a separate value model?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRPO: Main Idea
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) samples several responses for the same prompt.
For one prompt q_i:

\{o_{i,1}, o_{i,2}, \dots, o_{i,G}\}
\sim
\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid q_i)

Then compute rewards:

r_{i,j}=r(q_i,o_{i,j})


Instead of asking “how good is this response absolutely?”, GRPO asks “how good is this response compared with the other responses for the same prompt?”

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRPO Training Loop


theta = initial policy parameters


for iteration = 1, 2, …:


prompts = samplePromptBatch()


for each prompt q_i in prompts:


responses = sampleGroup(pi_theta, q_i, G)


rewards = scoreResponses(q_i, responses)


advantages = (rewards - mean(rewards)) / std(rewards)


theta_old = theta


ratio = pi_theta(o|q) / pi_theta_old(o|q)


objective = ppoStyleClippedObjective(ratio, advantages)


theta = optimizerStep(objective)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO vs. GRPO








Feature
PPO
GRPO




Policy update
Clipped policy-ratio objective
PPO-style clipped update


Advantage source
Often uses value-function critic
Group-relative rewards


Extra model
Critic/value model
No separate critic


Natural setting
General RL and RLHF
LLM reasoning-style training




GRPO keeps PPO’s conservative update idea, but changes how the advantage signal is estimated.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Useful References

Trust Region Policy Optimization, Schulman et al., 2015.
Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms, Schulman et al., 2017.
DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models, Shao et al., 2024.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

PPO limits policy updates by clipping the policy ratio.
The ratio compares the current policy to the policy that collected the data.
GRPO removes the critic by comparing responses within the same prompt group.
Both methods care about the same practical issue: stable policy improvement.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Value-Based Model-Free RL
Learn values from experience without knowing the transition or reward model.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Model-Based vs. Model-Free


Model-based
Assumes access to:

P(s'\mid s,a), \qquad R(s,a)

Then plans with the model.

Model-free
Learns directly from interaction.
No explicit P or R required.


Model-free methods learn from sampled experience alone.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Common Model-Free Methods








Family
Method
Main idea




Value-based
Monte Carlo
Learn from full returns


Value-based
TD
Bootstrap from next-state estimate


Control
SARSA
On-policy action-value learning


Control
Q-learning
Off-policy optimal action-value learning


Policy-based
REINFORCE, actor-critic, PPO
Directly learn a policy

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Monte Carlo Estimation
Monte Carlo waits until an episode ends, then updates from the full return.

G_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma r_{t+2}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-1}r_T


V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\left[G_t-V(s_t)\right]



Strength
Unbiased return estimate under the policy.

Weakness
High variance; must wait for episode end.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text: Monte Carlo vs. TD Timing

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Temporal-Difference Learning
TD learning updates before the episode ends.
It combines:

Learning from raw experience.
Bootstrapping from current value estimates.


“Temporal difference” means the update is driven by the difference between a current estimate and a one-step target.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(0) Target
From the Bellman expectation equation:

V^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}_\pi[r_{t+1}+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s]

Use the sampled target:

r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})

TD(0) update:

V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\left[r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\right]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(0) as Algorithm


observe transition (s, r, sNext)


target = r + gamma * V(sNext)


error = target - V(s)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Value Iteration
Value iteration repeatedly replaces each value by its best lookahead score. A sweep updates every nonterminal state once.


V = 0 for all states, including terminal F


repeat


old = copy(V)


for each nonterminal state s


V(s) = maxa LookAhead(s, a, old)


until largestChange(V, old) < threshold


return GreedyPolicy(V)


largestChange is the largest absolute value change across states. threshold is a chosen small positive stopping tolerance.

Every update in this sweep reads old. The terminal value stays zero. We call the estimates after k sweeps V_k.


This is synchronous value iteration, matching the numerical walkthrough. An in-place implementation is another valid variant but yields different intermediate sweeps. max ranges over actions available at s. With zero initial values, V_k can also be interpreted as an optimal k-step truncated-horizon value. A positive stopping threshold gives approximate values in general; it is not proof of exact convergence or a universal policy-error bound. Our small example happens to reach an exact fixed point after two sweeps. Reference: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/mdp/value-iteration.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Policy Iteration
Policy iteration alternates evaluation, computing the current policy’s values, with improvement, choosing better actions using those values.


pi = any deterministic policy


repeat


V = EvaluatePolicy(pi)


newPi = GreedyPolicy(V, keepTies=pi)


if newPi == pi: return pi


pi = newPi


EvaluatePolicy solves the fixed-policy Bellman equations. When several actions tie for the largest score, GreedyPolicy keeps the current action.

Evaluation predicts the current policy’s long-term outcome. Improvement compares all available first actions while using those evaluated future values.


Exact evaluation can solve a linear system or iterate the fixed-policy Bellman expectation updates to convergence. It is more than one value-iteration-style sweep. Stable tie handling avoids cycling among policies with equal value. There is no decision to evaluate or improve at F. Model-free algorithms later learn from sampled experience rather than requiring an exact model-based EvaluatePolicy call. Reference: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/mdp/policies-iteration.html.

Use the evaluated values V^{\pi_0}(D)=4, V^{\pi_0}(J)=2.6, and V^{\pi_0}(F)=0.

The next improvement changes D to pickup, since -1+0.9\cdot8=6.2>4.

All action scores in the table use the previous fixed policy’s values, not a partially improved successor policy. Call the first improved policy pi1: small at D and deliver at J. Evaluating pi1 gives (4,8,0). Improving again gives pi2: pickup at D and deliver at J. Evaluating pi2 gives (6.2,8,0). The following slide checks stability under this final evaluation. This explains why a policy-improvement round can change actions in stages.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Training: Differentiate, Then Update
A gradient measures how loss changes with a parameter. Backpropagation computes these derivatives backward through the network.


for each batch in trainingData


clearGradients(parameters)


prediction = forward(inputs, parameters)


loss = MSE(prediction, targets)


gradients = backpropagate(loss)


update(parameters, gradients, learningRate)


A batch groups examples; an epoch is one pass through the training dataset. Repeat passes as needed.

Backpropagation computes gradients. The optimizer uses them to change parameters. These are separate operations.


For the numerical walkthrough the batch contains one example. The pseudocode intentionally separates clearing stored gradients, evaluating the current computation, differentiating, and updating. A model can have correctly computed gradients and still make a poor optimization step if the learning rate is too large. Source: https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/optimization_tutorial.html.
