Heuristic Quality and Memory


More informative estimates

h=0 gives UCS priorities.
If 0\le h_1\le h_2\le h^*, h_2 provides a tighter lower bound.
A stronger estimate may cost more to compute.


Limited memory

A* stores frontier entries and search records.
Simplified Memory-Bounded A* (SMA*) can forget a worst leaf and retain its backed-up estimate.
Forgotten branches may need to be generated again.



Search time depends on both the number of expansions and the cost per expansion. Saving memory can require repeated work.


This is a brief connection to the archived lecture’s memory-bounded search topic. A tighter admissible heuristic is more informative, but equal-f tie breaking and evaluation overhead mean elapsed time does not always improve. SMA* bounds stored search nodes, not merely an arbitrary truncated heap. It backs forgotten estimates up to parents and regenerates promising branches. Its completeness and optimality depend on having sufficient memory for the relevant solution path. Do not present dropping queue entries without bookkeeping as an optimal memory-bounded algorithm. Details follow AIMA Chapter 3 and the original Lecture 7.

An overestimate does not force failure in every problem, but this counterexample shows that the optimality guarantee is lost. Even testing the goal on removal cannot repair an arbitrary overestimating heuristic.

Binary search works because a sorted line can be split in half.

Weak Heuristic

Many low-cost prefixes can look promising.


Strong Heuristic

A tighter lower bound can rule out more unpromising routes.
Even an exact heuristic may leave many tied optimal paths.



If two different optimal routes have the same total cost C^*, what can their frontier priorities be when h=h^*?


Both can have f=C^*. Tie-breaking and heuristic evaluation cost still matter, so a perfect heuristic does not guarantee O(d) runtime.

Representing a Game

Component
In this position

ACTIONS(s)
Place X in 6, 7, or 8


RESULT(s,a)
New board; O moves next unless play ends


TERMINAL(s)
Win or full board


UTILITY(s)
Score of a terminal position





An action is legal only in an empty square. A winning position ends the game immediately.


Square numbers run left-to-right, top-to-bottom, from 1 to9. Only empty squares are numbered in the picture. X starts, and the displayed state has three X and three O. It has no winner yet. Utility is defined for terminal states; a nonterminal estimate will be introduced separately. The diagrams use X as MAX throughout.

text:
Utility from MAX’s Viewpoint


MAX = X: prefer +1 to 0 to -1.
MIN = O: prefer -1 to 0 to +1.
The score’s meaning stays the same at every level.


At an O turn, choose the smallest X score. Do not change the sign just because the turn changes.


In a zero-sum model, O’s own utility is the negative of X’s. We can therefore store only X’s score. Terminal scores are stipulated by the rules; the values3,12,8 in the abstract example use a different utility scale. Do not add edge costs as in UCS or A*. A utility of0 here means an actual draw, not an unevaluated state.

text:
A Large Payoff May Be Unreachable


The largest leaf is 14. Which player chooses the final edge into that leaf?


MIN chooses at C and can select 2. MAX chooses a branch, not an arbitrary leaf inside it.


This abstract game ends after two plies. All bottom values are exact terminal utilities, not a depth cutoff. Edge labels A/B/C identify MAX’s options; there are no edge costs. The standard numerical example follows AIMA and https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/games/minimax.html. The image is redrawn locally in draw.io.

Back Up the Values

MAX chooses A, B, or C, then MIN chooses a payoff. Backing up values means computing each parent’s score from its children’s scores.


  
  
  



MIN: At A, \min(3,12,8)=3. Likewise, B=2 and C=2.


MAX: \max(3,2,2)=3 at the root. Choose A.



All bottom values are exact terminal utilities in a different game, not tic-tac-toe scores, edge costs, or probabilities. Before the first reveal, ask whether MAX can force the largest leaf, 14. MIN controls that final choice and can instead take 2. Then compute the minimum under each candidate move. The first reveal fills A=3, B=2, C=2 and highlights the selected leaves in gold. The second reveal chooses A at the root in teal. Reversing a reveal restores the previous diagram. The picture explains bottom-up values; an implementation can compute each subtree depth first instead of processing whole layers at once. Source: the standard AIMA example, also in https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/games/minimax.html. Redrawn locally in draw.io.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Minimax Pseudocode: Evaluate a State
VALUE(s) evaluates the child states, then returns their maximum if MAX moves or minimum if MIN moves.

  VALUE(s)
  if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
  if PLAYER(s) == MAX:
  v <- -infinity
  for a in ACTIONS(s):
  v <- max(v, VALUE(RESULT(s, a)))
  else: # MIN moves
  v <- +infinity
  for a in ACTIONS(s):
  v <- min(v, VALUE(RESULT(s, a)))
  return v


This child-to-parent calculation is a value backup. Search depth first, then return the parent’s value.


No depth parameter appears in exact VALUE: the stopping condition is terminal. The code assumes a finite game tree and at least one legal action in every nonterminal state. For a game with passing, a pass must be represented as a legal action. Terminal utility always refers to MAX. The loop accumulators use opposite infinities so they also handle all-negative MAX values or all-positive MIN values correctly. Source: standard minimax recurrence, rewritten as course pseudocode.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Minimax Pseudocode: Choose an Action
Precondition: the state is nonterminal and MAX moves next.

  CHOOSE_MOVE(s)
  best_value <- -infinity; best_action <- None
  for a in ACTIONS(s):
  value <- VALUE(RESULT(s, a))
  if value > best_value:
  best_value <- value
  best_action <- a
  return best_action


Whenever a better score appears, store its action too. With >, a tie keeps the first move found.


The recursive function computes scores. The outer loop remembers the move that produced the best score.


The strict comparison retains the first action among equally valued alternatives. The successor of a MAX move normally belongs to MIN; the state carries that turn, so the caller need not toggle a separate flag. This is the counterpart of retaining a parent/action in UCS and A*: computing a numeric value alone is insufficient to act. Standard tic-tac-toe utilities are finite.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why Minimax Is Correct
Assume a finite tree, correct game rules, and exact terminal utilities.

At a leaf: the utility is the actual outcome.
At a MAX node: if the child values are correct, MAX can choose the largest.
At a MIN node: MIN can choose the smallest, so MAX cannot count on anything larger.


Repeat the argument from the leaves to the root. Each backed-up value is correct once its children are correct.


Following minimax guarantees MAX at least the root value. This may still mean a win, draw, or loss against optimal play.


This is induction on subtree height. At MAX nodes there exists an action achieving the backed-up bound. At MIN nodes every legal reply has value at least the minimum, and an optimal MIN can attain that minimum. With perfect play by both sides the outcome equals the root value. For tic-tac-toe, exact value 0 means a draw under optimal play, not an unfinished calculation. The theorem relies on actual terminal utilities; arbitrary heuristic cutoffs lose the guarantee.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Search Cost
Exact search works for tic-tac-toe. For larger games, let b be the branching factor and m the maximum remaining plies.


Time
A full tree has
1+b+\cdots+b^m=O(b^m).
For b=3, m=10: 59,049 leaves and 88,573 total nodes.

Memory
Depth-first evaluation keeps the active recursion path and pending siblings.

O(bm) if each call stores its children.
O(m) if successors are generated one at a time.



You can evaluate a tree without storing all of it. The number of positions examined still grows exponentially.


These are search-node/record counts with state representation costs treated as fixed. The O(m) version assumes a constant-size successor iterator and no table retaining prior states. Eagerly storing the entire tree would instead take exponential memory. The full-tree formula assumes b greater than1; b=3 is a constructed branching example, not a claim about all tic-tac-toe positions. Tic-tac-toe branching decreases as squares fill, and some games end early. Standard depth-first minimax complexity follows AIMA.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Terminal Utility and Cutoff Evaluation
Large games may require stopping before a terminal state. Let d count plies still available.
VALUE_LIMITED(s, d):
    if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
    if d == 0:     return EVAL(s)
    # Otherwise use the same MAX / MIN recursion,
    # calling VALUE_LIMITED(RESULT(s, a), d - 1).







Leaf type
Returned score




Terminal position
Exact outcome U(s)


Nonterminal depth cutoff
Estimated value \operatorname{EVAL}(s)




Unlike A*’s remaining-cost estimate, EVAL estimates game value. Heuristic errors can change the move; optimal play is no longer guaranteed.


Check TERMINAL before d==0 so a terminal state at the cutoff receives its exact utility. EVAL always uses the same MAX viewpoint. Minimax over heuristic leaves is exact for those supplied leaf scores but is not guaranteed optimal in the actual game. Unlike A*’s admissible remaining-cost heuristic, there is no admissibility condition introduced here that restores exact play. Keep this as a bridge; Lecture10 covers practical cutoff methods and alpha-beta. Reference: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/games/minimax.html#322-evaluation-functions.

Your Turn: Three Decision Levels

Compute C, D, E, F, then A, B, then the root. Which first move should MAX play?


  
  


C=5,\ D=9,\ E=4,\ F=6. Then A=5,\ B=4. Root value 5; choose A.


Give pairs 2-3 minutes before revealing. The bottom decision layer is MAX, not MIN. Ask students to name the controlling player before each calculation. Follow-up after the solution: change only C’s leaf 5 to 1. Then C=max(3,1)=3, A=min(3,9)=3, B remains 4, and the root switches to B with 4. This checks whether students can update only the affected ancestors. The leaf 0 is a terminal payoff, not missing data. Transition: the recursive algorithm performs these same backups automatically. This exercise is an original course example.

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

A game state includes whose turn it is.
MAX takes the maximum; MIN takes the minimum, using one utility viewpoint.
Back up values, then retain the action that achieves the root’s best value.
Exact minimax gives the best worst-case guarantee, but its time cost is exponential.


Can we prove that some branches cannot affect the root’s decision before evaluating all their leaves?


Next lecture: alpha-beta pruning preserves the minimax value while avoiding unnecessary search.

Asset credits

Close by returning to the distinction between choosing a high leaf and choosing a guaranteed branch value. Leave alpha-beta bounds and pruning traces for Lecture10. For ties, pruning may change which equally optimal move is returned depending on implementation and ordering; the minimax value is preserved.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: The Chosen Move and Its Guarantee
text:
The Chosen Move and Its Guarantee







Result
Meaning




Value: 3
Best worst-case payoff


Action: A
Move to play now



Choosing A guarantees at least 3. If MIN selects 12 instead, MAX gets 12.


After each opponent reply, choose again from the resulting state. A strategy specifies how to act in every position that may arise.


With perfect play by both players the outcome is exactly 3. Against any legal opponent, MAX can guarantee at least 3 by following a minimax strategy. Minimax protects against the strongest replies without predicting that every real opponent will be optimal. The highlighted line is one possible optimal continuation, not a fixed plan the opponent must follow. In a longer game, recompute after each observed reply or store a contingent strategy. If child values tie, either action is optimal; the pseudocode will retain the first.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Minimax Rule

s: a state; a: an action; A(s): the legal actions in s.
\operatorname{Result}(s,a): the next state after action a in state s.
U(s): terminal score; V(s): score from s under optimal play.


V(s)=
\begin{cases}
U(s), & \text{if }s\text{ is terminal},\\[0.35em]
\max\limits_{a\in A(s)} V(\operatorname{Result}(s,a)), & \text{if MAX moves},\\[0.35em]
\min\limits_{a\in A(s)} V(\operatorname{Result}(s,a)), & \text{if MIN moves}.
\end{cases}


For MAX: \arg\max gives the action(s) with the largest child value. Choose one, a^*:
a^*\in\arg\max_{a\in A(s)}V(\operatorname{Result}(s,a)).


Read Result(s,a) as “the state reached after taking action a in state s.” It is the same operation as RESULT in the game representation and pseudocode. A(s) abbreviates ACTIONS(s), and U(s) abbreviates UTILITY(s). V(Result(s,a)) is therefore the value of a child state. The recurrence computes the score, whereas arg max identifies actions achieving the largest score. The symbol in between a* and arg max means “is one of,” allowing multiple equally good actions. The action-selection formula assumes MAX moves; use arg min at MIN’s turn. The same fixed MAX viewpoint applies throughout. Quick check: MAX with children -7, -2, -5 has value -2. Source: AIMA adversarial search chapter and Berkeley CS188 minimax notes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Tic-Tac-Toe
Tic-tac-toe is a two-player game on a 3\times3 board.





X starts. Players alternate, marking one empty square per turn.
The first player with three marks in a row, column, or diagonal wins.
A full board with no winner is a draw.



We choose X’s moves. Who chooses O’s replies?


The opponent controls O. Our plan must account for their choices, including moves that block our win.


Explain the rules before analyzing the position. Each player keeps the same symbol throughout the game. The board shown is a position partway through play; the small numbers label its empty squares and are not scores. A winning line ends the game immediately. Contrast with UCS and A*: in deterministic route finding, the agent controls every action along its chosen plan. Here we choose X’s moves but cannot choose O’s replies. A sequence that leads to a win is useful only if the opponent cannot avoid it. The next slide introduces the decision rule for handling those replies. Source: AIMA adversarial search chapter.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Minimax: The Basic Idea
Minimax chooses the move with the best worst-case outcome, accounting for an opponent who tries to make our outcome as bad as possible.
Give each outcome a utility, a numerical score from our viewpoint:

MAX is our player, seeking the highest score.
MIN is the opponent, seeking the lowest score for us.

For now, both players see the entire state, moves have no random effects, and every game eventually ends.

For each candidate move, consider the worst reply. Then choose the move whose worst outcome is best.


MAX and MIN abbreviate maximizing and minimizing. We use one numerical utility measured from MAX’s viewpoint; MIN wants the opposite outcome. This is a zero-sum model. Seeing the entire state is called perfect information, and known move results without randomness are deterministic. The rule considers replies throughout the remaining game, not just the opponent’s next move. Exact recursive minimax here assumes a finite game tree with two alternating players. Games with dice, hidden information, or shared objectives require extensions. Source: AIMA adversarial search chapter.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Same Minimax Value, Less Search
Pruning means skipping unexplored branches once we can prove they cannot improve the root’s decision.


Minimax checked all 9 leaves. Can we establish the same root value, 3, with less work?


Recall that MAX seeks the highest score and MIN the lowest, always using MAX’s viewpoint. This is exactly the example from Lecture 9, not a new game. Alpha-beta pruning preserves the minimax root value for the same tree and leaf evaluations. Equally optimal root moves can differ when move ordering or tie-breaking changes. Source: AIMA adversarial search chapter and the original Lecture 10 Beamer source.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Branch We Can Stop Searching
text:
A Branch We Can Stop Searching

Search depth first, left to right. Leaf numbers are terminal scores, measured from MAX’s viewpoint.


  
  
  
  



At A: \min(3,12,8)=3. MAX already has an option worth 3.


At B: seeing 2 proves B\le2. Skip its remaining leaves: MAX can choose A.


At C: check 14, 5, then 2. Root value 3, move A, only 7 of 9 leaves evaluated.



Before revealing each step, ask which player controls the node. After inspecting B’s first leaf, its eventual minimum can only stay at 2 or decrease. Therefore it cannot beat A’s exact value 3. Only the unvisited children of B are pruned; C must still be searched. At C, neither 14 nor 5 is low enough to stop, and the final 2 arrives after all its leaves have been examined. Crosses replace unevaluated leaf values. We know only B <= 2 from this search, even though the fully specified example’s true B value is 2. The returned bound is sufficient to reject B. Source: AIMA minimax example, extended with an alpha-beta trace.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Alpha and Beta: Options Already Available
text:
Alpha and Beta: Options Already Available

\alpha (alpha): MAX’s best lower bound so far along the search path.
\beta (beta): MIN’s best upper bound so far along the search path.
Start at the root with \alpha=-\infty, \beta=+\infty. Pass the current bounds to each child.





At B, MAX already has 3 elsewhere, so \alpha=3.
MIN finds a reply worth 2, lowering \beta to 2.
Prune when \alpha\ge\beta.


A cutoff can return a bound, not an exact subtree value. Here, knowing B\le2 is enough.


Alpha and beta describe alternatives on the active path, not the global largest and smallest leaves. At a MAX node the current best child raises alpha. At a MIN node the current best child lowers beta. The bounds are passed downward by value; they are not reset at every node. Alpha can only increase and beta can only decrease during one call. If the interval closes, an ancestor already has an option at least as good, so remaining siblings cannot improve its decision. Equality also permits pruning when seeking one optimal root action. On a cutoff, a MIN return is an upper bound and a MAX return is a lower bound on that subtree’s true minimax value. Only the full-window root result is necessarily exact. Source: AIMA alpha-beta algorithm.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Cutoff at a MAX Node
text:
A Cutoff at a MAX Node

Now the root is MIN. It can already choose A for 5. At B, MAX discovers a child worth 8.


  
  


Could B’s remaining child make MAX’s choice smaller than 5?


No. B\ge8, but MIN can keep 5. At B, \alpha=8\ge\beta=5, so skip the remaining child.


Emphasize the swapped root role. A is a MAX node with leaves 1 and 5, so its exact value is 5. That completed option provides the inherited beta bound for B. No matter what B’s unseen child contains, MAX at B can keep at least 8. MIN above will avoid it. This is the symmetric counterpart of the earlier MIN-node cutoff. All utilities still use MAX’s viewpoint. Original course example.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Alpha-Beta Pseudocode: MAX
AB searches state s; a is a legal action. Start with AB(root, -infinity, +infinity). This is the MAX case.

  AB(s, alpha, beta)
  if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
  if PLAYER(s) == MAX:
  v <- -infinity
  for a in ACTIONS(s):
  child <- RESULT(s, a)
  v <- max(v, AB(child, alpha, beta))
  alpha <- max(alpha, v)
  if alpha >= beta: break
  return v


MAX raises alpha. break skips the remaining actions at this node, then returns to the parent.


This is the MAX case of the same AB function whose MIN case follows. TERMINAL asks whether the game is finished, UTILITY gives the terminal score, PLAYER gives the side to move, ACTIONS lists legal actions, and RESULT produces the successor state including its player. The state carries the turn, so no separate Boolean flag is needed. The local variable v is the best returned child score so far. Each child receives the current bounds. Values are passed by value, not through shared global variables. At the root, additionally retain the action when a child strictly improves the best score, as in Lecture 9. This slide searches to terminal states; a later slide adds a depth cutoff. Source: AIMA algorithm, rewritten in the notation of Lecture 9.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Alpha-Beta Pseudocode: MIN
The MIN case of the same function. RESULT(s, a) is the state reached by taking action a in state s.

  AB(s, alpha, beta)
  if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
  if PLAYER(s) == MIN:
  v <- +infinity
  for a in ACTIONS(s):
  child <- RESULT(s, a)
  v <- min(v, AB(child, alpha, beta))
  beta <- min(beta, v)
  if alpha >= beta: break
  return v


MIN lowers beta. Both branches use the same stopping test: \alpha\ge\beta.


Compare the two cases: infinity, min/max, and the updated bound change; recursion and the stopping test stay the same. A cutoff return can be a bound rather than an exact value, which the calling algorithm handles through its own bounds. A nonterminal position must have a successor, including a legal pass where the rules require one. In HW2, neither player having a legal move is terminal; one player having no move is a pass. Keep the score from a fixed root-player viewpoint rather than switching perspective with every recursive call.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Quick Check: When Can We Stop?
text:
Quick Check: When Can We Stop?

MAX already has 4 from A. At MIN node B, the first leaf gives 6. Can we stop? What if the next leaf gives 3?


  
  


After 6, continue: 4<6. After 3, prune: \alpha=4\ge\beta=3. MAX keeps A, worth 4.


The values printed at untouched leaves are given problem data, not evaluations already performed. Ask for the comparison before revealing the answer. If the second leaf were exactly 4, equality would also allow pruning. If it were 5, we would still need the final leaf. Changing the skipped leaf to any number cannot make B exceed 3. The exact value of B could decrease further, but MAX’s root choice stays A. Original course exercise.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Move Ordering Changes the Work
Move ordering means trying promising moves first: high scores at MAX, low scores at MIN.




At C, try 2 before 14 and 5.



Search
Leaves checked




Plain minimax
9


Original order
7


Better reply order
5




With branching factor b and depth d, worst-case time is still O(b^d). Ideal ordering can reduce it to O(b^{d/2}).

Ordering changes which move we try first. Alpha-beta decides which remaining moves can safely be skipped.


Keep root order A, B, C and A’s replies unchanged. B still visits 2 first. Reorder C’s original replies 14,5,2 to 2,14,5, so C’s first reply closes the window. The visited leaf count is 3+1+1=5. We do not know exact child values in advance in real games; heuristics or earlier search results suggest an ordering. Best-case complexity describes balanced trees with ideal ordering, not a guaranteed practical runtime. Worst ordering can give little or no pruning. The root value remains 3; ties may change which equally optimal move is selected. Source: AIMA alpha-beta analysis.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Depth Limit Changes the Leaf Scores
text:
A Depth Limit Changes the Leaf Scores
Let d count the remaining plies, where one ply is one player’s move. At a depth limit, the game may still be unfinished.

  AB(s, d, alpha, beta)
  if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
  if d == 0: return EVAL(s)
  # Otherwise use the same MAX / MIN branches.
  # Each move calls AB(child, d - 1, alpha, beta).


UTILITY(s): exact score of a finished game.
EVAL(s): an estimate for an unfinished position, using the same player’s viewpoint.


With identical cutoffs and scores, alpha-beta matches depth-limited minimax. The heuristic estimate may still miss the best move in the full game.


Always check terminal before the depth cutoff. Alpha-beta is exact relative to the leaf scores supplied to it; it does not make inaccurate heuristic scores accurate. The demo notebook has explicitly supplied terminal leaves and no depth parameter. HW2 uses a function named utility for board evaluation in its search methods, so its name alone does not imply the position is terminal. In Reversi search, use a consistent depth convention and handle a forced pass explicitly. Source: AIMA imperfect decision making and Homework 2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Time Limits and Unstable Positions
Iterative deepening
Search depths 1, 2, 3, …. Keep the best move from the last completed search if time runs out. Its move ordering can help the next search.
Quiescence search
“Quiescent” means quiet or stable. Near a cutoff, extend selected forcing moves, such as a capture and immediate recapture, before evaluating.

Forward pruning skips moves because a heuristic judges them unpromising. Unlike alpha-beta’s bound test, it can change the minimax answer.


If depth 1 chooses A, depth 2 chooses B, and depth 3 is interrupted, use B from the completed depth-2 search. A partial deeper search has not compared every relevant root alternative. An implementation also needs a legal fallback if even the first iteration cannot finish. Quiescence addresses the horizon effect: a depth boundary may hide a forcing reply that reverses a seemingly good score. It usually extends a limited set of tactical moves and needs its own limits; it is not an instruction to search indefinitely until all play is calm. The HW2 GUI already supplies iterative deepening; implementing quiescence search is not part of HW2. Source: original Lecture 10 topics and AIMA adversarial search.

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Alpha-beta uses bounds to skip work while preserving the minimax root value.
MAX raises \alpha; MIN lowers \beta. Stop remaining siblings when \alpha\ge\beta.
Better move ordering can produce more pruning.
A depth cutoff needs a heuristic estimate and a consistent score viewpoint.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Searching for a Configuration
Local search keeps a current candidate and moves among nearby candidates. The goal is often a good final configuration.


An objective function scores each candidate. We will minimize a cost c(s): lower is better.


In systematic search we kept a frontier of alternatives and often stored parent links to recover a path. The single-state local methods here keep one current candidate, sometimes with a best-so-far record. They can use little memory, but they may stop without finding a goal or global optimum. A complete candidate may violate constraints. It is not necessarily a valid solution. Four queens is the smaller version of eight queens. Queens attack along rows, columns, and diagonals. The sliding puzzle remains a path-finding task. The scheduled GUI compares hill climbing and simulated annealing with A*, and records legal move sequences. Source: AIMA local search section and the original Lecture 11 Beamer source.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Queens: State, Cost, and Neighborhood

State s: one queen per column. Each list entry gives that queen’s row.
Cost c(s): pairs sharing a row or diagonal, counting each pair once. A solution has c(s)=0.
Neighborhood N(s): move one queen to a different row in its column.



With 4 queens, how many neighbors? With 8 queens?  4\times3=12 and 8\times7=56.


Rows are numbered top to bottom, columns left to right. Q denotes a queen. Starting with all queens present makes every state a complete assignment, even when queens attack. A pair attacks if it shares a row or if its row difference equals its column difference in absolute value. Sharing a column is impossible in this representation. There are six distinct pairs among four queens, so this starting cost is 6, not 12. Each of n queens has n-1 alternative rows, giving n(n-1) distinct neighbors. A systematic construction can instead add queens one at a time and backtrack when constraints fail. We use four queens to make the same eight-queens representation visible at a readable size. Source: AIMA n-queens local-search formulation. Worked boards are original course examples.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Greedy Queen-Move Trace
Hill climbing chooses a best immediate neighbor. For our cost, it moves downhill and accepts only a strict decrease.

  
  
  
  



Move column 2: cost 6 to 3. Choose one of the best moves if tied.


Move column 1: cost 3 to 1. Recompute neighbors from the new board.


Move column 4: cost 1 to 0. This run succeeds, but other starting states can get stuck.



At each step, consider all 12 neighbors, not just the selected queen. The chosen successor has minimum neighbor cost: 3, then 1, then 0. Equal best neighbors exist, so this is one valid greedy trace rather than a uniquely prescribed path. The gold queen marks the queen just moved. After the first move the three attacking pairs are columns (1,3), (1,4), and (3,4). After the second move only columns 3 and 4 attack. The last board [2,4,1,3] solves four queens. Source: original course example using the AIMA neighborhood.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Hill-Climbing Pseudocode
s is the current state, N(s) its neighbors, and K a move budget. LOWEST_COST chooses a neighbor with smallest c.

  HILL_CLIMB(s, K)
  for step in 1 .. K:
  if EMPTY(N(s)): return s
  n <- LOWEST_COST(N(s))
  if c(n) >= c(s): return s
  s <- n
  return s


Stopping means no strict local improvement or budget exhausted. Check the returned cost before calling it a solution.


This is steepest-ascent hill climbing expressed as cost minimization, also called steepest descent. It scans the neighborhood and chooses a best candidate. A streaming scan can retain only the best neighbor rather than materializing the whole set. Memory savings are therefore implementation dependent. Ties between equally good successors may be broken arbitrarily. The >= test prevents sideways moves, so a finite state space cannot cycle through accepted states. A known goal cost such as zero in n-queens permits an additional early stop. For general optimization, a low cost does not certify a global optimum. Source: AIMA hill-climbing algorithm, adapted to a cost and finite budget.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Local Minimum Can Stop the Search
text:
A Local Minimum Can Stop the Search
A local minimum is no worse than its neighbors. A global minimum has the lowest cost in the entire state space below.

  
  
  



From A, move to B: cost 8 to 5.


From B, move to C, cost 2. Then stop: B costs 5, D costs 4. The better state G is beyond a worsening move.



The graph is the whole state space for this toy problem. Edges define neighbors, and the numbers inside circles are state costs, not edge costs. The vertical placement only helps show lower and higher cost. C is a strict local minimum because both its neighbors have higher cost. G is the global minimum. If the goal were cost 0, hill climbing from A would fail to find an existing solution. With a score to maximize, the equivalent trap is a local maximum. Source: original course illustration of the AIMA landscape concept.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Plateaus and Restricted Moves
A plateau has equal-cost neighbors. A ridge for a score, or narrow valley for a cost, may point between the allowed move directions.


Limited sideways moves can cross a plateau but may cycle. A different neighborhood can help, when the problem permits it.


In the left graph, the current state is the first 2. Strict improvement halts immediately. Two equal-cost moves would reach the third 2, which has a lower-cost neighbor. A sideways-move budget or cycle detection prevents indefinite wandering, but does not guarantee success. In the right grid, lower numbers are better. From the bottom-right 3, up and left both give 5. A diagonal move would give 2, but it is outside this chosen neighborhood. This demonstrates how an apparently favorable direction may not be an available step. A narrow valley can produce slow zigzag progress or traps in a discrete neighborhood. We cannot arbitrarily introduce illegal puzzle moves. Source: AIMA plateaus and ridges, with original discrete course examples.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Simulated Annealing: Crossing a Cost Barrier
text:
Simulated Annealing: Crossing a Cost Barrier
Annealing heats a material and cools it. Simulated annealing borrows the temperature idea: it sometimes accepts a worse candidate.

  
  
  
  
  



Suppose we accept C to D: cost rises from 2 to 4.


Then propose E, cost 3. It improves on D, though C was better.


Then F, cost 1, improves the best record.


Then G, cost 0. This is one possible random trajectory, not a guaranteed route.



All comparisons use the current state, not the best state previously seen. E3 improves on current D4 and is accepted even though the earlier C2 was better. The gold circles mark previously visited states, and teal marks the current state. At C, the move to D is worsening and requires a probabilistic acceptance decision. Later steps also depend on which neighbor is proposed. The next slide quantifies the acceptance probability. The physical analogy is settling into low-energy configurations; avoid claiming that annealing always increases a material’s strength. Source: original Lecture 11 annealing motivation and AIMA simulated annealing. Graph and trajectory are original course examples.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Annealing Acceptance Rule
For current state s and proposed neighbor n, let \Delta=c(n)-c(s). Temperature T>0 controls acceptance of a cost increase.

P(\text{accept})=
\begin{cases}
1, & \Delta\le0,\\
\exp(-\Delta/T), & \Delta>0.
\end{cases}

For a proposed cost increase from 2 to 4, \Delta=2. Draw u uniformly from [0,1) and accept if u<P(\text{accept}).



Temperature T
Probability for \Delta=2
With u=0.30




4
e^{-0.5}\approx0.607
Accept


1
e^{-2}\approx0.135
Reject


0.25
e^{-8}\approx0.000335
Reject




P denotes probability. exp(z) is the exponential function e to the power z. The uniform random number is a fresh draw for each proposal; the fixed u=0.30 only illustrates how temperature changes the decision for the same draw. Improvements and equal-cost moves have probability one under this rule. As T decreases, a fixed positive delta has smaller acceptance probability. Larger cost increases are also less likely at a fixed temperature. The argument -delta/T is negative for worsening moves. If T is zero or negative, stop before evaluating the exponential. Source: AIMA simulated-annealing acceptance rule. Numerical probabilities are rounded.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Cooling and the Best-State Record
A cooling schedule lowers temperature: T(t)=T_0\rho^t, with starting temperature T_0>0 and cooling factor 0<\rho<1.


Cooling too fast can freeze the search near a local minimum.
Cooling slowly spends more of the budget exploring. Test several random seeds.


Current cost 4, best seen 2. Which state should we return?  The saved state with cost 2.


T0 is the starting temperature, rho the multiplicative cooling factor, and t the iteration count starting at zero. A rho closer to 1 cools more slowly for a fixed starting temperature and iteration count. Temperature has to be interpreted relative to the scale of cost differences. Multiplying the objective by 100 while keeping T fixed greatly reduces acceptance of worsening moves. The plotted sequence is an illustrative accepted-state history, not output from the notebook. At accepted move 4, current cost is 4 but best cost is 2. Save the state, not just its numeric score. Finite practical schedules do not guarantee the global optimum. Source: AIMA cooling discussion and original course trace.

title: Sliding Puzzle: Local Search and A*
text:
State and Legal Moves
The code blocks below are taken directly from the downloadable file. Their line numbers match that file. The full program is self-contained; the GUI sections are folded near the bottom.

Board Representation
A tuple stores the nine cells in row-major order. Zero is the blank. Immutable tuples can be dictionary keys for A*.
For this 3-by-3 puzzle, count inversions among numbered tiles: a pair is inverted when a larger number precedes a smaller one. A board can reach this goal exactly when that count is even. This formula is specific to odd-width boards; do not reuse it unchanged for a 4-by-4 puzzle.
GOAL = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 0)
TRAP = (1, 5, 2, 4, 3, 6, 7, 8, 0)
EASY = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 0, 7, 8)
MODES = ("Manual", "Hill climbing", "Simulated annealing", "A*")


def validate(state):
    if len(state) != 9 or set(state) != set(range(9)):
        raise ValueError("Use each number 0 through 8 exactly once.")


def is_solvable(state):
    tiles = [tile for tile in state if tile]
    inversions = sum(a > b for i, a in enumerate(tiles) for b in tiles[i + 1:])
    return inversions % 2 == 0  # This parity rule is for a 3-by-3 board.


The Neighborhood
Each neighbor swaps the blank with one tile directly above, below, left, or right. Diagonal moves and arbitrary tile swaps are not allowed. The helper returns both the moved tile and the resulting board.
def neighbors(state):
    blank = state.index(0)
    row, col = divmod(blank, 3)
    for dr, dc in ((-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)):
        nr, nc = row + dr, col + dc
        if 0 <= nr < 3 and 0 <= nc < 3:
            index = 3 * nr + nc
            board = list(state)
            tile = board[index]
            board[blank], board[index] = board[index], board[blank]
            yield tile, tuple(board)


Manhattan Distance
For each numbered tile, add its horizontal and vertical distance from its goal cell:

h(s)=\sum_{t=1}^{8}
\left(
|r_t-r_t^{\text{goal}}|
+
|c_t-c_t^{\text{goal}}|
\right).

The blank is excluded. One legal move changes this total by exactly +1 or -1, so this particular neighborhood has no equal-h moves. Manhattan distance never overestimates the required moves: each move shifts only one numbered tile by one cell.
def manhattan(state):
    total = 0
    for index, tile in enumerate(state):
        if tile:  # The blank is not a numbered tile.
            row, col = divmod(index, 3)
            goal_row, goal_col = divmod(tile - 1, 3)
            total += abs(row - goal_row) + abs(col - goal_col)
    return total


A Solvable Shuffle
Start from the goal and make legal moves. Avoid immediately undoing the preceding move during shuffling. The number of shuffle moves is not the shortest solution length. During search, all legal moves remain available, including undo moves.
def shuffled_board(rng, moves=40):
    state, previous = GOAL, None
    for _ in range(moves):
        # Avoid immediate undo only while shuffling, not during search.
        options = [(tile, board) for tile, board in neighbors(state)
                   if board != previous]
        previous, state = state, rng.choice(options)[1]
    if state == GOAL:
        state = next(neighbors(state))[1]
    return state

title: Sliding Puzzle: Local Search and A*
text:
Local Search

Run State
Each run gets its own seeded random-number generator. Resetting reproduces its choices without changing the initial puzzle. The current board and best-so-far record are separate; storing a best board does not teleport the current board to it.
class SearchRun:
    def __init__(self, initial, mode="Hill climbing", seed=42,
                 temperature=2.0, cooling=0.997, budget=2000):
        initial = tuple(initial)
        validate(initial)
        if mode not in MODES:
            raise ValueError("Unknown search mode.")
        if temperature <= 0 or not 0 < cooling <= 1 or budget < 1:
            raise ValueError("Use positive temperature/budget and 0 < cooling <= 1.")
        self.initial = self.state = initial
        self.mode, self.seed = mode, seed
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.start_temperature = self.temperature = temperature
        self.cooling, self.budget = cooling, budget
        self.records = []
        self.path = [initial]
        self.moved_tiles = []
        self.costs = [manhattan(initial)]
        self.best_costs = self.costs.copy()
        self.best_path = self.path.copy()
        self.planner = AStar(initial) if mode == "A*" else None
        self.status = "ready"
        if not is_solvable(initial):
            self.status = "unsolvable"
        elif initial == GOAL:
            self.status = "solved"

    @property
    def finished(self):
        return self.status in {"solved", "stuck", "budget", "unsolvable"}


Hill Climbing and Annealing
Hill climbing evaluates every legal neighbor and selects a minimum-h neighbor, breaking ties randomly. If no neighbor improves the current distance, it stops.
Annealing instead selects one random legal neighbor. With \Delta h=h(s')-h(s):

P(\text{accept})=
\begin{cases}
1, & \Delta h\leq 0,\\
\exp(-\Delta h/T), & \Delta h>0.
\end{cases}

Draw u uniformly from [0,1) and accept when u<P(\text{accept}). After each proposal, use T\leftarrow\max(0.05,\alpha T), where \alpha is the cooling factor. The positive temperature floor and finite proposal budget are practical demonstration choices, not a convergence guarantee.
    def advance(self, tile=None):
        if self.finished:
            return None
        if self.mode == "A*":
            return self.advance_astar()
        options = list(neighbors(self.state))
        if self.mode == "Manual":
            choice = next((move for move in options if move[0] == tile), None)
            return self.record(*choice) if choice else None
        if self.mode == "Hill climbing":
            best = min(manhattan(board) for _, board in options)
            if best >= manhattan(self.state):
                self.status = "stuck"
                return None
            tile, candidate = self.rng.choice([
                move for move in options if manhattan(move[1]) == best
            ])
            return self.record(tile, candidate)
        if len(self.records) >= self.budget:
            self.status = "budget"
            return None
        tile, candidate = self.rng.choice(options)
        delta = manhattan(candidate) - manhattan(self.state)
        probability = 1.0 if delta <= 0 else math.exp(-delta / self.temperature)
        proposal = self.record(
            tile, candidate, probability, self.rng.random(), self.temperature,
        )
        # Cool after every proposal, including a rejected proposal.
        self.temperature = max(0.05, self.temperature * self.cooling)
        if not self.finished and len(self.records) == self.budget:
            self.status = "budget"
        return proposal


Recording a Proposal
A proposal contains the before, proposed, and resulting boards. Rejections appear in the trace but not in the accepted move sequence.
@dataclass
class Proposal:
    step: int
    tile: int
    before: tuple
    candidate: tuple
    after: tuple
    h_before: int
    h_candidate: int
    delta: int
    temperature: float | None
    probability: float
    draw: float | None
    accepted: bool
The recorder updates the current board only on acceptance. It also keeps the best distance and a legal path from the original board to that best state. Only reaching h=0 counts as solving the puzzle; a low best-so-far distance is not enough.
    def record(self, tile, candidate, probability=1.0, draw=None, temperature=None):
        before = self.state
        h_before, h_candidate = manhattan(before), manhattan(candidate)
        accepted = draw is None or draw < probability
        if accepted:
            self.state = candidate
            self.path.append(candidate)
            self.moved_tiles.append(tile)
        proposal = Proposal(
            len(self.records) + 1, tile, before, candidate, self.state,
            h_before, h_candidate, h_candidate - h_before,
            temperature, probability, draw, accepted,
        )
        self.records.append(proposal)
        cost = manhattan(self.state)
        if cost < self.best_costs[-1]:
            self.best_path = self.path.copy()
        self.costs.append(cost)
        self.best_costs.append(min(self.best_costs[-1], cost))
        if self.state == GOAL:
            self.status = "solved"
        return proposal

title: Sliding Puzzle: Local Search and A*
Sliding Puzzle: Local Search and A*
text:
Questions and Answers

Why is the default board a local minimum even though it is solvable?
Why does a rejected annealing proposal count as a step but not a move?
Why must a retry reset to the same starting board?
Why can A* solve this board even though its first solution move increases h?
Does a lower best-so-far distance guarantee that annealing will solve the puzzle?



Answers


The current distance is 4, and both legal neighbors have distance 5. Strict hill climbing cannot leave it, but a legal six-move route reaches the goal.
The algorithm still sampled and evaluated a candidate. The rejection leaves the current board unchanged, so no tile moves, but the proposal budget and cooling schedule advance.
A different board is a different problem. Resetting the same board while changing the seed produces another stochastic attempt at the original task.
A* does not require each move to lower h. It maintains a frontier of alternatives and ranks total estimated path cost g+h.
No. Annealing may remain trapped after cooling, revisit states, or run out of proposals. A best-so-far record is useful evidence of progress, not a success guarantee.

class CostChart(QWidget):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.current, self.best = [0], [0]
        self.setMinimumHeight(120)

    def paintEvent(self, event):
        painter = QPainter(self)
        painter.setRenderHint(QPainter.RenderHint.Antialiasing)
        left, top, right, bottom = 38, 25, self.width() - 12, self.height() - 27
        maximum = max(2, max(self.current))
        painter.setPen(QColor("#58636b"))
        painter.drawText(left, 16, "Manhattan distance: current (blue), best (green)")
        painter.drawLine(left, bottom, right, bottom)
        painter.drawLine(left, top, left, bottom)
        painter.drawText(8, top + 5, str(maximum))
        painter.drawText(20, bottom + 4, "0")
        painter.drawText(left, self.height() - 5, "0")
        painter.drawText(right - 135, self.height() - 5,
                         f"Step {len(self.current) - 1}")
        for values, color in ((self.current, "#2463a5"), (self.best, "#18764d")):
            points = QPolygonF([
                QPointF(left + i / max(1, len(values) - 1) * (right - left),
                        bottom - value / maximum * (bottom - top))
                for i, value in enumerate(values)
            ])
            painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(color), 2))
            painter.drawPolyline(points)
            painter.drawEllipse(points[-1], 3, 3)

class SlidingPuzzle(QMainWindow):

    def build_ui(self):

        modes = QHBoxLayout()

Animation and Trace
Run, pause, reset, step, and trace
    def load_preset(self, index):
        self.initial = (TRAP if index == 0 else EASY if index == 1
                        else shuffled_board(random.SystemRandom()))
        self.reset_run()

    def new_shuffle(self):
        self.preset.blockSignals(True)
        self.preset.setCurrentIndex(2)
        self.preset.blockSignals(False)
        self.load_preset(2)

    def change_mode(self, mode):
        self.mode = mode
        self.reset_run()

    def reset_run(self):
        self.timer.stop()
        self.run = SearchRun(self.initial, self.mode, self.seed.value(),
                             self.t0.value(), self.cooling.value(), self.budget.value())
        self.trace.setRowCount(0)
        self.refresh()

    def toggle_run(self):
        if self.timer.isActive():
            self.timer.stop()
        elif not self.run.finished:
            self.timer.start(self.delay.value())
        self.refresh()

    def single_step(self):
        self.timer.stop()
        self.advance()

    def advance(self):
        # A* planning is batched while running, but One step expands one state.
        planning = self.run.planner and not self.run.planner.done
        batch = 100 if planning and self.timer.isActive() else 1
        for _ in range(batch):
            proposal = self.run.advance()
            if proposal:
                self.append_row(proposal)
            if self.run.finished or (planning and self.run.planner.done):
                break
        if self.run.finished:
            self.timer.stop()
        self.refresh()

    def manual_move(self, index):
        if self.mode == "Manual":
            proposal = self.run.advance(self.run.state[index])
            if proposal:
                self.append_row(proposal)
            self.refresh()

    def append_row(self, proposal):
        if self.trace.rowCount() == 500:
            self.trace.removeRow(0)
        row = self.trace.rowCount()
        self.trace.insertRow(row)
        values = [proposal.step, proposal.tile, proposal.h_before,
                  proposal.h_candidate, f"{proposal.delta:+d}",
                  "-" if proposal.temperature is None else f"{proposal.temperature:.3f}",
                  f"{proposal.probability:.3f}",
                  "-" if proposal.draw is None else f"{proposal.draw:.3f}",
                  "Accept" if proposal.accepted else "Reject", manhattan(proposal.after)]
        color = "#a44b18" if proposal.accepted and proposal.delta > 0 else "#1d6248"
        if not proposal.accepted:
            color = "#69747a"
        for column, value in enumerate(values):
            item = QTableWidgetItem(str(value))
            item.setTextAlignment(Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignCenter)
            item.setForeground(QColor(color))
            self.trace.setItem(row, column, item)
        self.trace.scrollToBottom()



Display State
Refresh the board and metrics
    def refresh(self):
        run = self.run
        last = run.records[-1] if run.records else None
        for index, button in enumerate(self.tiles):
            tile = run.state[index]
            highlighted = last and last.accepted and tile == last.tile
            background = "#e4e9ed" if not tile else "#d9eee4" if highlighted else "#dfeafb"
            button.setText(str(tile) if tile else "")
            button.setStyleSheet(
                f"background: {background}; color: #183042; font: bold 30px Arial;"
                "border: none; border-radius: 6px;"
            )
            button.setEnabled(self.mode == "Manual" and not run.finished and bool(tile))
            button.setAccessibleName(f"Tile {tile}" if tile else "Blank")
        self.metrics.setText(
            f"Distance h: {manhattan(run.state)}    Best h: {run.best_costs[-1]}\n"
            f"Steps: {len(run.records)}    Accepted moves: {len(run.moved_tiles)}"
        )
        messages = {
            "ready": "Ready.",
            "planning": "A* is planning. The board stays at the start until a route is found.",
            "replay": "A* found a shortest route. Playing its legal moves.",
            "stuck": "Hill climbing is stuck: every legal move increases the distance.",
            "budget": "Proposal budget exhausted without reaching the goal. This is not a solution.",
            "unsolvable": "This board cannot reach the goal (inversion parity).",
            "solved": ("Solved: shortest route (A*)." if self.mode == "A*"
                       else "Solved. This move sequence is not guaranteed shortest."),
        }
        message = messages[run.status]
        if last and run.status == "ready":
            decision = "Accepted" if last.accepted else "Rejected"
            message = f"{decision} tile {last.tile}: h {last.h_before} -> {last.h_candidate}."
            if last.temperature is not None:
                message += (f" P = {last.probability:.3f}, u = {last.draw:.3f}; "
                            f"accept when u < P.")
        self.status.setText(message)
        color = "#a44b18" if run.status in {"stuck", "budget"} else "#185b42"
        self.status.setStyleSheet(f"color: {color}; font-weight: 600;")
        options = ";  ".join(f"tile {tile}: h = {manhattan(board)}"
                              for tile, board in neighbors(run.state))
        self.candidates.setText(f"Legal neighbors of this board:\n{options}")
        if run.planner:
            self.search_info.setText(
                f"A* expanded: {run.planner.expanded}    "
                f"Frontier entries: {len(run.planner.frontier)}"
            )
        elif self.mode == "Simulated annealing":
            self.search_info.setText(f"Next T: {run.temperature:.4f}    "
                                     f"Cooling: {run.cooling:g}    Minimum T: 0.05")
        else:
            self.search_info.setText("")
        self.board_title.setText("Initial board (A* planning)" if run.status == "planning"
                                 else "Current board")
        self.chart.current, self.chart.best = run.costs, run.best_costs
        self.chart.update()
        self.path_label.setText("Solution: tiles moved into the blank" if run.status == "solved"
                                else "Accepted moves: tiles moved into the blank")
        self.path_text.setPlainText("  ".join(map(str, run.moved_tiles)) or "(none)")
        self.path_text.verticalScrollBar().setValue(self.path_text.verticalScrollBar().maximum())
        automated = self.mode != "Manual" and not run.finished
        self.play.setEnabled(automated)
        self.step.setEnabled(automated)
        playing = self.timer.isActive()
        icon = QStyle.StandardPixmap.SP_MediaPause if playing else QStyle.StandardPixmap.SP_MediaPlay
        self.play.setIcon(self.style().standardIcon(icon))
        self.play.setToolTip("Pause" if playing else "Run")
        for control in (self.t0, self.cooling, self.budget):
            control.setEnabled(self.mode == "Simulated annealing")
        self.seed.setEnabled(self.mode in {"Hill climbing", "Simulated annealing"})



Export the Full Run
Export JSON
    def export_run(self):
        self.timer.stop()
        self.refresh()
        filename, _ = QFileDialog.getSaveFileName(
            self, "Export run", "sliding-puzzle-run.json", "JSON files (*.json)",
        )
        if not filename:
            return
        run = self.run
        data = {
            "algorithm": run.mode, "status": run.status, "initial": run.initial,
            "seed": run.seed, "initial_temperature": run.start_temperature,
            "cooling": run.cooling, "minimum_temperature": 0.05, "budget": run.budget,
            "accepted_path": run.path, "moved_tiles": run.moved_tiles,
            "best_path": run.best_path, "proposals": [asdict(p) for p in run.records],
            "astar_expanded": run.planner.expanded if run.planner else None,
            "astar_route": run.planner.route if run.planner else None,
        }
        try:
            with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                json.dump(data, file, indent=2)
        except OSError as error:
            QMessageBox.warning(self, "Could not export", str(error))



Launch
Start the application

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Population-Based Search
A genetic algorithm (GA) searches with a population of candidate solutions. A generation is one round of reproduction and replacement.


Selection chooses parents using solution quality.
Crossover combines parents; mutation introduces random changes.


Unlike the single-state methods in Lecture 11, a GA keeps several candidates. More candidates do not guarantee a solution.


A candidate is often called an individual. The analogy to biological evolution motivates inheritance, selection, and variation, but a GA is a designed optimization procedure, not a literal model of natural evolution. Fitness is the task-specific score, introduced explicitly on the next two slides. The population is a collection that may contain duplicate candidates, not necessarily a mathematical set. This lecture develops one eight-queens example before connecting to the permutation representation used by the existing notebook. Source: AIMA genetic algorithms and the original Lecture 12 Beamer material.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Encoding an 8-Queens Board
Place eight queens so that no pair shares a row, column, or diagonal. Let x_i be the row of the queen in column i.

A gene is one entry x_i; a chromosome is the full candidate x=(x_1,\ldots,x_8).

One queen per column is automatic. Repeated rows are allowed in a candidate.


Rows and columns are numbered 1 through 8, with row 1 at the top. Every sequence of eight legal row values represents a board with one queen per column, even when the board is not a solution. There are 8^8 such encodings. The gene at column 6 has value 5; the entry is a row number, not a fitness value or tile label. Later we will impose a permutation constraint, which changes both the set of valid chromosomes and the operators. Source: the AIMA chromosome 24748552 carried over from the Spring 2025 lecture. Board redrawn for the course.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Fitness: Count Non-Attacking Pairs
There are \binom{8}{2}=28 unordered queen pairs. Let c(x) count attacking pairs; maximize fitness F(x)=28-c(x).


Is F(x)=24 a solution?  No. All 28 pairs must be non-attacking.


For columns i<j, queens attack when x_i=x_j or |x_i-x_j|=j-i. Column conflicts are impossible under this encoding. The four attacking pairs in this example are (1,8), (2,4), (3,8), and (6,7), so the fitness is 24. Fitness counts pairs, not the number of correctly placed queens. A board can have high fitness without any queen being in an independently correct final location. Minimizing conflict count and maximizing non-attacking pairs rank these boards identically. For n queens, the target is n(n-1)/2. Source: AIMA’s eight-queens genetic algorithm example; pair enumeration checked for this diagram.

Fitness-proportionate selection is also called roulette-wheel selection. The cumulative boundaries are 24/78, 47/78, 67/78, and 1. The four fixed draws are an illustrative sample, not an output claimed from the notebook. Selection copies or references parents for reproduction; the sampled parent list is not yet the final new generation. If all fitness values are zero, use a defined fallback such as uniform sampling rather than dividing by zero. This formula requires nonnegative weights. The notebook instead uses tournament selection, explained on the permutation slide. Source: the original AIMA population and scores, with explicit uniform draws added for the course.
