text:
One-Point Crossover
For the first selected pair B and A, choose a cut after gene 3. A child, or offspring, inherits a prefix from one parent and a suffix from the other.

  
  
  



Child 1: B’s prefix + A’s suffix.


Child 2 uses the other two segments. A valid encoding is preserved, but fitness need not improve.



One-point crossover chooses a boundary between genes. We fix the boundary after column 3 to make the inheritance visible. Pink genes come from B; teal genes come from A. B has fitness 23, A has 24, and the children have 23 and 22. Every gene remains a legal row value, so both children are valid chromosomes under the unrestricted row-vector encoding, even though neither solves the queens problem. The second pair B,C at the same cut produces 32715124 and 24452411, with fitness 22 and 18. These four children feed the replacement example. The pseudocode later creates one child per parent draw rather than requiring pairs of children; both are standard design choices. Source: AIMA one-point crossover, with these child scores independently calculated.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Mutation: Change a Gene
In this encoding, each gene may independently change to another row. For example, use mutation probability p_{\text{gene}}=0.10.

  
  


This mutation makes the child worse. Mutation introduces variation; it does not promise improvement.


The example changes only gene 6 in child 1 from row 5 to row 6. All other genes and the other three children remain unchanged in our worked generation. The chromosome becomes 32748652 and fitness drops from 23 to 21. Choosing a different replacement row would produce a different score; mutation samples a change instead of testing all changes and taking the best. With independent probability 0.10 per gene, a child may have zero, one, or multiple mutations. This is different from a probability of mutating the child once. Select the new row from the other seven values if a triggered mutation is required to actually change the gene. Source: original Lecture 12 mutation mechanism, with a course example chosen to demonstrate a fitness decrease.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Replacement and Elitism
Cross B and C at the same cut. Of the four children, mutate only child 1 from B and A.


How can we keep the best fitness from dropping?  Elitism: copy the best candidate unchanged, then fill the remaining slots with children.


Keeping one elite protects the best score, not the average. Keep the population size fixed.


This figure completes the same generation used on the selection, crossover, and mutation slides. The selected pairs B,A and B,C are both cut after gene 3. Only child 32748552 mutates, becoming 32748652. The offspring fitness values are consequently 21,22,22,18. The original best chromosome A has fitness 24 and is absent from those four children. In a size-four population with one elite, copy A unchanged and generate or retain only three children. This is a variant of full generational replacement, not an extra fifth individual. Protect an independent copy from later mutation. A separate best-ever record can preserve the returned answer even when the population itself loses it; elitism additionally keeps that candidate in the population. Source: original course continuation of the AIMA example and the notebook’s one-elite policy.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Genetic Algorithm Pseudocode
N is population size; G is the generation budget. EVALUATE assigns fitness F. This version keeps one elite.

  GENETIC(N, G, target)
  P <- RANDOM_POP(N); EVALUATE(P)
  best <- COPY(ARGMAX_F(P))
  for generation in 1 .. G:
  if F(best) = target: break
  next <- [COPY(ARGMAX_F(P))]
  while SIZE(next) < N:
  a, b <- SELECT(P), SELECT(P)
  child <- MUTATE(CROSSOVER(a, b))
  APPEND(next, child)
  P <- next; EVALUATE(P)
  if MAX_F(P) > F(best): best <- COPY(ARGMAX_F(P))
  return best


ARGMAX_F returns a highest-fitness candidate; MAX_F returns its score. For eight queens, target = 28.


P and next are populations; a and b are parents; child is a newly created chromosome. COPY makes an independent snapshot. N should be at least two for one-elite reproduction to produce new candidates. SELECT implements a stated selection rule, and CROSSOVER and MUTATE must preserve the chosen encoding without altering the parents. Mutation parameters can be passed to MUTATE or stored as configuration. All individuals are evaluated before comparison, including those produced in the last allowed generation. Returning best does not mean target was reached. With valid elitism, the best in P is already a best-ever candidate; the explicit best variable makes the return contract clear and remains useful in variants without elitism. Source: course pseudocode based on AIMA and the existing notebook, not a transcription of its implementation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Different Encoding: Permutations
Require each row number to appear exactly once. A permutation then prevents both row and column conflicts; only diagonals remain.


Operators must preserve the encoding. The notebook uses a permutation-preserving crossover, not ordinary one-point crossover.


The four-gene example is only an encoding check, not a claimed four-queens solution. Repeated rows were allowed under the earlier row-vector encoding, so 1212 was an encodable candidate there; it is invalid specifically under the permutation encoding. For eight queens there are 8! permutations instead of 8^8 unrestricted row vectors. The existing genetic_8_queen notebook uses random.sample(range(n),n) to create permutations and currently sets n=30. It also changes selection: tournament selection samples a group and chooses its highest-fitness member. The notebook samples ten candidates per tournament. That rule does not divide fitness by the population’s total. Source: existing genetic_8_queen.ipynb and standard representation constraints.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Permutation-Preserving Crossover
Copy a segment from A, then fill the gaps using unused values in B’s order.

  
  
  



Keep 7, 1, 8 fixed. B contributes 3, 2, 5, 4, 6.


The child is a permutation, but its fitness is 25, below A’s 27.



This example follows the supplied notebook’s implementation exactly: copy parent1[start:end], take unused values from parent2 in left-to-right order, then fill the child’s empty positions from left to right. With human column labels 3 through 5, the zero-based Python slice is [2:5]. The notebook’s comment calls this Order Crossover (OX), but its implementation does not use the cyclic fill order of some textbook OX definitions; describe the actual operation rather than relying on that abbreviation. In the figures, rows use labels 1 through 8. Subtract one from every row value when comparing with the notebook’s zero-based encoding; pairwise conflicts do not change. Source: genetic_8_queen.ipynb crossover function. These illustrative parents and scores are original course examples.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Mutation Depends on the Encoding
A permutation cannot freely replace one value: it could create a duplicate. Swap mutation exchanges two positions instead.








Row-vector example
Permutation notebook




0.10 chance per gene to replace its row
0.30 chance per child to swap two entries


Several genes may change independently
At most one swap per child




These rates describe different events. A swap preserves the permutation, but may improve or worsen fitness.


For this child, swapping the values at human columns 2 and 6 changes fitness from 25 to 26. Both positions must be distinct. The notebook’s mutate function draws one random value to decide whether to swap, then samples two positions. Thus mutation_rate=0.3 does not mean that each queen mutates with probability 0.3. By contrast, independent per-gene probability 0.1 on eight genes gives probability 1-0.9^8 of at least one triggered change, about 0.57. Parameter values cannot be compared meaningfully without knowing their events. Source: original lecture’s per-gene mutation and existing notebook’s swap mutation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Diversity and Stopping
Diversity means having different chromosomes in the population. Strong selection can make the population increasingly similar.


Can crossover alone create a new chromosome from identical parents?  No. Mutation can introduce variation that is missing from the population.


Stop at the target fitness or a time / generation budget.
Keep the best candidate; report whether it actually reached the target.
Compare several random seeds, including unsuccessful runs.


Premature convergence means losing diversity and concentrating around candidates before finding a sufficiently good solution. Mutation can help, but does not guarantee escape or success in a finite run. Excessive mutation can also disrupt useful combinations. Elitism preserves a maximum score but does not force average fitness to increase. Tournament size and fitness scaling affect selection pressure; larger tournaments generally favor the strongest candidates more aggressively. A generation limit is a resource limit, not evidence that the problem has no solution. Source: AIMA discussion of genetic search and the notebook’s exploration questions.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways








Design choice
Worked example
Existing notebook




Encoding
Row vector; repeats allowed
Permutation of rows


Parent selection
Fitness-weighted sampling
Tournament: best of 10 random candidates


Crossover
Exchange tails at one cut
Copy a segment, fill unused values


Mutation
Replace individual genes
Swap two positions


Replacement
Full replacement can lose the best
Keep one elite




Define the encoding and fitness first. Selection favors, crossover combines, and mutation varies candidates; none alone guarantees a solution.

Code: Genetic N-Queens notebook
Notebook defaults: n=30, target fitness 435, row indices 0 to 29.
Asset credits

A tournament selects the highest-fitness member of a randomly sampled group, not necessarily the best individual in the entire population. The notebook’s tournament size is ten, so its population must have at least ten candidates. Its default population size and generation limit are each 1000; these are experiment settings, not requirements of a GA. The file name retains eight queens even though the current experiment uses thirty. Slides explain the operators; runnable code remains on its own page. Source: genetic_8_queen.ipynb and original Lecture 12. The broader lesson applies beyond queens: representations should enforce structural constraints, while fitness measures the remaining objective.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Variables, Domains, and the Graph
Let X_A be A’s slot, with remaining domain D_A; use the same notation for B, C, and D.

A constraint graph has one node per variable. An edge joins two variables constrained together; here, each edge means different slots.

There is no B-C edge: B and C may share a slot. This is not a search tree or a travel map.


The graph encodes X_A != X_B, X_A != X_C, X_B != X_D, X_C != X_D. Node labels abbreviate the variables. Unary availability restrictions are stored in domains and need no graph edge. There is also no A-D edge. This simple graph view applies to binary constraints; constraints involving more variables need an additional representation or a decomposition. Source: AIMA constraint graphs and the course exam model.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Complete and Consistent
Complete: all variables have values. Consistent: assigned values are in their domains and violate no constraint among them.
Tuples below list (X_A,X_B,X_C,X_D) in that order.










Assignment
Complete?
Consistent?




X_A=1,\ X_B=2
No
Yes


X_A=1,\ X_B=1
No
No: AB


(1,2,2,2)
Yes
No: BD, CD


(1,2,2,3)
Yes
Yes







Only the last row is a solution. A consistent partial assignment is not yet a solution.


Reveal answers one row at a time. Partial means at least one variable remains unassigned. In the third row, B and C sharing 2 is allowed; D sharing their value violates both incident constraints. Consistency of a partial assignment does not assert that a completion exists; the later triangle gives a counterexample. Source: course exam example and standard CSP terminology.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Domain-Reduction Trace
Constraint propagation removes values ruled out by the constraints. A singleton domain contains just one value, so that value is forced.

  
  
  
  



X_A=1 removes 1 from D_B and D_C.


X_B=2 removes 2 from D_D.


X_D=3 removes 3 from D_C. Solution: (1,2,2,3).



Gold marks the variable causing the current reduction; teal marks affected neighbors. Initially: {1}, {1,2}, {1,2,3}, {2,3}. After A: {1}, {2}, {2,3}, {2,3}. After B: {1}, {2}, {2,3}, {3}. After D: {1}, {2}, {2}, {3}. All four inequalities hold at the end. Every deduction was forced by the original requirements, and this example has a unique solution. Propagation does not solve every CSP. Lecture 14 formalizes consistency. Source: course scheduling model.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One More Conflict
A student now takes both B and C. Add the rule X_B\ne X_C, keeping the same availability restrictions.

  
  


Can all requirements still be satisfied?


No. A, B, and D force slots 1, 2, and 3. C has no remaining value: D_C=\varnothing.


The new diagonal B-C edge is pink. The previous deductions forcing A=1, B=2, D=3 remain valid after adding a constraint. C must now differ from all three. This proves infeasibility, not just a failed attempt. A fourth slot for C, with C allowed to use it, would repair the model; ignoring the new shared student would not. If an empty domain instead follows a tentative search choice, it rules out that branch, not automatically the entire original problem. Source: course exam example.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Consistent Start Can Still Fail
text:
A Consistent Start Can Still Fail
A separate example has three exams, all conflicting with each other, and only slots 1 and 2. Assign X_A=1.

  
  


Consistent so far: X_A=1 violates no constraint among assigned exams. Can we assign B and C too, while satisfying every constraint?


No. B and C would both need slot 2, but they conflict. Starting with X_A=2 fails symmetrically.


This is a new three-variable model, not a modification of the four-exam example. Each initial domain is {1,2}. With only A assigned, no binary constraint has two assigned endpoints, so the partial assignment is consistent. There is nevertheless no extension. At the completely unassigned state, each value even has support on each individual edge, yet there is no joint solution; leave formal arc consistency to Lecture 14. Source: course triangle example.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Feasibility and Preferences








Kind
Meaning
Scheduling example




Hard constraint
Must be satisfied
No simultaneous exams for a shared student


Soft preference
Ranks feasible assignments
Prefer fewer exams in slot 3



For n exams with slots X_1,\ldots,X_n, one possible objective is
\min_X \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{X_i=3\}\quad\text{subject to all hard constraints}.
The indicator is 1 when exam i uses slot 3, and 0 otherwise.

A basic CSP seeks feasibility. Constraint optimization also compares feasible assignments.


The objective counts exams, not unique students. X denotes the vector of exam slots. This is a general scheduling extension; our four-exam instance has only one feasible assignment, so a preference cannot select a different solution without changing that model. A lower objective never excuses a hard-constraint violation. Source: existing lecture’s feasibility-versus-preference distinction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rows, Columns, and Blocks
A Sudoku unit is a row, column, or block. Each unit has an \operatorname{AllDifferent} constraint.

  
  
  



The same cell also participates in its column constraint.


And its block constraint. There are 27 units: 9 rows, 9 columns, 9 blocks.



A3 is gold throughout. Other cells in the displayed unit are teal. Each peer’s given digit forbids that same digit at A3. A peer is another cell sharing at least one unit; overlapping memberships are not separate variables. A cell has 20 distinct peers in standard Sudoku. The unit view avoids an unreadably dense graph. Source: original Lecture 13 row, column, and subgrid diagrams, consolidated into an animated draw.io figure.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Candidate Values for A3
Exclude digits assigned to A3’s peers: its row, column, or block.


Which values remain in D_{\mathrm{A3}}?


D_{\mathrm{A3}}=\{1,\ldots,9\}\setminus\{3,5,6,7,8,9\}=\{1,2,4\}.
Remaining candidates are not guaranteed to extend to a solution.


Row A excludes 3,5,7. Column 3 excludes 8. The upper-left block excludes 3,5,6,8,9. Repeated excluded digits are removed once. Set-minus means remove the listed values. Do not insert the known solution’s 4 simply because the puzzle is familiar; this local test leaves three candidates. Source: original puzzle and the candidate example in sudoku.ipynb.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Forced Values and Propagation
Using the same clues, the center cell E5 has only candidate 5.

  
  


E2 shares E5’s row and currently allows \{2,5\}. What follows?


Set E5 = 5, remove 5 from its peers, then E2 = 2 is forced. A deduction can trigger another deduction.


E5’s row excludes 1,3,4,8; its column excludes 1,2,6,7,8,9; its center block excludes 2,3,6,8. Their union leaves only 5. E2 originally allows 2 or 5. The figure highlights these two cells and their shared row; a full propagation operation also updates E5’s other column and block peers. These are forced deductions, not guesses. An unresolved empty domain signals contradiction; a singleton is forced. Source: original course Sudoku puzzle.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Search and Propagation
If propagation stalls, search may choose a variable and try a remaining value. A3’s local candidates illustrate possible branches:


Propagate: make deductions forced by current constraints.
Backtrack: undo a tentative choice if its branch fails, then try another.


For m blanks, there are at most 9^m complete fillings before constraints are used. This puzzle has m=51; pruning avoids exploring many of them.


The branches are alternatives, not simultaneous assignments or solved puzzles. Another variable may be a better choice; ordering heuristics belong to Lecture 15. The 9^m count is a loose count of complete fillings, not measured runtime or a tight solver bound. Fixed variable order gives at most nine value branches per level; do not multiply by the remaining variable count and explore many orders of identical assignments. Backtracking must restore all branch-specific domain changes. Source: original Beamer search and propagation content, with the assignment-count distinction made explicit.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Modeling Practice: A Lab Schedule
Experiments P, Q, R each take one of three equal, nonoverlapping slots \{1,2,3\}.


Write the variables, domains, and constraints. Give one valid schedule and one invalid schedule, with a reason.


Let students formulate the model before revealing the next slide. Each experiment lasts exactly one slot. Equal, nonoverlapping slots make precedence a strict inequality on slot indices. Nothing says P and R share equipment; do not invent that constraint. Source: existing Lecture 13 lab-scheduling practice.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Lab Schedule: A Formulation
X_P,X_Q,X_R are the slots. D_P=D_Q=\{1,2,3\} and D_R=\{2,3\}.
Constraints: X_P<X_Q and X_Q\ne X_R.




Assignment (X_P,X_Q,X_R)
Why invalid?




(2,1,3)
P does not finish before Q starts


(1,2,2)
Q and R need the shared equipment together




Multiple solutions are allowed; do not invent additional constraints.


The figure shows two valid schedules, not every solution. (2,3,2) is also valid because P and R may coincide: the only equipment conflict is Q-R. This catches an unstated AllDifferent assumption. Domains encode R’s unary restriction directly. Source: original course lab activity.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
N-Queens as a CSP
As in Lecture 12, let Q_i be the queen’s row in column i, with domain D_i=\{1,\ldots,N\}.




For each pair of columns i<j:
Different rows: Q_i\ne Q_j.
No diagonal attack: |Q_i-Q_j|\ne|i-j|.
One variable per column already enforces one queen in each column.


Same encoding, different formulation: instead of rewarding fewer conflicts, the CSP requires zero conflicts.


The figure uses N=4 for readability; equations apply to general N. It is a satisfying example, not the conflicted eight-queens chromosome from Lecture 12. Diagonal attack means the absolute row difference equals the absolute column difference. The unrestricted row-vector encoding needs row inequalities; a permutation enforces distinct rows structurally. A Boolean variable per square would need additional cardinality constraints such as exactly one queen per column. Source: AIMA N-queens CSP formulation and the previous lecture’s representation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways







Modeling question
What to specify




What decisions must be made?
Variables


What values may each decision take?
Domains, including fixed values


Which combinations are allowed?
Every required constraint


What counts as success?
A complete assignment satisfying all constraints




Consistency so far does not guarantee a valid completion.
Propagation removes impossible values; search handles unresolved choices.
A solver answers the model we give it, including its assumptions.


Next: how consistency checks prune domains systematically, and how to combine them with search.

Asset credits

An exit question: if the lab model returns (2,3,2), is the solver wrong? No, because P and R have no stated equipment conflict. A real-world mismatch may require changing the model rather than the search algorithm. Lecture 14 covers consistency and Lecture 15 covers CSP search with the Sudoku notebook. Source: AIMA and this lecture’s worked models.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Pruning Candidate Values
In a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP), propagation removes domain values that cannot belong to a solution.


Last time, forced exam slots triggered further deletions.
Today: check supports systematically, even before a variable is forced.
AC-3 (Arc Consistency Algorithm 3) manages these checks for binary constraints, which involve two variables.


Connect to the four-exam model from Lecture 13. Its final domains are all singleton, but this is not guaranteed for every problem. Domain consistency describes properties of the remaining candidate sets, not just whether the currently assigned variables conflict. The 3 in AC-3 identifies an algorithm, not 3-consistency. Unary restrictions are handled first. Suggested pacing: foundations and REVISE about 10 minutes; AC-3 and queue trace about 12; limits, stronger consistency, and cost about 8; notebook bridge and summary about 3; leave roughly 15 minutes for the AC-3 notebook. Sources: original Lecture 14 Beamer and AIMA, Figure 6.3.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Node Consistency
A unary constraint restricts one variable. Node consistency means every remaining value satisfies all its unary constraints.
Let D_X denote the domain of age X, with the rule X\ge18.

  
  


Keep D_X=\{20,25,30\}. Having just one valid value is not enough if invalid values remain.

If filtering empties a domain, the current problem or search branch has no solution.

Node consistency is also called 1-consistency. Filtering deletes every value that violates a unary constraint; it does not select a single age. An empty domain after an optional search choice rules out that branch. An empty domain using only the original restrictions rules out the original CSP. Definition checked against the CS50 AI constraint satisfaction notes: https://cs50.harvard.edu/extension/ai/2020/fall/notes/3/ .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Supports for a Binary Constraint
For X<Y, a support for x\in D_X is a value y\in D_Y that makes the constraint true. Lines below join allowed pairs.

  
  
  



X=3 stays: Y=4 is a support because 3<4.


X=4 goes: no value in D_Y is greater than 4.



Original Beamer example. Initial domains: X={1,2,3,4}, Y={2,3,4}. There are six allowed pairs. Every remaining X value needs at least one support, not a distinct support and not compatibility with every Y value. Several X values may use Y=4 as support. A support is a local witness for this one constraint, not a proof that x belongs to a complete solution.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Direction Matters
An arc (X,Y) asks whether each value of X has support in Y. Revising it can shrink X’s domain only.




Directed check
After removing 4 from D_X




(X,Y)
Each x\in\{1,2,3\} has a larger y


(Y,X)
Each y\in\{2,3,4\} has a smaller x




A binary CSP is arc-consistent when every directed arc passes. Reverse the check, not the rule: it is still X<Y.


Node-consistent binary CSPs that satisfy both directions have 2-consistency. Treat multiple constraints on a pair as their combined allowed-pair relation. In the reverse check, C_YX(y,x) expresses x<y, not y<x. Y=2 can use X=1; Y=3 can use X=1 or 2; Y=4 can use X=1,2,3. No Y value is deleted in this example. See https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/csp/filtering.html .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
REVISE: Remove Unsupported Values
D[i] is the current domain of X_i; C_{ij}(x,y) is true exactly when the pair is allowed.

  REVISE(i, j, D, C):
  changed ← false
  for x in COPY(D[i]):
  supported ← EXISTS y in D[j] with C[i,j](x,y)
  if not supported:
  REMOVE(D[i], x)
  changed ← true
  return changed


COPY lets us delete safely without skipping values during iteration.
The return value means “a deletion occurred,” not “a solution exists.”


REVISE mutates D[i], leaves D[j] unchanged, and returns a Boolean change flag. EXISTS stops once one supporting y is found. For the preceding example, REVISE(X,Y) deletes 4 and returns true; an immediate second call makes no change and returns false. The notebook collects values to delete in a separate list, an equally valid way to avoid changing a set during iteration. Pseudocode adapted from the supplied Beamer and AIMA Figure 6.3: https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
AC-3: Manage the Pending Checks
Q stores directed arcs awaiting revision. NEIGHBORS(i) lists variables constrained with X_i.

  AC3(D, C):
  if any D[i] is empty: return false
  Q ← queue of all directed arcs (both directions)
  while Q is not empty:
  (i, j) ← POP_FRONT(Q)
  if REVISE(i, j, D, C):
  if D[i] is empty: return false
  for k in NEIGHBORS(i) except j:
  ENQUEUE_IF_ABSENT(Q, (k, i))
  return true


A deletion may invalidate neighbors’ supports. true means no empty domain was found, not that a solution was found.


Use a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue for the trace. Any fair worklist order works; FIFO is not essential for correctness. ENQUEUE_IF_ABSENT avoids duplicate pending arcs, with a set of pending pairs as one implementation. The notebook allows duplicate pending arcs, which can do extra work but does not invalidate propagation. All domains change in place. Initialize with both directions for each combined binary constraint. Skip j on requeue: a removed value in D[i] had no support in D[j], so it could not have been the supporting value for any value in D[j]. This assumes the reverse arc checks the same relation with swapped argument positions. AIMA Figure 6.3 and Berkeley CS188 filtering notes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
AC-3 Trace: First Pass
Rules: A<B and B<C. The queue front is on the left; add an arc only if it is not already pending.

  
  
  
  



1. (A,B) deletes 3 from D_A: no larger B.


2. (B,A) deletes 1 from D_B: no smaller A.


3. (B,C) deletes 3 from D_B; put (A,B) back.



The initial domains are A={1,2,3}, B={1,2,3}, C={2,3}. Initially Q=[(A,B),(B,A),(B,C),(C,B)]. After step1 Q=[(B,A),(B,C),(C,B)], domains A12 B123 C23. After step2 Q=[(B,C),(C,B)], domains A12 B23 C23; (C,B) is already pending. After step3 Q=[(C,B),(A,B)], domains A12 B2 C23. Ask why A=2, which had support earlier, now needs another check. The figures show the most recently checked arc in teal, its first variable’s reduced domain in gold, and the queue after that check.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
AC-3 Trace: Rechecking
Continue the same problem and queue. A previously consistent arc may need checking again when its supporting domain shrinks.

  
  
  



4. (C,B) deletes 2 from D_C: B=2 requires C>2.


5. (A,B) deletes 2 from D_A: its old support B=3 is gone.



The queue is empty. Here we obtain a solution: A=1,\ B=2,\ C=3, and both inequalities hold.


After step4, Q=[(A,B)], domains A12 B2 C3. After step5, Q=[], domains A1 B2 C3. This instance happens to become fully solved. Checking (A,B) only once would leave the unsupported value A=2 behind. Domain values never reappear during this run; backtracking, which can restore saved domains, is a separate operation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why Incoming Arcs Return
When checking (B,C) removes 3 from D_B, A may lose a support.


Recheck (A,B): it asks whether A’s values still have support in B.
Checking (B,A) would prune B instead, missing the effect on A.
If an affected arc is already in Q, one pending copy is enough.


When D_i shrinks, reconsider arcs into X_i: neighbors were relying on its old values.


Why exclude the immediate reverse (C,B) from new enqueues after REVISE(B,C)? The deleted value B=3 had no compatible C value, so no C value was relying on it. In our trace (C,B) was already pending from initialization, so it is still checked when it reaches the front. Do not remove an existing queue item merely because the requeue rule would not newly add it. The relation is unchanged throughout: B<C.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Arc Consistency Has Limits
Three variables have domains \{1,2\}. Every pair must differ: A\ne B, A\ne C, and B\ne C.

  
  

Before any choice, every arc is consistent: 1 has support 2, and 2 has support 1.

Yet there is no solution. Choosing A=1 forces B=C=2; choosing A=2 fails symmetrically.


This is the two-value triangle, not the earlier chain. AC-3 on the original domains makes no deletions and returns true despite unsatisfiability. Different neighbor checks can use supports that cannot coexist globally. Once A is assigned, propagation would eventually produce an empty domain; the highlighted equal B and C values show the contradiction before that final deletion. The original graph is node- and arc-consistent, but not path-consistent. Source: AIMA and standard CSP consistency examples.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Stronger Consistency
Path consistency (3-consistency): every consistent assignment to two variables can be extended to any third variable.


k-consistency: every consistent k-1-variable assignment extends to any other variable.
Strong k-consistency: all levels 1,2,\ldots,k hold.


Stronger checks detect more contradictions, but cost more.


The pair A=1, B=2 satisfies its own inequality but has no extension to C. Path-consistency algorithms can remove allowed pairs, not just individual domain values. For binary CSPs this is the usual 3-consistency interpretation. Strong n-consistency, where n is the number of variables, permits successive extension without backtracking, but enforcing it is generally too expensive. Do not call every level above 2 path consistency. Source: original Beamer k-consistency definition and https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/csp/filtering.html .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Work and Termination
Domains are finite and only shrink. New queue entries are added only after a deletion, so the process eventually stops.
Let e be the number of directed arcs, and d the largest initial domain size.







Work
Basic AC-3 bound




One REVISE: try up to d supports for each of d values
O(d^2)


Rechecks of one arc as its supporting domain shrinks
O(d)


All directed arcs, with duplicate pending entries avoided
O(ed^3)





For this chain, what are e and d? e=4, d=3.


Each supporting domain can lose values on at most d separate occasions, and an arc is initially present once. Duplicate suppression keeps at most e arcs pending; queue storage is O(e), in addition to the domains and constraint representation. The simple REVISE implementation scans up to d squared pairs assuming an O(1) constraint test. This analysis is for basic AC-3, not an optimal arc-consistency algorithm. In our worked trace there are five REVISE calls, not e*d^3 calls. Reference: Berkeley CS188 filtering notes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Notebook’s Sum Constraints
All four variables initially allow digits \{0,1,\ldots,9\}. Each edge requires the indicated sum.


Can we freely combine values? No: a=0, b=2 violates a+b=3.

The notebook starts with 4 directed checks. Full AC-3 uses 8, including each reverse check. Both give these domains for this example.

Use the linked AC-3 notebook, keeping implementation details there. The supplied directed constraint triples are (a,b,3), (b,c,4), (c,d,2), (d,a,1); add (b,a,3), (c,b,4), (d,c,2), (a,d,1) for a standard bidirectional initialization. The notebook’s existing explanation discusses this distinction. Final domains with either list for this particular system: a={0,1}, b={2,3}, c={1,2}, d={0,1}. Exactly two solutions, in (a,b,c,d) order: (0,3,1,1) and (1,2,2,0). Fix a=0 and run ac3 again on those restricted domains to force b3,c1,d1. Calling solve again would recreate full initial domains. The four-check behavior must not be presented as generally equivalent to full AC-3.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Node consistency: remove values that fail a unary constraint.
Arc consistency: each remaining value has support across each binary constraint.
REVISE: prune the first variable’s domain.
AC-3: revisit affected incoming arcs after deletions.
Nonempty domains are not a proof of a solution.


Propagation removes impossible candidates. Search may still be needed to choose values that work together.

Open the AC-3 notebook
Asset credits

In the notebook, follow the domain changes, inspect why each removed value lacks support, compare the original queue with both directions, and then restrict a to 0 and propagate again. Keep the actual Python functions and their answers in the notebook, rather than duplicating them here. Lecture 15 adds search and variable/value ordering.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
After Constraint Propagation
A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) asks for values that satisfy every constraint. Propagation reduces domains, but may leave choices.







Remaining domains
Next step




Any domain is empty
Reject the current branch


Every domain is a singleton (one value)
Verify the complete assignment against every constraint


Some domains have multiple values
Choose a variable and try a value




Backtracking search tries a choice, continues recursively, and undoes the choice if the branch fails.

An empty domain after a tentative choice rules out that branch. Search can still try other choices.

Bridge from Lecture 14: AC-3 can return true without finding a solution. For node-consistent binary CSPs, if arc consistency has left every domain singleton, those values satisfy every binary constraint. The general solver should still validate all original constraints, especially when propagation handles only a subset. Start from a valid set of domains and fixed clues. Suggested pacing: worked search and basic pseudocode about 9 minutes, inference and restoration about 8, ordering and improved search about 10, advanced overview and notebook bridge about 6, leaving roughly 15 minutes for Sudoku. Sources: original Lecture 15 Beamer and AIMA’s CSP chapter.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Three-Exam Search Problem
Exams A, B, C all share students, so every pair must use different slots.
D_A=D_B=\{1,2\},\qquad D_C=\{2,3\}.


If we try C=2, have we violated a constraint among assigned exams? No. A and B are still unassigned.


This is a separate three-exam example, with C allowed slots 2 and 3. Its two solutions, in (A,B,C) order, are (1,2,3) and (2,1,3). The initial domains are arc-consistent. C=2 is locally legal as a partial assignment but has no completion. We intentionally start with C and try 2 first to show how backtracking recovers. A different ordering can find the solution sooner.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Backtracking Trace
Choose variables in the order C, A, B, trying smaller values first. The tree records choices; the triangle records constraints.

  
  
  
  
  



1. Try C=2.


2. A=1 leaves B no legal value. A=2 also conflicts with C.


3. Undo A and C, then try C=3.


4. A=1,\ B=2,\ C=3 satisfies every constraint.



No propagation is used in this first trace. At C=2, A=1 is the first legal value. B=1 violates A!=B, and B=2 violates B!=C. Return to A, undo A=1, and test A=2, which violates A!=C. A’s values are exhausted, so return to C, undo C=2, and try C=3. A=1 is legal; B=1 fails against A, while B=2 succeeds. A rejected candidate is never added to the assignment. The pink branch summarizes the failed checks; gold marks the current choice, and teal marks the successful path.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Assignment Order and Commutativity
Assigning A=1 then B=2 gives the same partial assignment as assigning them in the opposite order.

Let n count variables and d be the largest domain size. After k assignments, n-k variables remain.

Branching over variable-value pairs gives up to (n-k)d choices.
Selecting one variable first gives up to d value choices.


One variable per level avoids repeated assignment orders.


Commutativity concerns the resulting assignment for distinct variables, not an assertion that every ordering produces the same search effort or the same first solution. Before constraint pruning, an unconstrained n-variable problem with d values has d^n full assignments; considering every assignment order duplicates each one n! times. Standard CSP backtracking selects one variable at a node. A dynamic variable-selection rule is also valid. Source: supplied Lecture 15 Beamer and AIMA backtracking formulation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Basic Backtracking
a is a consistent partial assignment, D stores domains, and C stores constraints. Start with a=\{\}.

  BACKTRACK(a, D, C):
  if a is complete: return COPY(a)
  X ← SELECT_UNASSIGNED(a)
  for v in D[X]:
  if CONSISTENT(X, v, a, C):
  a[X] ← v
  result ← BACKTRACK(a, D, C)
  if result != FAILURE: return result
  REMOVE(a, X)
  return FAILURE

CONSISTENT checks constraints whose variables have all received values. REMOVE undoes X’s tentative assignment.

This is depth-first search over partial assignments. Each recursive call removes its own failed choice before returning failure. Domains are unchanged in this basic version. The invariant is that the current assignment violates no fully instantiated constraint; thus a complete assignment is a solution. COPY protects the returned dictionary from later mutations. If every value for X fails, return to the caller’s choice. Source: original course algorithm and AIMA Figure 6.5, https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Search with Inference
After trying X=v, restrict D_X to \{v\}, then remove values ruled out by the constraints.







Check
What it does after a choice




Check assigned values
Reject an immediate conflict with earlier assignments


Forward checking
Delete incompatible values from unassigned neighbors


Maintaining arc consistency (MAC)
Propagate deletions through the remaining constraint graph



AC-3 (Arc Consistency Algorithm 3) can implement MAC by continuing to recheck affected arcs.

Forward checking looks one step from the new assignment. MAC also follows the effects of those deletions.


For a binary CSP, forward checking revises incoming arcs (Y,X) for unassigned neighbors Y of the chosen X, without propagating consequences between those neighbors. MAC restores arc consistency after each search choice. If the parent domains were already arc-consistent, AC-3 can start with incoming arcs to the newly restricted X. Otherwise initialize all directed arcs. Full propagation costs extra work per choice but may avoid much larger failed subtrees; neither method is universally faster. Sources: course search/inference material, AIMA CSP chapter, and Berkeley CS188 filtering notes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Forward Checking and MAC
Return to the three exams. Every edge requires different slots. Try C=2.

  
  
  



Forward checking: D_A=D_B=\{1\}. Neither domain is empty yet.


MAC: revise (A,B). Value 1 has no unequal support, so D_A=\varnothing.



Propagation detects that the choice C=2 has no completion, before search assigns A and B.


At the first state, C is assigned but A and B remain unassigned. After basic forward checking they have forced values, but that method itself has not tested their mutual inequality. A solver may perform an additional check when assigning those singletons; MAC detects the conflict immediately by propagating between them. REVISE(A,B) leaves A empty while B remains {1}; stop on that first empty domain. This example explains a benefit of stronger propagation without claiming it always wins on runtime. The original domains are A12 B12 C23 and are arc-consistent before the choice.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Restoring a Failed Branch
The failed choice C=2 deleted values from several domains. Changing C alone does not repair the search state.

  
  


Restore the parent’s domains, then try C=3. The deletions belonged to the discarded branch.

Two common implementations: give each branch its own deep copy, or record deletions and undo them on return.

Restored domains are A={1,2}, B={1,2}, C={2,3}. Restoring to the parent means preserving earlier valid pruning, not blindly resetting to the original puzzle on every failure. Undo both assignments and domain changes when mutating shared state. A shallow dictionary copy that shares its sets does not isolate branches. The improved pseudocode uses branch-local deep copies, trading extra memory and copying work for simple state management.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Minimum Remaining Values
Minimum remaining values (MRV) selects the unassigned variable with the fewest current legal values.
A new four-exam example uses the edges shown below. All four exams are unassigned.


A, B, and D tie with 2 values. C has 3. Resolve a tie with another rule.

A singleton is forced. An empty domain signals failure. MRV often exposes difficult choices early.

Use current domains after filtering, not the size of the original unrestricted domains. A fixed order is still complete, but may postpone an important contradiction. MRV does not guarantee a smaller search tree on every instance. Here all four variables are unassigned and all pair constraints are inequalities. The domain sizes are A2, B2, C3, D2. Source: original variable-ordering material and https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/csp/ordering.html .

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Degree Tie-Breaker
For an MRV tie, the degree heuristic prefers the variable constraining the most other unassigned variables.


Which of A, B, and D should be selected? A: degrees are A: 3, B: 2, D: 1.


Most constrained: fewest values. Most constraining: most unassigned neighbors.


The graph has AB, AC, AD, BC. All unassigned neighbor counts are A3, B2, C2, D1, but C is not in the MRV tie. Count constraints to unassigned variables in the remaining problem, rather than always using the original graph degree. Further ties can be broken deterministically. This is a standard heuristic, not a guarantee of the most effective choice for every instance. Source: original Lecture 15 and AIMA.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Least-Constraining Value
Least-constraining value (LCV) preserves the most neighbor options. In our three-exam problem, select C and compare forward-checking deletions.




C’s value
New D_A
New D_B
Deletions




2
\{1\}
\{1\}
2


3
\{1,2\}
\{1,2\}
0




LCV tries C=3 first, avoiding the earlier failed branch.


This uses a one-step forward-checking score: add deletions across the unassigned neighbor domains. There are two deletions for C=2, one in A and one in B; there are none for C=3. More expensive LCV estimates may run fuller inference per candidate. Such simulations need copies or correct restoration as well. LCV changes value order; it does not discard the other values if the first attempt fails. It is particularly useful when seeking one solution. Source: original Lecture 15 and Berkeley CS188 ordering notes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Backtracking with Heuristics and AC-3
For a binary CSP, SOLVE uses domains as its state. CHECK_SOLUTION verifies every constraint and returns the assignment or FAILURE.

  SOLVE(D, C):
  if any D[X] is empty: return FAILURE
  if all domains are singleton: return CHECK_SOLUTION(D,C)
  X ← MRV_WITH_DEGREE(D, C)
  for v in LCV_ORDER(X, D, C):
  child ← DEEP_COPY(D)
  child[X] ← {v}
  if AC3(child, C):
  result ← SOLVE(child, C)
  if result != FAILURE: return result
  return FAILURE


Each branch gets its own domains. If it fails, discard that copy and try the next value using the intact parent state.


MRV_WITH_DEGREE selects a variable with more than one remaining value, since singleton variables are already fixed in this domain-based representation. Start with unary constraints enforced. AC3 checks all directed arcs in this version, so it need not assume the input state is already arc-consistent. Inference returning true permits recursion but does not establish success. Every branch strictly fixes a previously nonsingleton variable, so the finite search terminates and is complete if all domain values are tried when necessary. Unlike the basic algorithm, explicit assignment undo is unnecessary because state is isolated in child. The notebook implements this copied-domain search pattern with singleton propagation and MRV, rather than full AC-3, degree tie-breaking, or LCV. Source: original improved search pseudocode and AIMA Figure 6.5, adapted to make branch restoration explicit.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Backjumping and Constraint Learning
A separate example assigns A=1,\ B=2,\ T=1, in that order. D_X=\{1,2\}, with rules X\ne A and X\ne B. T is unrelated.


Conflict set: earlier choices that explain a failure. Here it is \{A=1,B=2\}.
Backjumping: revisit the most recent decision in that set, so change B before trying an unrelated T value.
Constraint learning: remember a no-good, a partial assignment that cannot lead to a solution. Here, forbid the combination A=1,\ B=2.


X=1 conflicts with A=1 and X=2 conflicts with B=2. The original domain of X is exactly {1,2}, so neither value works and the two decisions jointly explain failure. T was assigned more recently than B but contributes nothing. Jump to B, undoing later choices, including T. Conflict-directed backjumping also combines reasons from deeper failed subtrees. Basic backjumping’s immediate dead ends are already caught by forward checking, while more elaborate learning can retain explanations for future search. This is an introductory overview. Source: AIMA’s freely available CSP chapter, https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/newchap05.pdf , section on intelligent backtracking.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Complete Search and Local Repair
A CSP can also be approached through the local-search methods from Lecture 11.








Method
Search state
How it handles conflicts




Backtracking
A partial assignment
Reject choices and return to earlier decisions


Min-conflicts
A complete assignment that may violate constraints
Change a conflicted variable to a value with fewer conflicts



Min-conflicts can solve large instances quickly, but may get stuck or need restarts.

For finite domains, exhaustive backtracking can prove that no solution exists. A failed local-search run generally cannot.


A min-conflicts step typically selects a conflicted variable, evaluates the number of constraint violations for its possible values, and chooses a minimum-conflict value with randomized tie handling as appropriate. Unlike backtracking, the current full assignment may be invalid. This reconnects the CSP formulation to local repair without introducing another code demo. Source: original Lecture 15 Other Improvements and AIMA min-conflicts search.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Sudoku Notebook
Each blank is a variable. Row, column, and 3\times3 box constraints forbid repeated digits.





is_valid: test a digit against its row, column, and box.
solve: choose the first blank, recurse, and reset it to zero after failure.
infer: remove an assigned digit from peer domains.
solve_reduce: propagate, select with MRV, and try copied domains.



For general search, a guess must restrict its domain, and a failed branch must restore the previous state.


The notebook uses the same clue pattern as Lecture 13. Use the live notebook to show the actual Python functions. Its plain solver scans in row-major order. The inference solver keeps fixed cells as singleton domains, propagates through a queue, then uses MRV and branch-local copies when guesses are needed. The supplied puzzle is solved within one search call through propagation; the empty-grid example exercises guessing, and a locally legal wrong clue demonstrates an unsatisfiable case. The displayed saved counts are recursive calls, not timing measurements. Sources: course Sudoku notebook and the Wikipedia-derived original clue pattern credited in Lecture 13.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Backtracking tries choices and returns when a branch fails.
Forward checking and MAC prune after each choice.
MRV chooses a variable with few remaining values.
The degree heuristic breaks ties using remaining neighbors.
LCV tries values that preserve more options.
Every failed branch must restore its assignments and domains.


A reliable solver combines correct state management with good branching choices and useful propagation.

Open the Sudoku notebook
Asset credits

Return to the notebook: identify a legality check, the recursive call, and the reset to zero. Then compare candidate deletions with the copied-domain branching logic. In the inference solver, child_domains[cell] = {n} records a guess before recursion; each failed child is discarded. A complete assignment still needs to satisfy all constraints. Keep the backjumping and local-repair overview brief to protect notebook time.

title: Sudoku as Constraint Search
Sudoku as Constraint Search
text:
Search When Propagation Stalls
solve_reduce first propagates on copied state. If every domain is singleton, the board is complete. Otherwise, minimum remaining values (MRV) chooses an unresolved cell with the fewest candidates. Values are tried in increasing order.
Each guess restricts a fresh child domain to {n}. The recursive call propagates that decision before making another guess. If it fails, discard the child and try the next value; the parent’s board and domains stay intact. The function returns False only after propagation fails or every candidate branch fails.

num_reduce = 0

def solve_reduce(puzzle, possible_values):
    global num_reduce
    num_reduce += 1
    copy_possible_values = copy.deepcopy(possible_values)
    copy_puzzle = copy.deepcopy(puzzle)
    if not propagate(copy_puzzle, copy_possible_values):
        return False
    unresolved = [cell for cell in all_cells
                  if len(copy_possible_values[cell]) > 1]
    if not unresolved:
        print(f"Solved. Recursive calls: {num_reduce:,}.")
        draw_puzzle(copy_puzzle)
        return True
    cell = min(unresolved, key=lambda cell: len(copy_possible_values[cell]))
    for n in sorted(copy_possible_values[cell]):
        child_domains = copy.deepcopy(copy_possible_values)
        child_domains[cell] = {n}
        if solve_reduce(copy_puzzle, child_domains):
            return True
    return False

One propagation pass can do many candidate checks, so recursive-call counts are not a direct timing comparison. The final True is the returned success flag.

solve_reduce(puzzle, possible_values)

text:
Test a Puzzle That Needs Guessing
An empty grid has no singleton domains, so propagation alone cannot start. The solver must restrict a guessed cell to one digit before recursion. It returns the first valid completion; an empty grid has many solutions.
Each recursive choice fixes one unresolved cell. Every candidate receives its own branch-local domains.

empty_puzzle = [[0] * 9 for _ in range(9)]
num_reduce = 0
solve_reduce(empty_puzzle, make_domains(empty_puzzle))

Solved. Recursive calls: 48.









True

title: Sudoku as Constraint Search
section: Reject a Locally Legal Wrong Clue
text:
Reject a Locally Legal Wrong Clue
Digit 1 is locally legal at (0, 2) in the starting puzzle: it does not immediately repeat a row, column, or box digit. Fixing it there nevertheless makes this puzzle unsatisfiable. A local legality check does not guarantee a full completion.
Here the added fixed clue leads to an empty domain during initial propagation, so the solver returns False. When guessing is needed, a failed branch instead returns to its parent; the whole search fails only if every branch fails. A failed local-search run would not provide the same no-solution guarantee.

assert is_valid(puzzle, 0, 2, 1)
no_solution = copy.deepcopy(puzzle)
no_solution[0][2] = 1
num_reduce = 0
result = solve_reduce(no_solution, make_domains(no_solution))
print("Solver returned:", result)
assert result is False

Solver returned: False

(Intro to) AI
section: What Does the Rule Actually Permit?
text:
What Does the Rule Actually Permit?


A lab’s access rule says:

If a person has a valid badge, the door unlocks.


Must the door stay locked for everyone without a valid badge?


No. The rule requires unlocking for badge holders. It leaves other cases open.





Invite the viewer to choose an answer before revealing it. Return to this question after introducing implication and again in the final policy activity.
The lecture moves from representation to evaluation, then to equivalent formulas and policy debugging. Allow time to work through the truth tables and pause at the translation and policy questions. The next lecture introduces entailment and proof procedures.
The access example describes a simplified Boolean decision for one person at one time. It does not prescribe a real building’s safety or emergency policy.
[Sources] - Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 7. - Public-domain OpenClipart robot: https://openclipart.org/detail/325789/robot-2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Logic and Propositions
Logic represents knowledge precisely and supports reasoning from it.
A proposition is a statement that is true or false once its context is fixed.



Sentence
A proposition?




“The lab door is unlocked now.”
Yes, even if we have not checked


“Two plus three equals six.”
Yes, and it is false


“Unlock the door!” / “Is it unlocked?”
No, a command / question


“x is greater than three.”
Needs a value for x to stand alone




Classical logic uses T = true, F = false. Not knowing the value does not create a third value.


Connect to constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs): logical formulas also accept some assignments and reject others. An agent can use such rules to represent requirements and infer consequences. A correctly evaluated formula may still represent the wrong requirement.
Fix the person, door, and time when natural language leaves them implicit. The open expression involving x is not a closed proposition by itself. Specifying x makes it evaluable. Quantified statements come later.
[Sources] - Russell and Norvig, AIMA, Chapter 7. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/propositional.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One Symbol, One Stable Meaning
An atom is a proposition we treat as indivisible.
For one person, at one access decision:



Symbol
Atomic proposition




B
The person has a valid badge


V
The person is an approved visitor


E
An emergency is active


D
The door unlocks




Propositional logic combines atoms using logical connectives. A truth assignment gives each atom a value, T or F.


Keep B, V, E, and D fixed throughout the access example. Generic truth tables use P and Q, which can stand for any propositions. A symbol names a statement, not a numerical quantity or a command.
If the person or time changes, a new statement may be needed. An atom can describe a complicated fact in English, but propositional logic does not inspect its internal structure.

NOT and AND

Negation (NOT): \neg P flips the value of P.
Conjunction (AND): P \land Q is true only when both inputs are true.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Inclusive OR and Exclusive OR
Disjunction (OR) means at least one. Exclusive OR (XOR) means exactly one.


\underbrace{B \lor V}_{\text{at least one}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{(B \lor V) \land \neg(B \land V)}_{\text{exactly one}}


An approved visitor may also have a badge. Use ordinary OR if either method, including both together, is acceptable.


Read every column as one assignment. The first column is the difference between inclusive and exclusive OR. XOR’s first factor rules out neither, and its second factor rules out both. Clarify an English “or” before formalizing it.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: An Access Condition, Step by Step
text:
An Access Condition, Step by Step
“A valid badge or approved visitor, and no active emergency.”

\varphi = (B \lor V) \land \neg E

\varphi (phi) names this condition. Try B=\text{false}, V=\text{true}, E=\text{false}.

  
  
  
  




B \lor V = \text{true}.




\neg E = \text{true}.




\varphi = \text{true}.




First translate authorization as B OR V, no emergency as NOT E, then combine them with AND. Parentheses group the authorization condition. Phi names a formula, not a new independently assigned atom.
Pause before evaluating. Each advance highlights the corresponding operation. Evaluate from the assigned leaves upward. The operation uses its immediate child values, not the English wording again.
If E changes to true, NOT E becomes false and the root becomes false, even though authorization remains true. This gives the next truth table a concrete row to check.

title:

(Intro to) AI
section: Negation Scope and De Morgan’s Laws
text:
Negation Scope and De Morgan’s Laws
“Not both” means at least one fails. “Neither” means both fail.




English
Formula
Equivalent formula




Not both
\neg(B \land V)
\neg B \lor \neg V


Neither
\neg(B \lor V)
\neg B \land \neg V




De Morgan: negate each part and swap AND with OR. The symbol \equiv means logical equivalence.


With a badge but no visitor approval, not both is true and neither is false. One assignment with different outputs disproves equivalence between those two requirements.
Each row of the table gives a De Morgan equivalence. Keep parentheses until negation scope is clear. The next slide verifies the first law for arbitrary propositions P and Q.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Implication Has One Violating Case
Implication: B \rightarrow D means “if valid badge, then door unlocks.”
B is the premise. D is the conclusion.


An implication is false only when its premise is true and its conclusion is false.

A false premise makes the rule vacuously true: neither no-badge case violates it.

The diagram supplies the four rows of the implication truth table. Ask which case violates the rule before discussing the two cases without a badge.
The rule’s truth value is different from the door’s truth value: the rule can be true while D is false. Logical truth here describes compliance with a statement.
“Vacuously” is a technical term for the convention, not another truth value. A visitor or another access method could explain D when B is false. The formula does not claim such an explanation exists, only that this assignment is compatible with the rule.
Material implication describes truth conditions, not causation or timing. It does not itself specify a complete policy.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
“If” and “Only If”


B \rightarrow D: badge is sufficient, enough to guarantee unlocking.
D \rightarrow B: badge is necessary, required whenever unlocking occurs.


“The robot moves only if its battery is ready.” M = moves, R = ready. Which direction?


M \rightarrow R. Read it as “movement requires readiness.”


An English sentence may mention the conclusion first: “D if B” still means B implies D. Necessary does not mean sufficient. A ready battery need not force motion.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive
Equivalence (\equiv): formulas agree on every truth assignment.








Name
Formula
Equivalent to the original?




Original
B \rightarrow D
Yes


Converse: reverse the arrow
D \rightarrow B
No


Inverse: negate both parts
\neg B \rightarrow \neg D
No


Contrapositive: reverse and negate
\neg D \rightarrow \neg B
Yes




Try B=\text{false}, D=\text{true}. Which formulas are true?


Original and contrapositive: true. Converse and inverse: false.


Logical equivalence means agreement on every assignment. A single differing assignment refutes it. The contrapositive rules out exactly the original rule’s violating case: a valid badge but no unlock.
The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, though not to the original. “Not equivalent” does not mean they differ on every row.

“The door unlocks if and only if the badge is valid.”

Both arrows hold in the F/F row. Compare XOR: it accepts the two mismatching rows, whereas the biconditional accepts the two matching rows. This badge-only policy is a temporary example. The final policy allows visitors too.

Work through the T/F row: AND is false, so its negation is true. NOT P is false but NOT Q is true, so their OR is true. Matching every output establishes equivalence.
Agreement on only one row would be insufficient. A biconditional can be true in one assignment without its two sides being logically equivalent across all assignments.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Useful Equivalence Laws







Law
Equivalent formulas




Double negation
\neg\neg P \equiv P


Identity
P \land \text{true} \equiv PP \lor \text{false} \equiv P


Domination
P \lor \text{true} \equiv \text{true}P \land \text{false} \equiv \text{false}


Idempotence
P \land P \equiv PP \lor P \equiv P


Implication
(P \rightarrow Q) \equiv \neg P \lor Q


Distributivity: AND over OR
P \land (Q \lor R) \equiv (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R)


Distributivity: OR over AND
P \lor (Q \land R) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land (P \lor R)



OR over AND: either P is true, or both Q and R are true.

Explain the names with truth conditions rather than asking for memorization. Identity leaves the value unchanged. Domination fixes it regardless of P. Idempotence means a repeated input changes nothing. The implication law reproduces the implication’s four-row table.
Boolean logic has both distributive laws. The operator outside the parentheses distributes over the operator inside. AND over OR requires P and at least one of Q or R. OR over AND allows P alone, otherwise it requires both Q and R. For the second law, if P is true, both clauses on the right are true. If P is false, the right side reduces to Q AND R.
Optional check: rewrite NOT (P implies Q) as P AND NOT Q. This uses the implication law, De Morgan’s law, and double negation in that order.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Redundant Condition Disappears
AND over OR, used backward, factors out a shared requirement:

(P \land Q) \lor (P \land R) \equiv P \land (Q \lor R)

Both forms require P, together with at least one of Q or R.
B = valid badge, L = lab open.

(B \land L) \lor (B \land \neg L)


Here P=B, Q=L, R=\neg L. Factor out the shared B:

\equiv B \land (L \lor \neg L)



Since L \lor \neg L is always true, B \land \text{true} \equiv B.


The formula allows either value of L. Only the valid badge is required.


P, Q, and R are arbitrary propositions. In the left form, either successful branch requires P. In the right form, P is required once alongside the choice between Q and R. This is AND distributing over OR, used in reverse to factor out the repeated requirement.
The example says “valid badge and lab open, or valid badge and lab not open.” A valid badge is required in both branches. The law of excluded middle makes L or NOT L true. Identity finishes the rewrite. Neither the algebra nor the truth table decides whether the resulting policy is appropriate for the real task.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Testing an Incomplete Access Policy
Intended: unlock exactly when authorized and no emergency is active.
Proposed rules: Rule 1 ((B \lor V) \land \neg E) \rightarrow D and Rule 2 D \rightarrow \neg E.

Try B=\text{false}, V=\text{false}, E=\text{false}, D=\text{true}. Do both rules hold?


  
  
  



Rule 1: \text{false}\rightarrow\text{true} is true.


Rule 2: \text{true}\rightarrow\text{true} is true.



Counterexample: both written rules hold, but an unauthorized person gets in.


Point to the no-authorization state and the open door throughout the evaluation. The counterexample satisfies the written rules but violates the intended requirement. This does not make the two written rules logically inconsistent. They simply permit too many assignments.
Phi is the earlier condition (B OR V) AND NOT E. Rule 1 requires access for eligible people. Rule 2 prohibits unlocking during an emergency. Neither requires authorization whenever unlocking occurs. The missing direction is D implies B OR V.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Both Directions Specify the Decision

D \leftrightarrow ((B \lor V) \land \neg E)



What must D be in each case?








Situation
Required D




Valid badge, emergency active
F


Approved visitor, no badge, no emergency
T

F




The forward direction requires unlocking for eligible people. The reverse direction requires both authorization and no emergency whenever unlocking occurs. Adding D implies B OR V to the original pair gives the same complete Boolean decision.
This completes the simplified specification for these four atoms. It does not account for hardware failure, time delays, or other access mechanisms that the example omits.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Can the Robot Conclude It May Move?
text:
Can the Robot Conclude It May Move?


For this robot, define:

B: the battery is ready.
C: the corridor is clear.
M: movement is permitted.

It knows B and the rule (B\land C)\rightarrow M.

Must M be true, must it be false, or is it undetermined?





Lecture 16 gave us a language and its truth conditions. Now we ask what an agent can conclude from several sentences together. B, C, and M are defined for this robot example and keep these meanings throughout it.
Take a vote and ask what is missing. The answer is undetermined: B alone does not establish C. The rule is a sufficient condition for permission, not a biconditional or a command to move. Return to this question after identifying all models.
Allow about 15 minutes for models and entailment, 7 for model checking and inference rules, 12 for CNF with the paired exercise, and 12 for resolution and propagation. Reserve the remaining time for the robot exit question. Pause at each answer reveal.
[Sources] - Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 7. - Original robot example for this course. - Public-domain OpenClipart robot: https://openclipart.org/detail/325789/robot-2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Facts, Rules, and a Query
A knowledge base (KB) is a collection of sentences assumed true.



Role
Robot example




Fact
B: the battery is ready


Rule
(B\land C)\rightarrow M


Query
Does M follow from these sentences?



All sentences must hold together:

\text{KB}=B\land\bigl((B\land C)\rightarrow M\bigr)


Inference finds consequences of the encoded facts and rules. It does not verify that a sensor report is correct.


A fact and a rule are both formulas. A set of KB sentences is interpreted as their conjunction. The query need not be stored in the KB, and it can be a compound formula rather than a single atom.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, knowledge-based agents. Original robot encoding. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Assignments and Models
An assignment gives every atom T or F. A model of the KB is an assignment that makes every KB sentence true.
\text{KB}=B\land\bigl((B\land C)\rightarrow M\bigr)


The KB leaves three possible worlds. T = true, F = false.


Read each tile in B, C, M order. The top row has B=true. The second tile, B=true, C=true, M=false, violates the implication. The remaining three top-row worlds are models. All bottom-row worlds fail because the KB includes B as a fact, even when the implication itself is true.
Textbooks sometimes call any assignment a model and then ask whether it satisfies a sentence. Here, a model of the KB always means a satisfying assignment. These are logical possibilities under the assumptions, not probability estimates.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, models and satisfaction. Original enumeration and editable draw.io illustration. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/propositional.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Entailment
\text{KB}\models\alpha
Read: “The KB entails \alpha.” The query \alpha is true in every model of the KB.


To disprove entailment, find one world where the KB is true and the query is false.


Alpha names the query formula. The double turnstile is the semantic entailment symbol. The diagram depicts an entailed query in general, not yet the robot query M. The query can be true outside the KB’s models, so the reverse inclusion is unnecessary.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, entailment. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/inference.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Robot’s Permission Is Undetermined
The three models of B\land((B\land C)\rightarrow M):



Model
B
C
M

T

F



A countermodel satisfies the KB but makes the query false.

\text{KB}\models B: all three models have B=\text{true}.


\text{KB}\not\models M: model 3 is a countermodel.


\text{KB}\not\models\neg M: model 1 is a countermodel.


Not entailed does not mean false. The KB permits both values of M.


Return to the opener. Ask students to identify a countermodel before each reveal. Model 2 also disproves entailment of NOT M. These three assignments exhaust the KB models over B, C, M.
The distinction is about what follows from our knowledge. Every individual assignment still has only the two classical truth values. Treating an unreported fact as false would be an extra closed-world assumption.
[Sources] - Original robot example, with the classical entailment definition from AIMA Chapter 7. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Validity and Satisfiability
Satisfiable: at least one assignment makes the formula true.



Classification
Across all assignments
Example




Valid / tautology
Always true
P\lor\neg P


Unsatisfiable / contradiction
Always false
P\land\neg P


Contingent
Sometimes true, sometimes false
P\rightarrow Q




For P\rightarrow Q, give one satisfying and one falsifying assignment.


P=\text{false},Q=\text{false} satisfies it. P=\text{true},Q=\text{false} falsifies it.


Valid and contingent formulas are both satisfiable.


Validity classifies a single formula across all assignments. Entailment relates a KB to a query. The table’s three categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Satisfiable is a broader yes/no property, not a fourth exclusive category.
An implication is not automatically valid. Remind students of its one violating row rather than treating the arrow as a proof that Q is true.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, validity and satisfiability. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Entailment as a SAT Test
The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) asks whether a formula has a satisfying assignment.

\text{KB}\models\alpha
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{KB}\land\neg\alpha\text{ is unsatisfiable}








\text{KB}\land\neg\alpha
What it tells us




Has a satisfying assignment
A countermodel exists: \alpha does not follow


Has no satisfying assignment
\alpha follows from the KB



This is refutation: assume the conclusion is false and look for a contradiction with the KB.

A consistent KB has at least one model. Check this first: C\land\neg C has none and entails every query in classical logic.


Explain the negated query in words: can the premises all hold while the proposed conclusion fails? No such world means entailment. The negation is essential.
The consistency warning concerns classical logic. If the KB has no models, the universal condition for entailment is vacuously true. This does not make contradictory sensor reports trustworthy or make every claim about the physical world true. Repair the premises before interpreting an entailment result as useful evidence.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, proof by refutation and satisfiability. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/inference.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Model Checking
Conceptual pseudocode: enumerate complete truth assignments.
def entails(kb, query):
    symbols = symbols_in(kb, query)
    for model in all_assignments(symbols):
        if evaluate(kb, model):
            if not evaluate(query, model):
                return False
    return True

symbols_in: collect distinct atoms from both inputs.
all_assignments: enumerate all 2^n assignments for n atoms.
evaluate: apply the connectives’ truth tables.


Why is return True after the loop?


One countermodel gives False. True requires exhausting the loop.


The helpers describe operations, not a complete runnable Python implementation. Follow the highlights: enumeration, testing a model, and accepting only after exhaustion. Rows violating the KB do not constrain the query. This procedure also returns True for an inconsistent KB, as classical semantics requires.
Use the robot’s model 3 as a witness for query M. If querying a fresh atom X, symbols_in must include X even though it is absent from the KB. Counting 2^n assignments omits the additional cost of evaluating each formula.
[Sources] - Simplified teaching pseudocode based on AIMA truth-table entailment: https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Entailment and Derivation







Notation
Meaning




\text{KB}\models\alpha
True in every KB model: a statement about meaning


\text{KB}\vdash\alpha
Derived by our proof rules: a statement about a proof





Sound: every derived conclusion is entailed. Complete: every entailed conclusion can be derived.


Read the single turnstile as derives and the double turnstile as entails. The arrows in the diagram denote set inclusion, not implication between object-language atoms. A system that is both sound and complete has exactly the right consequences.
Completeness is relative to the logic and proof system. It does not mean that a particular unfinished proof search will find every consequence, or that modus ponens alone proves every propositional entailment. Propositional resolution is complete for refutation when all needed resolvents are explored.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, inference systems, soundness, and completeness. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens
These are inference rules: patterns that derive a conclusion from known premises.


Modus Ponens
\frac{P\rightarrow Q\qquad P}{Q}
The premise P holds, so the rule requires Q.
If the battery is ready, a light is on. The battery is ready. Therefore the light is on.

Modus Tollens
\frac{P\rightarrow Q\qquad\neg Q}{\neg P}
If Q is false, P cannot hold without violating the rule.
The same rule holds, but the light is off. Therefore the battery is not ready.


Knowing Q and P\rightarrow Q does not establish P. The light might have another power source.


Explain the fraction-like notation before using it: the formulas above the line are premises, the formula below is the derived conclusion. The Latin names identify these two reasoning patterns. Ponens affirms the antecedent; tollens denies the consequent. Both are sound because the implication excludes P=true, Q=false.
The light example is a separate simplified rule with generic atoms P and Q. The caveat is logical, not probabilistic: P=false, Q=true satisfies Q and the rule while falsifying P. Affirming the consequent is therefore unsound.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, standard propositional inference rules. Original battery/light example. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Conjunctive Normal Form
Conjunctive normal form (CNF) is an AND of clauses.
 (P\lor\neg Q)\land(Q\lor R)\land\neg R 




Term
Meaning




Literal
An atom or its negation, such as P or \neg Q


Clause
An OR of literals, such as P\lor\neg Q


Unit clause
Just one literal, such as \neg R




All clauses must hold. Within each clause at least one literal must hold. A unit clause is already a clause and needs no extra literal. P, Q, and R are generic atoms for this section.
Ask which clause forces R to be false. If R=false, the second clause then forces Q=true, and the first forces P=true. This also anticipates unit propagation.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, CNF. Original annotated draw.io illustration. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
CNF Conversion, Step by Step
Convert \neg(P\rightarrow Q)\lor R without changing its models.







Step
Equivalent formula




1. Remove the implication
\neg(\neg P\lor Q)\lor R


2. Move NOT inward
(P\land\neg Q)\lor R


3. Distribute OR over AND
(P\lor R)\land(\neg Q\lor R)



The distributive law used in step 3:
X\lor(Y\land Z)\equiv(X\lor Y)\land(X\lor Z)

The result has two clauses. When R=\text{false}, both forms require P=\text{true} and Q=\text{false}.


Predict each expression before revealing it. Step 1 uses P implies Q equivalent to NOT P OR Q. Step 2 uses De Morgan and double negation. Step 3 first commutes R to the left, then substitutes X=R, Y=P, Z=NOT Q in the displayed distributive law.
CNF needs OR over AND. AND over OR is also a valid distributive law, but expansion in that direction produces an OR of conjunctions instead. To remove a biconditional, rewrite P iff Q as (NOT P OR Q) AND (NOT Q OR P). Repeated distribution can greatly enlarge a formula, so this direct method is for small examples.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, equivalent CNF rewrites. Original worked formula. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
