(Intro to) AI
section: CNF Practice: One Clause or Two?
text:
CNF Practice: One Clause or Two?
Convert both formulas. First remove the implication.


One Premise, Two Consequences
P\rightarrow(Q\land R)

\neg P\lor(Q\land R) \equiv(\neg P\lor Q)\land(\neg P\lor R)
Two clauses: P requires Q and also R.


Two Conditions, One Consequence
(P\land Q)\rightarrow R

\neg(P\land Q)\lor R \equiv\neg P\lor\neg Q\lor R
One clause: only P and Q together require R.



The position of AND matters. Negating an AND and distributing over an AND are different steps.


Give a short pair exercise before clicking. Keep both answers hidden initially and reveal each solution separately. In the first, distribute OR over AND. In the second, negating the premise changes its AND into OR by De Morgan, so no distribution is needed.
Use P=true, Q=false, R=false to distinguish the original formulas: the first is false but the second is true. This tests whether students changed the rule while rearranging it.
[Sources] - Original practice using AIMA Chapter 7 equivalence laws. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Resolution
Resolution combines two clauses containing a complementary pair, P and \neg P.

P is the pivot atom. A,B are the remaining disjunctions. Add the derived resolvent; keep both parents.



If both parents are true…
Then…




P=\text{false}
The first clause forces A


P=\text{true}
The second clause forces B




Either way, A\lor B is true. Resolution is sound.


P is the pivot atom. A and B here stand for the remaining literals or disjunctions, not the robot’s battery atom. The case split proves soundness without guessing P’s truth value.
Resolution derives a consequence; it generally does not produce an equivalent replacement for both parents. A refutation procedure retains existing clauses and adds the resolvent.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, propositional resolution. Original draw.io parent/resolvent diagram. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Unit Resolution and the Empty Clause
text:
Unit Resolution and the Empty Clause
A unit clause has only one literal, so resolving can leave a shorter clause or no literals at all.


One Literal Remains
\frac{P\qquad\neg P\lor Q}{Q}
The fact P eliminates \neg P. The remaining clause is Q.

No Literals Remain
\frac{P\qquad\neg P}{\bot}
The empty clause, written \bot, cannot be true under any assignment.


Deriving \bot proves the starting clauses cannot all hold together.


The first pattern is modus ponens after rewriting the implication as a clause. Read bottom as contradiction. Some sources denote the empty clause by a square or empty braces. An OR over zero literals is false.
Distinguish the empty clause, which is false, from an empty set of clauses, whose conjunction is true. A resolution derivation of bottom shows inconsistency of the starting clause set. When those starting clauses are KB plus the negated query, this establishes the original query by refutation.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, unit resolution and the empty clause. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Reachability by Refutation
L: left route open. R: right route open. G: the goal is reachable.

\text{KB}=(L\lor R)\land(L\rightarrow G)\land(R\rightarrow G)
To prove G, add \neg G and convert to clauses:



ID
Clause
Origin




1
L\lor R
At least one route is open


2
\neg L\lor G
L\rightarrow G


3
\neg R\lor G
R\rightarrow G


4
\neg G
Negated query, added for the proof




This is a new example; L and R name two route-open propositions, not costs. Ask whether a reachable goal necessarily tells us which route is open. No: either one or both could be open. The KB is consistent, for example L=true, R=false, G=true satisfies it.
The diagram represents the alternative routes, not a shortest-path search. Clause 4 is a temporary assumption, not a reported fact about the goal. Refutation checks whether it can coexist with the original KB.
[Sources] - Original route example and draw.io diagram, using AIMA Chapter 7 refutation. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Resolution Proof, Step by Step
text:
A Resolution Proof, Step by Step
Numbers identify clauses. Each new clause records its parents and pivot.

  
  
  
  
  



5: resolve 2 and 4 on G to get \neg L.


6: resolve 3 and 4 on G to get \neg R.


7: resolve 1 and 5 on L to get R.


8: resolve 6 and 7 on R to get \bot. Thus \text{KB}\models G.



One click reveals one inference and highlights its parent clauses, connecting arrows, and new result. Step backward to revisit a deduction. Clause 4 is used twice; the two copies in the proof diagram denote the same negated-query clause.
Ask students to predict each resolvent before revealing it. Deriving bottom disproves the extra assumption NOT G when combined with the KB. It proves G, not NOT G. Keep every clause, even when it is no longer used in the displayed derivation. Other valid proof orders are possible.
[Sources] - Original checkable refutation trace. AIMA Chapter 7, propositional resolution. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Resolution Uses One Complementary Pair
Consider P\lor Q and \neg P\lor\neg Q.

Can we cancel both P,\neg P and Q,\neg Q to conclude \bot?


No. P=\text{true},Q=\text{false} satisfies both parent clauses.


Resolve only on P:
\frac{P\lor Q\qquad\neg P\lor\neg Q}{Q\lor\neg Q}


The resolvent is a tautology, not a contradiction. A sound rule cannot derive \bot from satisfiable parents.


This is a useful counterexample to an overgeneralized cancellation rule. Resolving on Q gives P OR NOT P instead. A complementary pair across the two parent clauses is the pivot for one resolution step. Complementary literals in the resulting clause make it tautological, not empty.
[Sources] - Original error-checking example based on AIMA’s resolution rule. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Unit Propagation
A unit clause forces its only literal to be true. Substitute that assignment and repeat.
For the route clauses \{L\lor R,\ \neg L\lor G,\ \neg R\lor G,\ \neg G\}:


Like constraint propagation, forced assignments reduce search. If they do not decide the formula, branching may still be needed.


CSP means constraint satisfaction problem, as in Lectures 13-15. The clause NOT G first forces G=false. Simplifying NOT L OR G and NOT R OR G produces the unit clauses NOT L and NOT R. These force both routes closed, making L OR R false.
This is the same inconsistency as the resolution proof, viewed as successive forced assignments. Unit propagation alone is not a complete general SAT solver. No remaining unit clause does not imply a satisfying assignment or unsatisfiability.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 7, SAT and unit clauses. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/inference.html - Original draw.io propagation diagram. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: New Facts Change the Robot’s Conclusions
text:
New Facts Change the Robot’s Conclusions
B: battery ready. C: corridor clear. M: movement permitted.
Original KB: B and (B\land C)\rightarrow M.
The rule becomes \neg B\lor\neg C\lor M. Resolving with B gives \neg C\lor M.
Consider these separate updates to the original KB:


Add C: Does M Follow?

\frac{\neg C\lor M\qquad C}{M}
Yes. The rule now has both required conditions.


Add \neg M: Does \neg C Follow?

\frac{\neg C\lor M\qquad\neg M}{\neg C}
Yes. A clear corridor would contradict the rule and known facts.



The original KB left M undetermined. An added fact removes possible worlds.


Allow a brief individual attempt before each reveal. The updates are alternatives, not cumulative: adding C and NOT M together would make this KB inconsistent. For each update students can also filter the three models on the earlier slide.
The second conclusion follows from this encoded sufficient-condition rule and B. It is not a claim that a movement restriction always measures real corridor safety. A refutation proof for either conclusion would add its negation and derive bottom from the displayed unit result.
[Sources] - Original robot exercise using AIMA Chapter 7 inference and resolution. [/Sources]

title: Homework 3: Logic Toolkit
text:
Reference Sheet (Supporting Material)

Background
Propositional logic treats each symbol such as P or Q as one truth-valued statement. First-order logic adds objects, predicates, variables, and quantifiers. State a nonempty domain and use parentheses to make each quantifier’s scope clear.








Form
Read as
Useful equivalence




\neg P
not P
flips the truth value


P\land Q
P and Q
true only when both are true


P\lor Q
P or Q
false only when both are false


P\rightarrow Q
if P, then Q
\neg P\lor Q


P\leftrightarrow Q
P exactly when Q
(P\rightarrow Q)\land(Q\rightarrow P)



Classification: a tautology is always true, a contradiction is always false, and a contingent formula has both true and false assignments. A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes it true. Both tautologies and contingent formulas are satisfiable.


Equivalence Laws
De Morgan’s laws:
\neg(P\land Q)\equiv\neg P\lor\neg Q,
\qquad \neg(P\lor Q)\equiv\neg P\land\neg Q.
Quantifier negation:
\neg\forall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,\neg P(x),
\qquad \neg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv\forall x\,\neg P(x).
OR over AND, the distribution used to form CNF:
X\lor(Y\land Z)\equiv(X\lor Y)\land(X\lor Z).


Clause-Form Workflow

Eliminate \leftrightarrow and \rightarrow.
Move negations inward with De Morgan’s laws, double negation, and quantifier negation.
Rename bound variables to avoid collisions. For example, (\forall x\,P(x))\land(\exists x\,Q(x)) can use y in the second part.
If moving quantifiers to the front, preserve scope: do not capture a variable that was free in another part of the formula.
Skolemize each existential with a fresh constant or function. Record its dependencies on surrounding universal variables. This step preserves satisfiability.
Distribute OR over AND.
Write the result as a set of clauses, with universal quantifiers implicit. A clause is an OR of literals. The whole clause set requires all clauses to hold.

For instance, \forall u\,\exists v\,R(u,v) uses a fresh g(u) for v, while \exists v\,\forall u\,R(u,v) uses a fresh constant k.


Unification and Resolution
A substitution replaces variables with terms and applies consistently throughout each expression. An MGU avoids unnecessary bindings. The occurs check rejects a binding such as x\mapsto f(x) because the replacement contains x itself. Different constant symbols do not unify syntactically.
Resolution combines clauses containing one complementary pair. In FOL, first rename variables in different parent clauses apart if needed, then find a unifier for the atoms. Apply that substitution to the entire parent clauses, remove the complementary literals, and join the remaining literals with OR.
For a refutation proof, add the negated query to the KB. Deriving the empty clause shows that the KB together with the negated query is unsatisfiable:
\text{KB}\models\alpha\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{KB}\land\neg\alpha\text{ is unsatisfiable}.
The empty clause has no literals and is false. It is different from an empty clause set, which has no requirements and is true.


Lecture References

Lecture 16: Propositional Logic
Lecture 17: Propositional Inference
Lecture 18: First-Order Logic


← Homework 2Homework 4 →

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Objects and General Rules


First-order logic (FOL) describes objects and their relationships.
Instead of a separate rule for each person:
\text{HumanSocrates}\rightarrow\text{MortalSocrates}
write one rule about all people:
\forall x\,\bigl(\text{Human}(x)\rightarrow\text{Mortal}(x)\bigr).
The domain is the nonempty set of objects that variables range over. Here, choose all people.




Read the quantifier as “for every x.” Human and Mortal are predicates, whose arguments refer to people. The propositional atom HumanSocrates does not expose an object argument. A finite collection can be enumerated propositionally, but FOL states the general rule directly, including for people we have not named.
Keep this lecture to about 30-35 minutes, leaving time for Homework 3 and midterm questions. Spend most of that time on quantifier scope, matching, and the single clause-form example. Lectures 17 and 18 are excluded from the upcoming midterm, as stated in the schedule.
[Sources] - Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapters 8-9. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/first-order-logic.html - Public-domain OpenClipart connections artwork, credited on the course asset page. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Terms and Predicates
A term refers to an object. An atomic formula makes a claim about objects.








Building block
Example
Meaning




Constant
\text{Ada}
A named person


Variable
x
A person whose value may vary


Function term
\text{Mother}(\text{Ada})
An object: Ada’s mother


Predicate
\text{Knows}(\text{Ada},x)
A claim: Ada knows x



Connectives \neg,\land,\lor,\rightarrow,\leftrightarrow combine formulas as before.

Does \text{Mother}(\text{Ada}) itself have a truth value?


No. It denotes an object. \text{Human}(\text{Mother}(\text{Ada})) makes a truth-valued claim about that object.


The domain is people. In this simplified model, Mother assigns one person to every person. Functions are total and single-valued. A relation such as Advises may hold for several pairs or none, so it should generally be a predicate rather than a function. Different names need not denote different objects unless the model or premises say so.
A FOL interpretation specifies the domain, the objects named by constants, functions on that domain, and the relations represented by predicates. An assignment supplies values for free variables. A model of a closed KB makes every sentence in the KB true.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 8, first-order syntax and semantics. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Universal and Existential Quantifiers
Domain: people. \text{Happy}(x) means “x is happy.”


Universal: \forall
\forall x\,\text{Happy}(x)
Every person is happy.
One unhappy person makes the statement false.

Existential: \exists
\exists x\,\text{Happy}(x)
At least one person is happy.
One happy person is a witness that makes it true.


The quantifier binds x in its scope. In \forall x\,(\text{Human}(x)\rightarrow\text{Mortal}(x)), the parentheses put both predicates in that scope.


Existence does not mean exactly one. A witness is an object that satisfies the quantified condition. In Happy(x) alone, x is free: we must assign it a value to evaluate the formula. A closed sentence has no free variables.
On a finite domain, universal quantification behaves like AND across all objects, while existential quantification behaves like OR. This is an intuition for evaluation, not a claim that all FOL domains are finite.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 8, quantifiers and scope. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Quantifier Order
Domain: people. An arrow from x to y means \text{Knows}(x,y).


\forall x\,\exists y\,\text{Knows}(x,y)
Each person knows someone. The witness may depend on x.

\exists y\,\forall x\,\text{Knows}(x,y)
One person is known by everyone. The same witness works for all x.



The left world satisfies only the first statement. The right world satisfies both.


Both diagrams use the same three-person domain, Ada, Bo, and Cy, with no additional Knows pairs. The left and right columns within each diagram are source and target copies of the same objects. Bo knowing Bo is allowed: we have not imposed an irreflexivity condition. Knows is directed and need not be symmetric.
The right-hand statement entails the left-hand one on a nonempty domain. Swapping mixed quantifiers can change meaning, but swapping two adjacent universals, or two adjacent existentials, does not.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 8, nested quantifiers. Original finite relation examples and draw.io illustration. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Translating “Every” and “Some”
Domain: people. \text{Student}(x) and \text{Advisor}(y) identify roles. \text{Advises}(y,x) means “y advises x.”
Every Student Has an Advisor
\forall x\,\bigl(\text{Student}(x)\rightarrow
  \exists y\,(\text{Advisor}(y)\land\text{Advises}(y,x))\bigr)
Some Student Has an Advisor

\exists x\,\exists y\,\bigl(\text{Student}(x)\land
  \text{Advisor}(y)\land\text{Advises}(y,x)\bigr)


Use implication to restrict a universal rule to students. Use AND to require an existential witness to be a student.


Ask for the second translation before revealing it. Under a universal quantifier, Student(x) AND … would claim that every person is a student. Under an existential quantifier, Student(x) implies … can be satisfied by a nonstudent, so it does not establish a student witness.
The first statement does not assert that any students exist. If there are no students, every implication in it is true. The second does assert the existence of at least one student and an advisor, who need not be a different person unless inequality is added.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 8, translating quantified English. Original advising example. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Negating Quantifiers
Moving NOT inward flips the quantifier:
\neg\forall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,\neg P(x) \neg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv\forall x\,\neg P(x)

“Not everyone knows someone.” Rewrite \neg\forall x\,\exists y\,\text{Knows}(x,y) with NOT next to the predicate.


\exists x\,\forall y\,\neg\text{Knows}(x,y)
There is a person who knows nobody.


“Not everyone” means at least one exception. It does not mean “nobody.”


P(x) here stands for any condition on x. Move the negation across one quantifier at a time. Across a compound condition, also apply De Morgan’s laws. This prepares students for Homework 3, Problem 3, without solving its specific formula.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 8, quantifier negation. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Instantiation
Instantiation replaces a quantified variable with a term.


Universal Instantiation (UI)
\forall x\,\text{Human}(x)
Any particular instance follows:
\text{Human}(\text{Ada}).
The rule applies to every object, including Ada.

Existential Instantiation (EI)
\exists x\,\text{Happy}(x)
Give a witness a fresh name k:
\text{Happy}(k).
We have not learned whether that witness is Ada.


A fresh witness name adds no claim that it differs from all known people. It simply avoids assuming which person satisfies the existential.


UI is ordinary logical consequence. EI is a witness introduction in an extended vocabulary for proof or satisfiability reasoning. Happy(k) is not an unrestricted consequence about an arbitrary preinterpreted name k. In natural deduction, the fresh-name assumption has a local scope and must not leak into an unjustified conclusion.
For a standalone existential with no surrounding universal dependency, the fresh name is a Skolem constant. For a nested existential we may need a function, covered later. UI also permits suitable function terms. Avoid variable capture when applying a substitution under quantifiers.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 9, universal and existential instantiation. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Most General Unifiers and Failure
A most general unifier (MGU) matches expressions without unnecessary bindings.
R(x,f(y))\qquad R(\text{Ada},f(z))

An MGU is \{x\mapsto\text{Ada},\ y\mapsto z\}. It leaves z unrestricted. Here R is a predicate and f a unary function.








Expressions
Why unification fails




P(\text{Ada}) and P(\text{Bo})
Different constant symbols cannot match syntactically


P(x) and P(f(x))
Occurs check: x occurs inside f(x)




The occurs check rejects x\mapsto f(x): ordinary first-order terms must be finite.


R is any binary predicate, P any unary predicate, and f a unary function symbol. An MGU allows every other unifier to be obtained by further substitution. For example, additionally setting z to Bo also unifies the pair but is more specific. Reversing y maps to z is an equivalent MGU up to variable renaming.
Syntactic unification does not infer equalities between distinct constant symbols even if a possible interpretation maps them to the same object. Equality reasoning is a separate extension. In the occurs-check case, substitution cannot turn the finite term assigned to x into exactly that same term with an extra f around it. This is about finite syntactic terms, not whether a semantic function could have a fixed point.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 9, most general unifiers and the occurs check. - https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/courses/atp/lectures/10-unif.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Skolem Constants and Functions
Skolemization replaces existential variables with fresh witness symbols.







Quantified statement
Witness representation




\exists y\,\forall x\,\text{Knows}(x,y)
\forall x\,\text{Knows}(x,k): one fresh constant k


\forall x\,\exists y\,\text{Knows}(x,y)
\forall x\,\text{Knows}(x,f(x)): a fresh function f





The function’s arguments record the surrounding universal variables on which a witness may depend. Different inputs may still share a witness.


The diagram shows one possible interpretation of f for the left world from the quantifier-order slide. Skolemization does not compute this function or claim that the relation has a unique witness. It chooses one permissible witness per input when such witnesses exist.
The symbols must be new to the whole problem. Skolemization preserves satisfiability in an expanded vocabulary, not logical equivalence over a fixed interpretation of the new symbols. This is why it is suitable for refutation. For several surrounding universal variables, use f(x1,…,xn). A standalone existential has no such dependency, so a constant suffices.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 9, Skolemization. - https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs257/slides/Lecture_7.pdf [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Clause Form for Resolution
Conjunctive normal form (CNF): AND of clauses, each an OR of literals. In FOL, atoms can contain terms, such as \text{Human}(x).



Step
Operation




1
Remove \rightarrow and \leftrightarrow


2
Move NOT inward, including across quantifiers


3
Rename bound variables to avoid collisions


4
Skolemize existentials with the correct dependencies


5
Distribute OR over AND and list the clauses




All remaining variables are implicitly universal. Skolemization preserves satisfiability. The other formula rewrites preserve equivalence.


To rename bound variables apart, (forall x P(x)) AND (exists x Q(x)) can use x in the first part and y in the second. Also standardize variables in different clauses apart before resolving, so variables with the same spelling in independent clauses are not accidentally tied together.
Parentheses still matter. Quantifiers may be moved to a prefix after safe renaming, provided their scope and dependencies are preserved. In A OR forall x B, pulling forall x outward requires that x not be free in A. Dropping the written universal quantifier is a clause notation convention, not replacement by a single named object.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 9, first-order clause conversion. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One Rule, Two Clauses
Every student has an advisor. Abbreviate: S(x) = student, A(y) = advisor, T(y,x) = y advises x.
\forall x\,\bigl(S(x)\rightarrow\exists y\,(A(y)\land T(y,x))\bigr)







Step
Result




Remove implication
\forall x\,\exists y\,(\neg S(x)\lor(A(y)\land T(y,x)))


Skolemize y with f(x)
\forall x\,(\neg S(x)\lor(A(f(x))\land T(f(x),x)))


Distribute OR over AND
(\neg S(x)\lor A(f(x)))\land(\neg S(x)\lor T(f(x),x))




Two clauses, using the same f(x):
C_1=\{\neg S(x),A(f(x))\},\qquad C_2=\{\neg S(x),T(f(x),x)\}.


The original formula comes from the translation slide. The first row combines implication elimination with pulling the existential outward, valid because y is not free in S(x) and the domain is nonempty. No negations need pushing further inward, and x and y are already distinct.
Introduce f fresh for this example, independent of the earlier Knows example’s f. The last formula has implicit universal x. The clauses require one chosen individual f(x) both to be an advisor and to advise the student x. Using unrelated functions for the two occurrences would allow two different people and could weaken the original requirement. For a nonstudent, both clauses hold through NOT S(x).
Set notation uses an inner set for the OR of literals and an outer set for the AND of clauses. C1 and C2 name the two clauses, not new logical atoms.
[Sources] - Original worked advising example, using AIMA Chapter 9 clause-conversion rules. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Resolution with Unification
Resolve clauses whose opposite-sign atoms match under a substitution:
C_1=\neg\text{Human}(x)\lor\text{Mortal}(x),
\qquad C_2=\text{Human}(\text{Socrates}).


Unify \text{Human}(x) and \text{Human}(\text{Socrates}):

\theta=\{x\mapsto\text{Socrates}\}.



Apply \theta to the whole clauses, then remove the complementary pair.

C_3=\text{Mortal}(\text{Socrates}).


The substitution affects the remaining literals too. Keep both parent clauses when adding the resolvent.


The negation signs differ, but the atoms Human(x) and Human(Socrates) unify. Do not try to unify a negated formula with a positive formula directly. The resolvent is the disjunction of the remaining substituted literals. Here only Mortal(Socrates) remains.
This example has one variable-bearing parent and one ground fact, so variable renaming between parents is unnecessary. In general, standardize parent clauses apart first. AIMA’s full FOL resolution procedure also includes factoring. We do not present this single example as a complete implementation of that procedure.
[Sources] - AIMA Chapter 9, resolution in first-order logic. - https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/logic/first-order-logical-inference.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Refutation: A Complete Small Proof
Query: \text{Mortal}(\text{Socrates}). Add its negation as clause 3.

  


4. Parents 1 and 2, \theta=\{x\mapsto\text{Socrates}\}: derive \text{Mortal}(\text{Socrates}).


5. Parents 4 and 3, no binding needed: derive \bot, the empty clause.


The KB and negated query cannot both hold. Therefore \text{KB}\models\text{Mortal}(\text{Socrates}).


Animate the same proof as the preceding slide, now completing refutation. Initial clauses are 1: NOT Human(x) OR Mortal(x), 2: Human(Socrates), 3: NOT Mortal(Socrates). Clause 3 is a temporary assumption for refutation, not an extra fact asserted by the original KB. The diagram highlights the currently used parents and derived clause at each step.
The empty clause has zero literals and is always false. It is different from the empty clause set, a conjunction of zero clauses that is true. We use bottom here as in Lecture 17. The square symbol used in HW3 names the same empty clause.
[Sources] - Standard Human/Mortal example from AIMA Chapters 8-9, original draw.io proof layout. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Quick Check
Domain: people. \text{Knows}(x,y) means “x knows y.”

For \forall x\,\exists y\,\text{Knows}(x,y), may we replace y with one fixed constant k? Why?


In general, no. Different people may need different witnesses. Use a fresh function f(x).


Do P(x,x) and P(\text{Ada},\text{Bo}) unify?


No. The first position requires x\mapsto\text{Ada}; the second requires x\mapsto\text{Bo}. One substitution cannot satisfy both.


P is a binary predicate here. Ada and Bo are constant symbols. Pause for an answer before each reveal. These check witness dependency and consistent substitution, the main new skills needed for Homework 3.
[Sources] - Original questions using AIMA Chapter 9 definitions. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

State the domain and define every predicate.
Quantifier order determines whether a witness may depend on another variable.
Unification uses one consistent substitution across each expression.
Skolem terms record witness dependencies in clause form.
Refutation proves entailment by deriving the empty clause from the KB and negated query.


Homework 3: Logic Toolkit. Show intermediate steps. Due Friday, October 23, 11:59 PM Eastern.

Asset credits

Point students to the five required problems before the optional reference section. No code or starter download is required. Reserve the remaining class time for homework clarifications and review questions about Lectures 1-16 for the October 12 midterm, rather than expanding this deck with another full recap.
[Sources] - Course schedule and Homework 3 specification. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Planning Task
Planning finds an action sequence from an initial state (starting arrangement) to a goal (required final conditions).


Can we put A onto B immediately? What must happen first?


C blocks A. A plan must first make A movable.


Use this one arrangement throughout Lectures 19 and 20. A is teal, B gold, C rose. We model a move as a complete transfer of one block, with no separate pickup or hand state. Ask for a proposed sequence before introducing formal notation.
[Sources] - Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, fourth edition, Section 11.1 and the blocks-world example in Figure 11.4. - https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf - Original editable draw.io illustration of that example. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Classical Planning Assumptions
Our planner uses a deliberately simplified model:







Assumption
Meaning in this example




Fully observable
The current arrangement is known


Deterministic
A legal move has one predicted result


Static environment
Blocks stay put unless the agent moves them


Finite, discrete states
Finitely many distinct arrangements, described by true/false facts


Sequential actions
One complete move at a time




A classical plan is a fixed action sequence. Unexpected outcomes may require replanning: computing a new plan from the observed state.


These assumptions describe classical planning, not every planning method. We also ignore action duration and use one unit of cost per move. Real robot control would need geometric feasibility, perception, grasping, and failure handling, which are outside this symbolic model.
[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Section 11.1. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Action Schemas and Ground Actions
Objects are named things in the problem: blocks A,B,C and \text{Table}.
An action schema is a reusable action description. A template means it has variables as placeholders, like blanks in a form.








Form
Example
Meaning




Action schema
\text{Move}(b,\text{src},\text{dst})
Move block b from source \text{src} onto destination \text{dst}


Ground action
\text{Move}(B,\text{Table},C)
Move B from the table onto C



Grounding fills the placeholders: b=B, \text{src}=\text{Table}, \text{dst}=C.
A ground action has specific objects in every slot, with no variables left. The schema also defines when the action is allowed and what it changes.

Planning searches over states. Each legal ground action supplies one edge. The chosen objects must still meet the action’s requirements.


An object is an individual named entity in the domain, not necessarily a Python object. Here B and C name particular blocks, and Table names their shared support. The lower-case b and the descriptive names src and dst are variables to replace, not extra objects.
The full action schema includes preconditions and effects, introduced on later slides. Grounding substitutes the chosen objects throughout those rules as well as in the action’s name. For example, Clear(b) becomes Clear(B). Ground means variable-free, not a physical location or a move onto the ground.
Move(B,Table,C) is applicable in the initial arrangement because B is on the table and B and C are clear. Move(A,Table,B) is also ground, but is initially inapplicable because C blocks A. Grounding and checking applicability are different steps.
This connects planning to the earlier search lectures: a node represents a world state, an applicable ground action supplies an edge to Result(s,a), the goal test checks the required facts, and a solution is an executable action sequence.
[Sources] - AIMA Sections 11.1-11.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Blocks-World Vocabulary
A constant names one object: A,B,C or \text{Table}. A predicate describes a property or relation, such as \text{Clear} or \text{On}.







Fact
Meaning




\text{Block}(A)
A has type (object category) block; this never changes


\text{On}(C,A)
C rests directly on A


\text{On}(B,\text{Table})
B rests on the table


\text{Clear}(B)
No block is on top of B




For blocks, Clear means an empty top. \text{Clear}(\text{Table}) is a special, always-true convention: the table can accept several blocks.


We follow AIMA’s two-schema model, which includes Clear(Table). It does not mean that the table has no blocks. A move’s destination must be a block, so Move never deletes Clear(Table). MoveToTable handles the table destination separately.
On and Clear can change. Block facts and the Clear(Table) convention stay fixed. The diagrams show only block arrangements, not every predicate.
[Sources] - AIMA Figure 11.4, available in https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Complete Initial State
A state s is the set of facts currently true in the world.


Where blocks rest:
\begin{aligned}
&\text{On}(A,\text{Table}),\quad\text{On}(B,\text{Table}),\\
&\text{On}(C,A).
\end{aligned}
Clear facts: \text{Clear}(B),\text{Clear}(C).
Fixed facts: \text{Block}(A),\text{Block}(B),\text{Block}(C) and \text{Clear}(\text{Table}).




Closed-world assumption: facts absent from this complete state are false. In particular, \text{Clear}(A)=\text{false}.


A state is a set of true ground atoms. All the listed facts must hold together, so commas in a set are interpreted conjunctively. Supplying the Clear facts is essential: a planner cannot infer them unless we implement a separate derivation rule.
Contrast with Lecture 17’s logical KB, where an unreported fact could be undetermined. Here the state description is complete under the closed-world convention. This is a modeling assumption, not a rule that missing sensor data proves a physical claim false.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1 and Figure 11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Partial Goal
A partial goal specifies only the facts we require at the end.
G=\{\text{On}(A,B),\ \text{On}(B,C)\}
The symbol G names the set of required goal facts.



Required
Left unspecified by G




A directly on B
What C rests on


B directly on C
Other facts and additional objects




The goal test G\subseteq s means every fact in G is in state s. Extra true facts are allowed. Both required facts must hold together.


In this exact three-block, acyclic physical domain, C must be on the table in a valid final arrangement. The formula itself does not state this: the domain constraints supply it. With additional blocks, C could rest on another block. Avoid claiming several valid three-block final arrangements for this particular goal.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1, goal representation. Original discussion of the three-block domain. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Preconditions and Effects
Preconditions say when an action is allowed. Effects say what it changes.







Set
Role




\text{Pre}(a), or PRE
Preconditions: facts required before action a


\text{Add}(a), or ADD
Add effects: facts made true


\text{Del}(a), or DELETE
Delete effects: facts removed, hence made false



An action is applicable (executable now) when \text{Pre}(a)\subseteq s. Its next state is:
\text{Result}(s,a)=\bigl(s\setminus\text{Del}(a)\bigr)\cup\text{Add}(a).
Here \setminus removes facts and \cup combines fact sets.

The frame problem asks how to represent unchanged facts. Facts outside the effect sets persist: moving C leaves \text{On}(B,\text{Table}) true.


Explain set difference as remove and union as add. The basic fragment used here has positive preconditions and disjoint add/delete lists. Negative effects are entries in the delete list, not negated atoms stored in a state. This is the STRIPS style of representation, named for Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver, with typing and inequality constraints on schema instances.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1, action applicability and the state transition function. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Maintaining the Clear Facts
For a block b, \text{Clear}(b) means no block x rests on b:
\neg\exists x\,\text{On}(x,b).
We store this summary as a fact and update it after each move.







A move changes…
Clear fact to update




The old supporting block loses its top block
Add \text{Clear}(\text{src})


The destination block gains a top block
Delete \text{Clear}(\text{dst})


The moving block’s own top
Nothing: it remains clear




The initial state and action effects must keep these summary facts consistent with the arrangement.


The quantified formula explains the meaning for block arguments only. It is not a formula evaluated by the state-set engine. Clear(Table) has the separate capacity convention already stated. Adding Clear(Table) after moving a block off it is harmless because that atom was already true.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1, blocks-world Clear predicate. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Moving Onto a Block
b and \text{dst} are distinct blocks. \text{src} is a block or Table, different from both.


Move(b, src, dst)


PRE: On(b, src) and Clear(b) and Clear(dst)


ADD: On(b, dst), Clear(src)


DELETE: On(b, src), Clear(dst)


Example: \text{Move}(B,\text{Table},C) puts B onto C.

Why must the schema delete \text{Clear}(C)?


B now occupies C’s top. Leaving \text{Clear}(C) true would allow an impossible second block to move onto C.


PRE, ADD, and DELETE refer to the three sets just defined. Type and inequality guards in the sentence above the code are part of the schema, even though we omit their fixed predicates from the displayed PRE line. dst cannot be Table. src may be Table, in which case its Clear atom stays true.
[Sources] - AIMA Figure 11.4, with explicit parameter restrictions and add/delete presentation. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Moving Onto the Table
b and \text{src} are distinct blocks. The table is a constant, not a block.


MoveToTable(b, src)


PRE: On(b, src) and Clear(b)


ADD: On(b, Table), Clear(src)


DELETE: On(b, src)



No occupied-top check or delete effect is needed for the table. It has space for multiple blocks in this model.


This action moves onto the table. Its source must be a block, which excludes the useless MoveToTable(b,Table) instance. The earlier Beamer source mislabeled this as handling moves off the table. Explain the direction from the actual arguments rather than preserving that wording.
[Sources] - AIMA Figure 11.4, MoveToTable action. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Grounding an Action
Use the same replacements in every rule: b=C and \text{src}=A.
\text{MoveToTable}(b,\text{src})\quad\leadsto\quad\text{MoveToTable}(C,A).



Grounded set
Facts




Preconditions
\text{On}(C,A),\ \text{Clear}(C)


Add
\text{On}(C,\text{Table}),\ \text{Clear}(A)


Delete
\text{On}(C,A)



The object restrictions also hold: C and A are different blocks.

After this action, does B remain on the table?


Yes. \text{On}(B,\text{Table}) appears in neither effect set, so it persists.


The leadsto arrow denotes schema instantiation, not logical implication. All dynamic preconditions are true initially. The effect both clears A and keeps C’s own top clear.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1. Worked instance of Figure 11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Plan, Step by Step
Goal: \text{On}(A,B)\land\text{On}(B,C).

   


1. \text{MoveToTable}(C,A) adds \text{Clear}(A).


2. \text{Move}(B,\text{Table},C) achieves \text{On}(B,C).


3. \text{Move}(A,\text{Table},B) achieves \text{On}(A,B).


At each reveal, ask whether the next move is applicable. Before step 2, C and B are clear. After step 2, B remains clear while C is not. Before step 3, A and B are clear. The two goal facts now hold together.
[Sources] - AIMA Figure 11.4 solution sequence. Original animated draw.io frames. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Checking a Proposed Plan
For k actions a_1,\ldots,a_k, s_i is the state after action i:

Start with the complete initial state s_0.
Check \text{Pre}(a_i)\subseteq s_{i-1} before every action.
Compute s_i=(s_{i-1}\setminus\text{Del}(a_i))\cup\text{Add}(a_i).
Check G\subseteq s_k at the end.


What is wrong with starting our plan with \text{Move}(A,\text{Table},B)?


The action needs \text{Clear}(A), which is false initially. Achieving a goal fact is insufficient if the action is not executable.


Define i as the action index and k as the sequence length. s_i denotes the state after i actions. A validator can reject a plan at the first failed precondition without running a physical robot. It validates the encoded model, so model accuracy still matters.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.1, solution definition. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Effect-Set Practice
Suppose all three blocks are separate on the table. Execute \text{Move}(B,\text{Table},C).

Which facts change? Is B still clear afterward?


Add: \text{On}(B,C),\ \text{Clear}(\text{Table}).
Delete: \text{On}(B,\text{Table}),\ \text{Clear}(C).


\text{Clear}(B) persists. Adding \text{Clear}(\text{Table}) is redundant because that fixed fact already holds.


This is the middle action of the plan. Ask students to distinguish the moving block’s top from the destination block’s top. The effect set is the schema’s specification, while the set of actually changed truth values omits the redundant Clear(Table) addition.
[Sources] - Original exercise using AIMA Figure 11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Candidate Actions and Applicability
A candidate is a ground action allowed by the object rules: correct types and different objects where required.
With five blocks and one table:








Schema
Parameter choices
Candidates




\text{Move}(b,\text{src},\text{dst})
5 moving blocks, 4 destinations, 4 sources
5\times4\times4=80


\text{MoveToTable}(b,\text{src})
5 moving blocks, 4 block sources
5\times4=20


Total
Before state-dependent checks
100




For example, \text{Move}(A,\text{Table},B) is a candidate but initially cannot run: A is not clear. Candidates still need state-dependent precondition checks.


For Move, choose distinct b and dst among the five blocks. src can be any of the six objects except b and dst, giving four choices. For MoveToTable, src must be one of the four other blocks. Blind enumeration over all six objects would yield 216 plus 36 assignments, but many violate fixed type and inequality guards. We count the well-formed candidates here, not the branching factor of a particular state.
[Sources] - Original calculation for the restricted AIMA Figure 11.4 schemas. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
State Growth and Model Constraints
Each Boolean fact is true or false. A truth assignment chooses these values for all m facts, giving up to 2^m combinations.
A state constraint is a rule for a valid arrangement:

Each block has exactly one support.
A block supports at most one block.
No cycles: A on B and B on A is forbidden.
Clear facts agree with the arrangement.


An invariant is a rule preserved by every legal action. Our schemas preserve these constraints if the initial arrangement is valid.


m counts dynamic atoms, not objects. For three blocks there are nine possible On atoms and three Clear atoms, yielding 4096 raw assignments, but only 13 valid arrangements in this simplified domain. The Block atoms and Clear(Table) are fixed. We do not need a complexity-class detour to explain why representation and pruning matter.
The schemas preserve the stated invariants from valid states because they move only a clear block onto a clear distinct block or the table. They do not repair an already inconsistent input state. A validator should check the model’s initial state too.
[Sources] - AIMA Sections 11.1-11.2. Original three-block counting example. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

A plan must satisfy every action’s preconditions in sequence.
Grounding fills a schema’s variable slots with named objects.
Add/delete effects update a complete state. Other facts persist.
A partial goal tests only its required facts.
Type restrictions and state constraints remove invalid candidates.


Next: search forward from the initial state or backward from the goal to find an action sequence.

Asset credits

[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Section 11.1, in both U.S. and Global editions. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Same Planning Problem

Goal: G=\{\text{On}(A,B),\text{On}(B,C)\}.
Recall: a state is its true facts. The Move and MoveToTable schemas are reusable rules with preconditions and effects.

How could an algorithm discover the three-move plan, rather than having us supply it?


Retain the exact initial facts from Lecture 19: On(A,Table), On(B,Table), On(C,A), Clear(B), Clear(C), the three Block facts, and Clear(Table). A schematic plan path is only one branch of the search. All moves have unit cost.
[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Sections 11.1-11.2 and Figure 11.4. - Original draw.io arrangement from Lecture 19. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Progression: Forward State Search
Progression starts at the initial state and applies actions whose preconditions hold in the current state s.







Operation
Rule




Choose an action a
\text{Pre}(a)\subseteq s


Compute the next state (successor)
(s\setminus\text{Del}(a))\cup\text{Add}(a)


Check the goal
G\subseteq s



In our initial state, both actions below are legal:

\text{MoveToTable}(C,A) clears A.
\text{Move}(B,\text{Table},C) achieves one goal fact but puts B on top of C.


Preconditions determine legal choices. Search decides which to explore.


The second move builds B on C while C is still on A. To free A later, we must move B off C before moving C off A, undoing the partial goal. It is a useful example of why immediate goal progress can be misleading. The first move is part of a shortest plan, but forward search must evaluate alternatives.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.1. Original comparison in the AIMA blocks domain. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Breadth-First Progression
Pseudocode. Immutable means each stored state stays unchanged.
def breadth_first_plan(initial, goal):
    frontier = deque([(initial, [])])
    seen = {initial}
    while frontier:
        s, plan = frontier.popleft()
        if goal <= s:
            return plan
        for a in applicable_actions(s):
            nxt = result(s, a)
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                frontier.append((nxt, plan + [a]))
    return None

Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue. deque stores the queue. popleft() removes its oldest entry.
frontier stores (state, plan) pairs. seen records visited states.
goal <= s tests whether every goal fact holds in state s.


FIFO means first in, first out. deque is Python’s double-ended queue from collections, and popleft removes the oldest item. An immutable frozenset is one possible state representation. applicable_actions tests the typed ground actions’ preconditions. result implements the add/delete update from Lecture 19.
This is teaching pseudocode, not a complete runnable implementation. The highlighted groups cover initialization, goal checking, expansion with repeat prevention, and failure after exhaustion. Under unit costs, BFS finds a shortest action sequence. Unequal costs require uniform-cost search or a suitable heuristic search.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.1 and standard graph BFS, adapted to the planning representation. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Regression: Backward Goal Search
Regression searches backward: which facts must hold before an action achieves goal set G? Its search nodes are requirements, not complete states.
A useful action must:

Add at least one required fact: \text{Add}(a)\cap G\ne\varnothing.
Delete none of the required facts: \text{Del}(a)\cap G=\varnothing.

Here \cap means shared facts and \varnothing is the empty set. The previous requirements are:
\text{Regress}(G,a)=\bigl(G\setminus\text{Add}(a)\bigr)\cup\text{Pre}(a).

Keep goals that the action does not establish. Add every precondition of that action.


This formula is for positive conjunctive goals and positive-precondition add/delete actions. Regression nodes are sets of requirements, not complete world states. The search stops when the initial state satisfies the regressed set. Additional invariant tests may prune physically impossible combinations.
Fixed type constraints are handled during grounding. A backward graph search should also record chosen actions and avoid repeated goal sets. It then executes the selected actions in reverse order of selection.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Regressing the Last Move
Goal: G=\{\text{On}(A,B),\text{On}(B,C)\}.
Choose a=\text{Move}(A,\text{Table},B) as the last action.







Step
Required facts




Remove the goal that a adds
\text{On}(B,C)


Add all preconditions of a
\text{On}(A,\text{Table}),\text{Clear}(A),\text{Clear}(B)




Before that last move, B must already be on C, while A is on the table and both A and B are clear.


The chosen action also adds Clear(Table), but it was not a goal requirement, so it removes nothing else from G. It deletes On(A,Table) and Clear(B), neither of which is in the target goal set. This makes it compatible with G.
The regressed set describes potentially many predecessor states. Do not draw it as a single fully specified block arrangement and call that the regression node.
[Sources] - Original worked application of AIMA Section 11.2.2 to Figure 11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Backward Trace
For compact notation, \text{Tbl} denotes the table on this slide.

   








Set
Requirements




G_3
\text{On}(A,B),\text{On}(B,C)


G_2
\text{On}(B,C),\text{On}(A,\text{Tbl}),\text{Clear}(A),\text{Clear}(B)


G_1
\text{On}(A,\text{Tbl}),\text{On}(B,\text{Tbl}),\text{Clear}(A),\text{Clear}(B),\text{Clear}(C)


G_0
\text{On}(A,\text{Tbl}),\text{On}(B,\text{Tbl}),\text{On}(C,A),\text{Clear}(B),\text{Clear}(C)




All facts in G_0 hold initially. Execute the selected actions forward: \text{MoveToTable}(C,A), \text{Move}(B,\text{Tbl},C), \text{Move}(A,\text{Tbl},B).


G_i denotes the required facts before the final 3-i actions. Regress G3 through Move(A,Table,B), then G2 through Move(B,Table,C), then G1 through MoveToTable(C,A). The three operations select actions last to first. The resulting G0 includes On(C,A) and Clear(C), but no longer requires Clear(A), because the first move establishes it.
Tbl abbreviates the Table object. Fixed Block predicates and Clear(Table) remain true and their type guards are already checked in these ground actions.
[Sources] - Original regression trace using AIMA Sections 11.1-11.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Actions That Threaten a Goal
An action threatens a goal if it deletes a required fact. Consider a new goal for our initial arrangement:
G=\{\text{Clear}(A),\text{Clear}(B)\}.
This goal is feasible: both facts hold when all three blocks are on the table.

Could a=\text{Move}(C,A,B) be the last action just because it clears A?


No. It adds \text{Clear}(A) but deletes \text{Clear}(B).
\text{Del}(a)\cap G=\{\text{Clear}(B)\}\ne\varnothing.


\text{MoveToTable}(C,A) achieves both goals directly. The rejected move can still occur earlier in a longer plan.


Use the same initial arrangement: C rests on A, while B is separate on the table. Only the goal changes for this example. The two goal facts can hold together, and MoveToTable(C,A) achieves them in one step.
Move(C,A,B) is legal initially: C is on A, and C and B are clear. It adds On(C,B) and Clear(A), but deletes On(C,A) and Clear(B). The delete intersection with G is therefore exactly {Clear(B)}, so regression rejects it as the last action for this goal set.
This is a rejection of an action choice at this backward-search node, not a claim that the action is always unusable. A valid longer plan is Move(C,A,B), followed by MoveToTable(C,B). The second move restores Clear(B), while Clear(A) persists.
[Sources] - Original check using the relevance and consistency conditions of AIMA Section 11.2.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Heuristics for Planning
A heuristic h(s) estimates remaining plan cost, here the number of moves.
An easy starting point counts goal facts not yet true. |X| means the number of facts in set X:
h_{\text{goal}}(s)=|G\setminus s|.
In our initial state, both goal facts are missing, so h_{\text{goal}}=2. A shortest plan needs 3 moves because C must first leave A.

Goal counting misses prerequisite moves. It can also overestimate: one switch could turn on two lights, achieving two goal facts in one action.


This heuristic is a simple illustration, not a general admissible heuristic. Admissible means never overestimating the true optimal remaining cost. A* needs an appropriate heuristic and repeat-handling policy for its optimality guarantee.
A relaxed problem omits some constraints and supplies a more systematic estimate. The next slide introduces the common delete relaxation. No action-cost asymmetry is present in the blocks example.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.3, planning heuristics. Original comparison against the shortest three-move plan. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Delete Relaxation
A relaxation drops rules to make a problem easier. Delete relaxation ignores delete effects but keeps preconditions and add effects.
Robot example: L,R are locations; \text{At}(L) means the robot is at L. \text{Go}(L,R) requires \text{At}(L), adds \text{At}(R), and deletes \text{At}(L).

Fast Forward (FF) is a planner. It estimates cost by counting actions in a relaxed plan, one that solves the easier problem.

The relaxed robot can be “in both places.” This easier problem guides search, but its plan may violate the real model.


The optimum cost of a delete-relaxed plan is a lower bound on optimum real cost, because every real plan is valid in the relaxed positive-precondition model. Computing that optimum can still be hard. FF, expanded as Fast Forward, extracts a practical relaxed-plan estimate that is not generally admissible.
In positive-precondition delete relaxation, facts accumulate rather than disappear. This can make later actions available without undoing earlier achievements. We return to a different reachability structure, the planning graph, on the next slide.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.3. - Hoffmann and Nebel, The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search, https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0675. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Planning Graph
A planning graph alternates layers (levels): possible facts S_t after t steps, then possible actions A_t.
A no-op (no operation) keeps a fact true in the next layer. Mutex means mutually exclusive: facts cannot hold together, or actions conflict at that step.


Moving gives \text{At}(R); staying gives \text{At}(L). S_1 lists both possibilities, not one state where the robot is in both places.


This uses the robot model from the preceding slide. The layer indexes represent increasing planning depth. Go deletes At(L), so it conflicts with the no-op that keeps At(L). Their resulting facts have inconsistent support at S1 and are mutex.
A planning graph summarizes many possible histories and may overapproximate what can jointly hold. It is distinct from the earlier state-space graph, whose nodes are individual complete states. Unlike plain delete relaxation, this graph retains mutex information. Static connectivity is implicit in the single allowed Go action.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.4 and Section 11.3, planning graphs. - https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15281/coursenotes/classicalplan/ - Original draw.io robot graph. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Mutex and Graphplan
An action supports a fact if it makes that fact true. For example, \text{Go}(L,R) supports \text{At}(R).
Actions can conflict when:

One deletes another’s precondition or effect.
Their preconditions are mutually exclusive at the preceding fact layer.

Graphplan grows the graph, then performs plan extraction: a backward search for compatible actions whose effects achieve the goals.

If all goal facts appear in a layer, do we already have a valid plan?


No. The goals may be mutex, or the actions supporting them may conflict. Even non-mutex goals still need a successful plan extraction.


Fact mutex also includes opposite literals and inconsistent support: every possible pair of supporting actions is mutex. Pairwise non-mutex goals are a useful test, not a complete guarantee that a plan exists. Graphplan includes backward extraction and records failures rather than simply reading a path through the reachability graph.
Depending on the encoding, Graphplan permits nonconflicting parallel action sets and seeks a small number of layers. This need not minimize the number of sequential actions, so do not equate its objective with our BFS unit-action optimum.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.4. - https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~avrim/graphplan.html [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Planning as Boolean Satisfiability
Boolean satisfiability (SAT) asks whether true/false values can satisfy all constraints in a formula. A working choice is a satisfying assignment, also called a SAT model.
An encoding translates planning rules into Boolean constraints. Fix a horizon T: the number of available action steps. Represent states at t=0,\ldots,T and actions at t=0,\ldots,T-1.



Horizon for our blocks task
A plan within that horizon?




T=0,1,2
No


T=3
Yes: the three-move plan




Unsatisfiable means no truth assignment works. At T=2, this rules out plans within two steps. Longer plans may still exist.


Here T is a time-step horizon. Use a sequential encoding with at most one real action per step and allow idle steps, so the question is existence within T steps. Under these conditions the minimum horizon matches the fewest unit-cost actions. Alternative parallel encodings measure a different objective.
The numbers follow from the block task: A and B must each move to their goal supports, and C must leave A first. This gives a lower bound of three, achieved by the displayed plan.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.3. Original bounded-horizon application to Figure 11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
SAT Encoding Ingredients
Each Boolean variable is true or false, recording a fact at a time or whether a ground action occurs.







Constraint
What it enforces




Initial state
Every initial fact’s true or false value at t=0


Goal
Required facts hold at t=T


Action preconditions
A chosen action is applicable


Action effects
Its add/delete changes occur at t+1


Frame constraints
Only actions that add/delete a fact can change it


Action choice
At most one action per step in our sequential model




Frame constraints enforce persistence. Without them, the solver could invent \text{On}(A,B) even when no action puts A onto B.


Unlike a state set that leaves false facts implicit, an SAT encoding must constrain their initial values too. Otherwise unspecified initial variables can be chosen to make an easier problem. Frame constraints connect each next-state atom to its current value and the actions that may add or delete it. The serial action constraint is an encoding choice rather than a requirement of every SAT planner.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.2.3 and Section 7.7.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A One-Step SAT Example
Robot model: the only real action is \text{Go}(L,R).
Variables: p_t means at L at time t, q_t means at R at time t, and m_0 means the action occurs in step 0.
\rightarrow means “if … then.” \leftrightarrow means “if and only if.”







Requirement
Boolean constraint




Initial state and goal
p_0\land\neg q_0\land q_1


Precondition
m_0\rightarrow p_0


At L afterward: there before and no move
p_1\leftrightarrow(p_0\land\neg m_0)


At R afterward: there before or a move
q_1\leftrightarrow(q_0\lor m_0)




q_0=\text{false} and q_1=\text{true} force m_0=\text{true}: the robot must move.


The biconditionals give both causal change and persistence for the one-action model. If m0 is false, both locations keep their initial values. If m0 is true, the robot leaves L and arrives at R, with the precondition requiring it to start at L. These are all the constraints needed for this deliberately small one-step example, in addition to the usual Boolean variable domains.
If we kept only m0 implies q1, the assignment m0=false, q1=true could invent arrival. The reverse causal direction is therefore essential. This is an illustration of SAT planning rather than the full blocks-world encoding.
[Sources] - Original encoding using AIMA Section 11.2.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Bounded SAT Planning
Conceptual Python pseudocode. The bound max_horizon is the largest number of action steps to try.
def sat_plan(problem, max_horizon):
    for T in range(max_horizon + 1):
        formula = encode(problem, T)
        model = solve_sat(formula)
        if model is not None:
            return extract_actions(model)
    return None

encode builds all constraints for that horizon.
solve_sat returns a satisfying assignment or None.
extract_actions reads the selected actions in time order.


None here means no plan within the tested bound. Validate an extracted plan against the original action model.


The helpers are conceptual, not a standalone implementation. An actual solver may also return unknown or time out, which must not be treated as a proof of unsatisfiability. Increasing horizons indefinitely can fail to terminate on an unsolvable task, so this version has an explicit bound. An empty assignment can be a valid model, hence the explicit is not None check.
For exact, complete sequential encodings with idle steps, the first satisfying horizon gives a minimum-action plan. If actions carry unequal costs, minimizing the horizon alone does not minimize cost.
[Sources] - Teaching adaptation of SATPlan from AIMA Section 11.2.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Hierarchical Task Network Planning
A hierarchical task network (HTN) arranges tasks and their required order.

Abstract task: a high-level request, such as “build the tower.”
Method: a rule for refinement (decomposition): splitting a task into subtasks.
Primitive task: an executable action, such as \text{MoveToTable}(C,A).



Each primitive action must still satisfy its preconditions.


This diagram shows one method suitable for the initial arrangement of our example, not a universal recipe for every tower task. A complete domain can contain alternative methods with different applicability conditions. The arrows between subtasks indicate ordering constraints, not state transitions or causal implication.
HTN planning can restrict search to decompositions supplied by domain knowledge. A state-space plan might exist but be excluded by the available methods. This is why a method library’s coverage matters.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 11.4. Original tower-method illustration. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Planning Approaches Compared








Approach
Search representation
Key check




Progression
Complete states
Action applicable now?


Regression
Required fact sets
Action achieves goals without deleting others?


Planning graph / Graphplan
Possible facts and supporting actions by layer
Can chosen actions jointly achieve the goals?


SAT planning
Boolean assignments over time
All encoded constraints satisfied?


HTN planning
Task decompositions
Valid task splits and executable final actions?




Heuristics can guide progression or regression, so heuristic search is not necessarily a separate representation family. Planning graphs can also supply heuristics. The table compares representations rather than claiming one method always dominates the others.
[Sources] - AIMA Sections 11.2-11.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Quick Check

Why must regression keep goal facts that the chosen action does not add?


Those facts must already hold beforehand and survive the action. Replacing the entire goal with only the preconditions can lose requirements.


The SAT formula is unsatisfiable at horizon 2. Can we conclude that the task has no plan?


No. Test a longer horizon. Our blocks example first has a solution at horizon 3.


Pause before revealing each answer. These check two common errors: discarding unachieved goals during regression, and interpreting bounded SAT failure as global impossibility.
[Sources] - Original questions using AIMA Section 11.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Progression searches executable state transitions. Repeated-state handling prevents cycles.
Regression preserves remaining goals and adds action preconditions.
Relaxed problems help estimate cost. Planning graphs also flag conflicts.
SAT planning needs full transition constraints and a stated horizon.
HTN methods guide decomposition, with primitive actions checked against the model.


Every returned plan must work under the original preconditions, effects, and goal test.

Asset credits

[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Sections 11.2-11.4, in both U.S. and Global editions. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Uncertainty in AI
An alarm sounds. Does that prove a robot has a defective part?



Observation
Possible explanation




Alarm sounds
A defective part triggered it


Alarm sounds
A working part triggered a false alarm



Probability assigns numbers to uncertainty under a stated model.

Would the same alarm mean the same thing if defects were common rather than rare?


We need both the alarm’s behavior and how common defects are. We will calculate this near the end of the lecture.


Connect to the deterministic models in planning: an observation can have several explanations. The robot example is hypothetical, not measured equipment reliability. Probability can guide decisions, but choosing an action also requires a cost or utility model.
[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Sections 12.1-12.2 and Appendix A.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Probability Rules
An axiom is a starting rule. The basic axioms require nonnegative probabilities, P(\Omega)=1, and additivity for disjoint events.







Rule
Meaning




0\le P(A)\le1
Every event has a valid probability


P(A^c)=1-P(A)
A^c is the complement: outcomes outside A


P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) if A\cap B=\varnothing
Disjoint events have no shared outcomes


P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)
Otherwise, subtract the overlap counted twice



\cup means or, \cap means and, and \varnothing is the empty set.
For the die, even A and at-least-4 B overlap at 4,6:
P(A\cup B)=\frac36+\frac36-\frac26=\frac46.

The upper bound 1 and complement rule follow from the axioms. General additivity applies to countably many pairwise disjoint events. The finite examples here avoid measure-theory details. The union is {2,4,5,6}, checking the arithmetic by counting.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.2 and Appendix A.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Mean and Variance
The expectation or mean is a probability-weighted average:
\mu=E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x).
The variance measures spread using squared distances from the mean:
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2].
For our head count, the PMF is (1/4,1/2,1/4) at x=0,1,2.

\begin{aligned}
E[X]&=0\left(\frac14\right)+1\left(\frac12\right)+2\left(\frac14\right)=1,\\
\operatorname{Var}(X)&=(0-1)^2\left(\frac14\right)+(1-1)^2\left(\frac12\right)+(2-1)^2\left(\frac14\right)=\frac12.
\end{aligned}


An expected value is an average, not a guaranteed outcome. A fair die has mean 3.5, even though no roll produces 3.5.


The sum runs over every possible value of X. Variance uses squared units, and standard deviation is its square root. Var(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2 gives 1.5-1=0.5 here.
[Sources] - AIMA Appendix A.3 and Stanford CS229 probability review, Sections 2.4-2.5. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Linearity of Expectation
Linearity means that the expectation of a sum equals the sum of the expectations:
E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y].
Let X be 1 if the first fair coin toss is heads and 0 otherwise. Define Y the same way for the second toss.
E[X]=\frac12,\qquad E[Y]=\frac12,\qquad E[X+Y]=1.

Does the identity still hold if Y=X, so the variables are completely dependent?


Yes: E[X+X]=2E[X]. Linearity does not require independence, provided the expectations exist. This is useful for adding waiting times in HW4.


These 0/1 variables are indicators: they mark whether an event occurs. Their expectations equal their event probabilities. For HW4, divide the total collection time into stages and add stage expectations without first proving stage independence. No full assignment derivation is needed here.
[Sources] - AIMA Appendix A.3 and Stanford CS229 probability review, Section 2.4. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Continuous Variables and a PDF
A continuous variable takes values along a range. Its probability density function (PDF) f_U(u) gives probability per unit length. Area gives probability.
Let U be uniform on [0,2]: equal-length intervals are equally likely. Its density is 1/2 on that interval and 0 outside it.

P(0.5\le U\le1)=\int_{0.5}^1 f_U(u)\,du=(1-0.5)\left(\frac12\right)=\frac14.

Here P(U=u)=0. Density can exceed 1. Only area gives probability.


The entire area is 2 times 1/2, which equals 1. A uniform density on [0,0.1] has height 10. A cumulative distribution function (CDF) gives F_U(u)=P(U<=u), accumulating area up to u. This prepares students for uniform angular positions in HW4.
[Sources] - AIMA Appendix A.3 and Stanford CS229 probability review, Sections 2.1-2.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Joint Distribution
A joint distribution assigns probability to combinations of variable values.
Toy model: W is weather and U is umbrella use. These symbols are local to this model.



P(W=w,U=u)
U=\text{Yes}
U=\text{No}




W=\text{Sunny}
0.10
0.60


W=\text{Rainy}
0.20
0.10



All four entries are nonnegative and sum to 1.

Which entry represents rain and an umbrella? Which entries represent rain regardless of umbrella use?


Rain and umbrella: 0.20. Rain regardless of umbrella: 0.20+0.10=0.30.


A comma inside P(W=w,U=u) means the two events hold together. P(w,u) abbreviates the same thing once variables are clear. Every cell in a full joint table shares one total sum of 1. These numbers match the model at the start of Lecture 22.
[Sources] - AIMA Sections 12.2-12.3. Original course weather model. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Marginal and Conditional Distributions



Weather w
P(w,U=\text{Yes})
P(w,U=\text{No})




Sunny
0.10
0.60


Rainy
0.20
0.10



Marginalization sums over a variable we do not keep:
P(W=\text{Rainy})=\sum_u P(W=\text{Rainy},U=u)=0.20+0.10=0.30.
Conditioning fixes a variable to its observed value:
P(W=\text{Rainy}\mid U=\text{Yes})=\frac{0.20}{0.10+0.20}=\frac23.

Ignoring umbrella use and observing an umbrella answer different questions. For continuous variables, marginalization integrates the joint density instead of summing it.


The marginal P(U=Yes)=0.3 provides the denominator. Conditioning keeps its Yes column and normalizes it. An unobserved variable in a marginal is not assumed to be No.
For continuous X,Y, the counterparts are f_X(x)=integral f_X,Y(x,y) dy and f_X|Y(x|y)=f_X,Y(x,y)/f_Y(y) when f_Y(y)>0. The weather variables in the table are discrete.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.3 and Appendix A.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Spam Given a Keyword
Let S mean spam and K mean an email contains a particular keyword. The toy model gives:
P(S)=0.30,\qquad P(K\mid S)=0.60,\qquad P(K\mid\neg S)=0.20.


The law of total probability adds the spam and non-spam routes:
P(K)=P(K\mid S)P(S)+P(K\mid\neg S)P(\neg S)=0.18+0.14=0.32.


P(S\mid K)=180/(180+140)=0.5625. The keyword raises the spam probability from 30\% to 56.25\%.


The frequencies describe a hypothetical population matching the probabilities, not an observed dataset. Out of 320 keyword emails, 180 are spam. This equals (0.60 times 0.30)/0.32. Both keyword-producing routes belong in the denominator.
Total probability sums over a disjoint, exhaustive partition. Here S and not S form that partition.
[Sources] - Spam example from the supplied course material. AIMA Section 12.5. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rare Defects and False Positives
Defective: D. Flagged: F. Base rate: P(D)=0.01 (1% defective).

True-positive rate: flags 95% of defective parts, P(F\mid D)=0.95.
False-positive rate: flags 5% of working parts, P(F\mid\neg D)=0.05.



Among the flagged parts, what fraction are actually defective?


P(D\mid F)=95/(95+495)\approx16.1\%. Most flagged parts are working.


This uses the supplied false-positive example’s numbers in hypothetical parts inspection. A false positive is a positive prediction for an item without the condition. The flagged fraction is 0.95(0.01)+0.05(0.99)=0.059. The posterior is 0.0095/0.059, or 95/590.
The base rate changes the interpretation even if the conditional alarm rates stay fixed. Choosing a repair policy also requires repair and failure costs.
[Sources] - Numerical teaching example from the supplied course material, adapted to robot parts. AIMA Section 12.5. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Joint-Probability Practice
An image classifier predicts a handwritten digit. Let:

X be image brightness, scaled to [0,1].
Y be the predicted digit, one of 0,1,\ldots,9.

Suppose P(Y=3)=0.15 and P(X>0.5\mid Y=3)=0.60.

What is the probability that an image is bright and predicted as digit 3?


P(X>0.5,Y=3)=P(X>0.5\mid Y=3)P(Y=3)=0.60(0.15)=0.09. This describes 9\% of images under the model.


X is continuous, but X>0.5 is an event with nonzero probability, so ordinary event probability applies. Y is the classifier’s prediction, not the true digit. The calculation therefore does not measure accuracy.
[Sources] - Image-classification example from the supplied course material. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Define the sample space, events, and variables before calculating.
Conditioning keeps the observed event and rescales its probabilities.
Independence is a property of the model, not a default assumption.
PMFs assign mass to values. PDFs give probabilities through area.
Bayes’ rule combines likelihoods and base rates to update beliefs.
Linearity lets us add expectations without assuming independence.


Homework 4: Probability in Motion: geometric probability, random walks, and coupon collection. Define your events and show the reasoning behind each step.

[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Appendix A.3 and Sections 12.1-12.5. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Inference from an Observation
Someone has a toothache. How likely is a cavity?
Probabilistic inference uses a probability model and observed information to calculate probabilities of unknown quantities.



Term
Meaning
Our question




Query
What we want to find out
Is there a cavity?


Evidence
What we have observed
There is a toothache




Could a toothache have another explanation? What would that mean for our answer?


The answer is a probability under the model. An observation can support an explanation without proving it.


Connect to Lecture 21’s alarm example. Today the model is already supplied: inference computes answers from it, rather than learning its probabilities from data. A probability alone does not choose an action without a cost or utility model.
The dental example is an illustrative AIMA model, not clinical guidance or measured medical reliability. Work through the table slowly enough for students to track the changing denominators. Leave time for the two-evidence exercise, robot practice, and HW4 questions.
[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Section 12.3. - UC Berkeley CS 188, Inference: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/bayes-nets/inference.html. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Model Variables and Notation
Each variable is Boolean, or binary: it takes either \text{true} or \text{false}.







Variable
What true means




C: cavity
The tooth has a cavity


T: toothache
The person has a toothache


H: probe catches
The tip of a dentist’s small examining tool gets stuck on the tooth



We use the shorthand C for the event C=\text{true}, and \neg C for C=\text{false}. The same convention applies to T and H.
P(C,T)=P(C\text{ and }T),\qquad P(C\mid T)=\text{probability of }C\text{ given }T.

A comma means that both listed events occur. The vertical bar means given. A probe catch is a separate observation from toothache. The letter H is simply the label used in this course for that observation.
An uppercase letter sometimes names a random variable and sometimes its true event; the shorthand above makes that convention explicit. A distribution over C has two outcomes, true and false.
[Sources] - Supplied Spring 2025 Beamer lecture, toothache example. AIMA Sections 12.2-12.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
The Full Joint Table
A full joint distribution assigns probability to every complete assignment: one value for each variable.





T,H
T,\neg H
\neg T,H
\neg T,\neg H

0.144
