For example, P(C,T,\neg H)=0.012: cavity and toothache and no probe catch.

Which entry means toothache and a probe catch, but no cavity?


P(\neg C,T,H)=0.016. All eight entries are nonnegative and sum to 1. Individual rows need not sum to 1.


These are joint probabilities over the whole hypothetical population, not conditional probabilities within a row. There are eight assignments because three Boolean variables have 2^3 combinations. The table’s cavity row totals 0.2 and no-cavity row totals 0.8.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.3, toothache/cavity/catch full joint distribution. Values preserved from the supplied Beamer lecture. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Query, Evidence, and Hidden Variables
We want the cavity probability given a toothache: P(C\mid T).



Role
Variable
Operation




Query
Cavity C
Keep its true and false outcomes separate


Evidence
Toothache T
Fix it to the observed value, true


Hidden
Probe catch H
Add over both possible values



A hidden variable is in the model but is neither queried nor observed.

We did not observe a probe result. Would setting H=\text{false} still answer our question?


No. That adds an observation we do not have and changes the question to P(C\mid T,\neg H).


Variable roles depend on the query, not on permanent labels in the model. H becomes evidence if a probe result is observed. If the query were P(H given C), H would be the query, C evidence, and T hidden.
[Sources] - UC Berkeley CS 188, Inference by Enumeration. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Step 1: Filter by the Evidence
Filtering keeps only complete assignments that match what we observed. Here, T=\text{true}.



Cavity C
Probe catch H
Retained joint probability

The four assignments with T=\text{false} do not match the evidence.

The retained entries sum to P(T)=0.20. They are still joint probabilities. We have not rescaled them yet.


Filtering here means selecting rows of a joint table. It is not the separate time-series filtering problem discussed in temporal models. If the original table is laid out as two rows and four columns, this operation keeps its two toothache columns. The long-form table here lists the four surviving assignments explicitly.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.3. UC Berkeley CS 188, Inference by Enumeration. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Step 2: Sum the Hidden Values
Add the two probe possibilities separately for each cavity outcome.

Each total is an unnormalized weight: a nonnegative value before rescaling to sum to 1.
w_C=P(C,T)=0.12,\qquad w_{\neg C}=P(\neg C,T)=0.08.

The hidden variable H has been summed out. Cavity status C remains the query.


These particular weights are joint probabilities with the observed event. Weights in other algorithms can have a different common scale; normalizing still works if they are proportional to the desired probabilities and their sum is positive. The subscripts on w label the true and false cavity outcomes.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.3. Original draw.io diagram using the AIMA table entries. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Step 3: Normalize the Weights
Normalization divides each nonnegative weight by the sum of all the weights. Here that sum is P(T)=0.12+0.08=0.20.




Query outcome
Weight
Conditional probability




Cavity
0.12
P(C\mid T)=0.12/0.20=0.60


No cavity
0.08
P(\neg C\mid T)=0.08/0.20=0.40





The normalizing constant \alpha is the reciprocal of the total. Multiplying by it gives the same result:
\alpha=\frac{1}{0.20}=5,\qquad \alpha(0.12,0.08)=(0.60,0.40).


The total must be positive. If the evidence has probability 0 in this discrete model, this conditional probability is undefined.


The two conditional probabilities sum to one. Do not divide by the full table’s total of one: after observing a toothache, the relevant total is 0.20. Alpha is not a new probability; its value can exceed one.
Zero-probability evidence may reveal an inadequate model or an input error. It does not justify silently substituting a uniform distribution.
[Sources] - Supplied Beamer lecture, normalization using alpha. AIMA Section 12.3. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Inference by Enumeration
Enumeration means checking possible complete assignments in the model.

For P(C\mid T), we kept the toothache assignments, summed over the probe result, and divided by 0.20.

This is exact inference: it computes the model’s probabilities without estimating them from random samples. Its accuracy still depends on the model.


An exact calculation is exact relative to the supplied distribution, even if that distribution is a simplified description of reality. The method extends to multiple query variables: preserve each joint query assignment until the final normalization.
[Sources] - UC Berkeley CS 188, Inference by Enumeration: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/bayes-nets/inference.html. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Two Possible Probe Results
With a toothache, P(C\mid T)=0.60. Now observe the probe result.




Catch H
No catch \neg H




Cavity C
0.108
0.012


No cavity \neg C
0.016
0.064




Compute P(C\mid T,H) and P(C\mid T,\neg H).


P(C\mid T,H)=\frac{0.108}{0.108+0.016}\approx0.871.


P(C\mid T,\neg H)=\frac{0.012}{0.012+0.064}\approx0.158.


More evidence can raise or lower a particular explanation’s probability.


Allow students to choose the relevant column and write both denominators before revealing the answers. No hidden variable remains once both T and H are observed in this three-variable model. The displayed numbers remain joint masses from the original table, so each selected column must be normalized separately.
[Sources] - AIMA toothache distribution. Two-evidence practice written for this course. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Reversing a Conditional
From the joint table, P(C)=0.20, P(H)=0.34, and
P(C,H)=0.108+0.072=0.18.



Question
Calculation




Probe catches, given cavity
P(H\mid C)=0.18/0.20=0.90


Cavity, given probe catches
P(C\mid H)=0.18/0.34\approx0.529




Why do the answers differ even though the numerator is the same?


The given events differ. Each denominator is the probability of the event after the bar.


P(H)=0.108+0.072+0.016+0.144=0.34. The numerator is the same intersection in both directions, but conditioning selects different reference populations. This connects directly to Bayes’ rule from Lecture 21.
[Sources] - AIMA Sections 12.3 and 12.5. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Marginal Independence
Marginal independence is ordinary independence: learning one variable leaves the other’s distribution unchanged, without conditioning on a third variable.
Let X and Y be the results of two fair coin tosses. Our model gives:









First toss X
Y=\text{heads}
Y=\text{tails}
Marginal P(X)




heads
0.25
0.25
0.50


tails
0.25
0.25
0.50


Marginal P(Y)
0.50
0.50
1.00




P(X=\text{heads}\mid Y=\text{heads})=\frac{0.25}{0.50}=0.50.
The first toss stays 50% heads after learning the second result. Every joint cell also equals the product of its two marginals: 0.25=0.50(0.50).


The right column and bottom row contain marginal probabilities, obtained by summing over the other toss. The bottom-right 1.00 is the total probability, not an additional outcome. The four inner cells form the full joint distribution of X and Y.
The supplied joint table is the modeling assumption: fairness alone does not imply independence of two tosses. All four pairs have probability one quarter here. Check factorization for every pair, or equivalently note that conditioning on either possible second result leaves the first toss’s full distribution unchanged. The same statement holds with the two tosses interchanged.
Marginal independence is ordinary independence. The qualifier marginal emphasizes the contrast with conditional independence, rather than naming a different notion. It describes X and Y without conditioning on a third variable. The next slide returns to the dental example to introduce independence within a known group. These are different models; the coin example does not claim that the dental observations are marginally independent.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.4, independence. Original fair-coin example and joint table. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Conditional Independence
Back to the toothache model: conditional independence means that, once cavity status is known, learning the probe result gives no further information about toothache.









Known group
P(T\mid\text{group})
P(H\mid\text{group})
P(T,H\mid\text{group})




Cavity
0.60
0.90
0.54=0.60(0.90)


No cavity
0.10
0.20
0.02=0.10(0.20)



The joint probability equals the product within each group.

We write T\perp H\mid C: \perp means independent, and \mid C means given cavity status, for both values of C.


Here C after the bar names the conditioning random variable, not only its true event. The condition holds for both its true and false groups. In the cavity group, P(T,H|C)=0.108/0.20=0.54. In the no-cavity group, 0.016/0.80=0.02. Checking the true-true cell together with the two Boolean marginals establishes factorization for all four T,H outcomes in each group.
This is a property of this toy distribution, not a universal claim about dental observations. Marginal dependence and conditional independence can coexist because mixing different cavity-status groups creates a dependence.
[Sources] - AIMA Section 12.5.2, combining evidence using conditional independence. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Compact Probability Models
A full table for n binary variables has 2^n entries: each new variable doubles its size. At n=50, that is about 10^{15} entries.
A Bayesian network is a graph of variables with local probability tables. Arrows identify the variables each local probability conditions on.

Factorization writes the joint as a product of smaller distributions:
P(C,T,H)=P(C)P(T\mid C)P(H\mid C).

Conditional independence makes this model compact. Exact inference can still be expensive in larger networks.


In the graph, a node represents a random variable. An arrow identifies a variable used in the target’s local conditional probability. This is a preview; the next lecture defines the graph rules and tables in detail. Graph structure by itself is not proof of causation.
A general chain rule gives P(C,T,H)=P(C)P(T|C)P(H|C,T). The conditional-independence property lets us replace the last factor with P(H|C). For example, 0.20 times 0.60 times 0.90 reproduces 0.108. A full binary table has 2^n entries but only 2^n-1 independent free probabilities because they sum to one.
[Sources] - Supplied Beamer lecture, full-joint storage growth. AIMA Sections 13.1-13.2. [/Sources]

Location

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Identify the query, observed evidence, and hidden variables.
Filter by evidence, sum hidden values, then normalize.
Unknown does not mean false. Keep query outcomes separate.
Divide by the evidence probability, which must be positive.
Check independence before replacing a joint probability with a product.
Conditional independence can make a model smaller.


Before calculating, say what is known, what is unknown, and which probability belongs in the denominator.

[Sources] - AIMA fourth edition, Sections 12.3-12.5 and 13.1-13.2. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Graph and Local Probabilities
A Bayesian network combines a graph with local probability tables.


A node is a random variable. Here, each is binary: true or false.
An arrow goes from a parent to a child; a root has no parents.
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) has arrows but no directed cycle: following arrows cannot bring us back to the starting node.

Here C: cavity; T: toothache; H: the dentist’s probe catches on the tooth.

Arrows specify the local conditioning structure, not proof of causation.


The model and illustrative probabilities follow AIMA, fourth edition, Sections 13.1-13.4. These are teaching probabilities, not clinical data. A redundant edge need not imply actual dependence. See https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/bayes-nets/representation.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Local Probability Tables
A conditional probability table (CPT) gives a distribution for each parent assignment. A root uses a prior: its distribution before evidence.



Node
Parent value
Probability true
Probability false




C
No parent
0.20
0.80


T
C=\text{true}
0.60
0.40


T
C=\text{false}
0.10
0.90


H
C=\text{true}
0.90
0.10


H
C=\text{false}
0.20
0.80




Each row sums to 1. The entire table does not need to sum to 1.

For short, C means C=\text{true}; \neg C means C=\text{false}, and similarly for T,H.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Factorization: Local to Joint

Factorization writes the joint probability as a product: each variable is conditioned only on its parents.

P(C,T,H)=P(C)\,P(T\mid C)\,P(H\mid C).


For one complete assignment, all three variables true:

P(C,T,H)=0.20\times0.60\times0.90=0.108.



Use the same product rule for every true/false assignment, selecting the appropriate CPT entries.


The first formula uses the conventional distribution notation; the worked line uses the true-event shorthand defined on the previous slide. Generally, P(X_1,…,X_n) is the product of P(X_i | Parents(X_i)).

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Storage and Inference Cost
A free parameter is a probability we must specify. For a binary variable, the other probability in that row is 1-p.








Binary variables
Full joint: free parameters
Bayesian network: free parameters




Our 3-node network
2^3-1=7
1+2+2=5


50 nodes: one root, one parent per other node
2^{50}-1\approx10^{15}
1+49\times2=99



The saving comes from the network’s conditional-independence assumptions.

A compact model can still require expensive sums for exact inference in a large network.


These counts are free parameters, not the number of stored table cells. For the 50-node example, assume a binary DAG with exactly one root and exactly one parent for each remaining node. General inference difficulty depends on structure as well as node count; tree-structured networks have efficient exact methods.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: One Exact Answer as a Benchmark
text:
One Exact Answer as a Benchmark
Target: P(C\mid T), the posterior probability of a cavity after observing a toothache.

Query variable: what we want to infer, C.
Evidence: an observed value, T=\text{true}.
Hidden variable: unobserved and not the query, here H.

Summing over H leaves these two possibilities:



Cavity status
Joint probability with toothache




True
P(C,T)=0.20\times0.60=0.12


False
P(\neg C,T)=0.80\times0.10=0.08




Normalize: P(C\mid T)=\dfrac{0.12}{0.12+0.08}=0.60.


Summing the H factor gives P(H | C) + P(not H | C) = 1 for either value of C. This small network is easy to solve exactly; it provides a check for approximate methods.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Monte Carlo: Estimate by Random Sampling
text:
Monte Carlo: Estimate by Random Sampling
A sample is one randomly generated assignment, such as (C,T,H)=(\text{true},\text{false},\text{true}).
Monte Carlo estimation approximates probabilities using random samples.



Illustrative batch
Cavity true
Cavity false




20 independent draws from the model
5
15




\widehat{P}(C)=\frac{5}{20}=0.25
\qquad\text{versus the model's }P(C)=0.20.

The hat marks an estimate, not an exact probability from the model.

More independent samples tend to reduce sampling error, but an estimate need not improve after every new draw.


The counts are illustrative, not a measured run. Sampling estimates the specified model, not whether the model describes reality correctly. To estimate a posterior such as P(C | T), we must also account for the evidence.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rejection Sampling: The Algorithm
Evidence is T=\text{true}. Let N be the number of prior draws; counts records the two cavity outcomes.


function EstimateCavity(N)


counts = {true: 0, false: 0}


repeat N times


C, T, H = PriorSample()


if T == true


counts[C] += 1


total = counts[true] + counts[false]


if total == 0: return no_estimate


return counts[true] / total



Divide by the number accepted, not by N. If none match, we have no estimate.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One Weighted Sample
draw_true(p) returns true with probability p, otherwise false. Here w is the sample’s weight for the observed toothache.


function WeightedSample()


C = draw_true(0.20)


T = true


w = 0.60 if C else 0.10


H = draw_true(0.90 if C else 0.20)


return (C, T, H, w)


Across many samples:

\widehat{P}(C\mid T)=\frac{\text{sum of weights for }C=\text{true}}{\text{sum of all weights}}.


If the total weight is zero, the ratio is undefined and there is no estimate from that batch. All weights in this toy model are positive. H is included to illustrate a complete weighted sample; it could be omitted when computing this particular query.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
One Gibbs Update, Worked Out
Suppose the current state has T=\text{true} and H=\text{true}. Resample C while holding these two values fixed.



Candidate value of C
Joint probability with T,H




True
0.20\times0.60\times0.90=0.108


False
0.80\times0.10\times0.20=0.016




P(C\mid T,H)=\frac{0.108}{0.108+0.016}\approx0.871.
Draw a new C: true with probability 0.871, false otherwise.


Next, resample H using the new C: probability 0.90 if C is true, 0.20 otherwise. The evidence T never changes.


Unnormalized means proportional to the desired conditional probability, before dividing by the sum. Given C, H is conditionally independent of T in this graph, so its Gibbs conditional is just its local table. The update illustrated here is a different starting H value from the preceding diagram.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
How the Methods Use Evidence








Method
What happens to evidence?
Main limitation




Prior sampling
Sample it like any other variable
Joint draws alone are not a posterior estimate


Rejection sampling
Discard draws that do not match
Rare evidence wastes draws


Likelihood weighting
Fix its value; weight by its likelihood
A few large weights may dominate


Gibbs sampling
Fix its value; update other variables
Dependent states may explore possibilities slowly




If only 1 in 10,000 prior samples matches the evidence, which method immediately wastes most draws?


Rejection sampling. Fixing the evidence avoids those rejections, but does not guarantee a fast, accurate estimate.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Short Practice: Two Observations
Observe a toothache and no probe catch. Estimate P(C\mid T,\neg H) by likelihood weighting, fixing both observations.
Suppose 1,000 prior draws of C give these counts:



C
Draws
P(T\mid C)
P(\neg H\mid C)




True
200
0.60
0.10


False
800
0.10
0.80




What is each sample’s weight? What is the normalized estimate?


Weights: 0.60\times0.10=0.06 and 0.10\times0.80=0.08.


Total weights: 200\times0.06=12, 800\times0.08=64.
\widehat{P}(C\mid T,\neg H)=\frac{12}{12+64}\approx0.158.


Again these batch counts are illustrative. Because they exactly match the C prior proportions, the estimate equals the exact model answer in this particular example. Contrast with the .60 posterior for toothache alone: no probe catch is evidence against a cavity.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Graph + local tables specify a joint distribution.
Conditional independence makes the representation compact.
Identify the query, evidence, and hidden variables first.
Rejection, weighting, and Gibbs sampling differ in how they use evidence.
An approximate answer still needs enough useful samples; no method is always best.


Same model, same query, different routes to an estimate. Check against an exact answer when one is available.

Asset credits

AIMA, fourth edition, Sections 13.1-13.4. Leave time for questions about HW3, due today. No additional implementation is required by this deck.

The Dental Example, Illustrated




C: Cavity
A small hole caused by decay in a tooth.


T: Toothache
Pain in or around a tooth.


H: Probe catches
A dentist’s pointed tool snags on a rough spot.




Toothache and probe catch are observations, not proof of a cavity.


Read “catches” as “snags” or “gets stuck,” not “finds the tooth.” H records the result of an examination, while T records a symptom. A cavity can exist without either observation, and either observation can occur without a cavity in this simplified probability model. The cartoons illustrate the words, not guaranteed causal relationships or a clinical diagnostic procedure.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Training and Prediction
A model maps an input to an output. A label is an example’s supplied target answer, such as the digit in an image.
One example using labeled data:


Training (or fitting) prepares the model using the available examples.
Prediction applies that model to a new input.


The new input’s label is not an input to the prediction step.


For k-NN, training largely stores the reference examples. Other algorithms fit numerical parameters. The learned model is a hypothesis about the input-output relationship as well as an executable prediction procedure. AIMA Sections 19.1-19.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Three Learning Settings
The feedback available to the learner determines the setting.








Setting
Available feedback
Example




Supervised learning
Inputs paired with target labels
Image and its digit answer


Unsupervised learning
Inputs without target labels
Group similar images


Reinforcement learning (RL)
Reward: numerical feedback from interaction
Learn moves that lead a robot to an exit




Are we given target answers, only inputs, or feedback from actions?


These are three major settings, not an exhaustive taxonomy. Labels can be categorical or numerical. A reward need not identify the correct action, and can arrive after several actions. AIMA Sections 19.1-19.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Supervised Tasks: Categories or Numbers
Features are the input measurements. The label is the target output supplied for each training example.








Task
Output
Features and label




Classification
A category
Pixel intensities; digit category 0-9


Regression
A numerical value
Floor area and location; house price



The digit 7 is a category here, not an amount to be averaged.
A loss scores prediction error. Examples: 0 for a correct category and 1 for a wrong one, or squared error for a numerical prediction.

The task determines what a good prediction means and how we measure its error.


Digit labels happen to be encoded as integers, but their numeric distances do not define classification error. A 7 predicted as 8 is simply a wrong category under 0-1 loss. AIMA Section 19.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
k-Nearest Neighbors
k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) stores labeled examples. For a new input, it finds the k closest stored examples and lets their labels vote.
Let q=(q_1,q_2) be the query, the new input. Let x=(x_1,x_2) be a stored example with two numerical features.
Euclidean distance is straight-line distance:
d(q,x)=\sqrt{(q_1-x_1)^2+(q_2-x_2)^2}.
For N stored examples, choose an integer k with 1\leq k\leq N.

For classification, the most frequent label among the selected neighbors wins. k-NN can also do regression by averaging their numerical targets.


Instance-based learning means retaining training instances and doing much of the work when a prediction is requested. In more than two dimensions, sum squared differences across all features before taking the square root. Reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neighbors.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Neighbor Vote, Worked Out
Two features are already on comparable scales. The query is q=(0,0); letters A and B are class labels.



The three nearest examples:



Example
Features
Distance




A1
(1,0)
1


B1
(0,2)
2


B2
(2,2)
\sqrt{8}\approx2.83






With k=1, A1 alone votes: predict A.


With k=3, the votes are A, B, B: predict B.


The fourth example A2 has distance sqrt(10), about 3.16, so it is outside the first three. There are no distance or voting ties for the two choices of k shown. All coordinates are constructed for this example. Small k is sensitive to individual examples; a larger neighborhood may include points from other classes.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
k-NN Prediction Algorithm
Let D contain N stored (features, label) pairs. mostVotes returns the most frequent label. Assume 1\leq k\leq N.


function KNNPredict(q, D, k)


distances = []


for each (x, label) in D


append(distances, (d(q, x), label))


sortAscendingByDistance(distances)


neighbors = first k entries of distances


return mostVotes(neighbors)


Fix a rule for ties, such as a fixed class order. An odd k does not prevent all ties when there are more than two classes.

Store examples during training. Compute distances and vote during prediction.


The pseudocode uses a fixed rule for equal distances as well as equal vote counts. The notebook sorts with NumPy and its Counter vote resolves equal counts by label encounter order. The details of tie-breaking can affect predictions. Full sorting is a simple implementation, not a requirement for every k-NN algorithm. The stored-example search is different from fitting neural-network weights.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Feature Scales Change the Neighbors
Suppose the features are an object’s height and mass.



Object
Height (cm)
Mass (g)




Query
10
100


A
11
150


B
20
102




Using cm and g: distance to A \approx50.01, to B \approx10.20. B is closer.


Convert mass to kg: distance to A \approx1.001, to B \approx10.000. A is closer.


Choose meaningful feature scales. Estimate any scaling settings from training data, then apply the same transformation to new inputs.


Raw distances are sqrt(1^2 + 50^2) and sqrt(10^2 + 2^2). After conversion to kg they are sqrt(1^2 + .05^2) and sqrt(10^2 + .002^2). This illustrates how relative feature scales weight the distance. Applying the same nonzero scale factor to every feature does not change Euclidean neighbor ordering. In particular, the notebook’s common transformation from pixel range [0,1] to [-1,1] scales all pixel differences equally.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Evaluation on Unseen Examples
Generalization means performing well on new examples. A hyperparameter is a chosen setting, such as k.







Data split
Purpose




Training
Fit a model, or store reference examples for k-NN


Validation
Compare choices such as different values of k


Test
Evaluate the final choice without using these answers to select it



Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that match the labels:
\text{accuracy}=\frac{\text{number correct}}{\text{number evaluated}};\qquad \frac{12}{15}=0.80.

A test score stops being an independent final check if we repeatedly use it to choose k.


The 12-of-15 count is illustrative. The notebook fixes k=3 and uses the provided MNIST training/test split. It does not create a validation split or tune k. To compare hyperparameters, reserve validation data from the training portion. If preprocessing learns statistics, fit them without using the validation or test examples. AIMA Section 19.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Notebook Example: Handwritten Digits
MNIST (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology) contains 28\times28 grayscale digit images.


Features: flatten the image into 28\times28=784 pixel values. The distance compares all 784 values.
Label: the digit category, 0 through 9.
This notebook stores 10,000 training examples, then predicts using k=3. Its fit method stores examples rather than learning weights.

KNN on MNIST notebook
Asset credits

The figure is an unchanged saved output from the course notebook, not a newly run experiment. The code takes the first shuffled batch of 10,000 training images, not the entire MNIST training set. Prediction uses NumPy on the CPU even when the setup prints another available device. Test labels are used only in evaluation and result display, not in finding neighbors. The notebook includes its own runnable code, explanations, and saved results. Dataset reference: https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.datasets.MNIST.html.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Unsupervised Learning Tasks
We have inputs but no supplied target answers.








Task
Meaning
Example




Clustering
Group similar examples
Group handwriting styles without digit labels


Dimensionality reduction
Represent inputs with fewer coordinates
Compress hundreds of pixel features


Anomaly detection
Find examples unusual relative to the data
Flag an unusual image for inspection




A discovered group or unusual example still needs interpretation. An unusual transaction, for example, is not automatically fraud.


These methods may also be used inside larger supervised pipelines. Calling a method unsupervised describes which target information it uses, not whether its output is automatically meaningful. AIMA Section 19.1.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Robot Navigation: Rewards and a Policy
text:
Robot Navigation: Rewards and a Policy
A policy chooses up, down, left, or right for each square. Reaching the exit ends the run.



Illustrative rewards:



Outcome
Reward




Ordinary move
-1


Attempt to enter a wall: stay put
-3


Enter the exit
+10






The marked route has six moves: five ordinary moves, then the exit. Total reward: 5(-1)+10=5.


The robot learns which moves lead to reward. We do not supply a correct-move label for every square.


Rewards are mutually exclusive per transition: entering the exit yields +10 rather than +10 and a separate -1. The displayed route is illustrative, not an experimental learned policy. A policy maps every relevant state to an action, whereas a route is one resulting sequence of actions. For this fully known deterministic maze, search could compute a path directly; RL illustrates learning from interaction when transitions or useful decisions are not supplied in advance. Exploration means trying actions to gain information, while exploitation means using what has already been learned. Improvement is not guaranteed after every interaction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Quick Check: What Feedback Is Available?
text:
Quick Check: What Feedback Is Available?

Predict tomorrow’s temperature using past weather records paired with the next day’s temperature.
Group handwriting images without being given their digit labels.
Let a robot try moves and receive rewards for reaching an exit.


1. Supervised regression: the training examples have numerical targets.


2. Unsupervised clustering: no target groups are supplied.


3. Reinforcement learning: feedback comes from interaction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways

Features describe inputs. Labels supply targets in supervised learning.
k-NN predicts using nearby stored examples. The choice of features, scales, and k matters.
Validation helps choose settings. Unseen test examples check the final choice.
PCA finds directions of large variation without using labels.
Reinforcement learning uses rewards from interaction to learn decisions.


A useful model must work on new examples, beyond the data used to prepare or choose it.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Fitting Data and Generalizing
Generalization means predicting well on new routes. Observations may include noise: variation not predictable from the recorded inputs, such as random waiting delays.







Data
Role




Training
Fit coefficients using our 50 completed routes


Validation
Compare model choices on separate routes, without refitting


Test
Check the final choice on further routes used for neither fitting nor choosing




If a model remembers every training route’s duration, must it predict the next route accurately?


No. Matching the training observations can include matching their noise.


The supplied Spring 2025 lecture motivates generalization through linear regression. The examples here assume fresh examples come from the same distribution as training data. A representative independent test set estimates generalization performance, but is not a guarantee about every future input. The notebook’s comparisons across many model sizes are an experiment, not a procedure for selecting a deployed model using its test set.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Linear Regression and Its Parameters
A parameter is a number fitted from data. For one-stop routes, try predicting duration from distance alone:
\hat y=b+wz.




b: intercept, predicted minutes at z=0.
w: slope, extra minutes per kilometer.
\hat y: predicted duration; y: recorded duration.

The dots are observations. The line is one candidate model.



For b=8, w=2, and a 3 km route: \hat y=8+2(3)=14 minutes.


The displayed line is a candidate, not the least-squares optimum for these three observations. Its intercept is the model’s prediction at z=0, an extrapolated baseline, not a claim that zero-distance deliveries necessarily occur. The later constructed full rule is 5+2z+3c. For the one-stop subset c=1, its mean is 8+2z, so this candidate agrees with the assumed mean but need not minimize the observed noisy sample loss. In neural-network terminology an intercept is sometimes called a bias parameter; that is different from the statistical bias discussed later. The letter z is route distance; later x denotes a vector of features.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Residuals and Mean Squared Error
A residual is observed minus predicted output: y_i-\hat y_i. Here i identifies an observation, and n is the number of observations.
Mean squared error (MSE) averages the squared residuals:
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat y_i)^2.



Distance (km)
Observed (min)
Predicted (min)
Squared residual




1
11
10
1


2
11
12
1


3
16
14
4




\text{MSE}=(1+1+4)/3=2\ \text{min}^2. Minimizing this loss is least squares.


These predictions use b=8, w=2 from the previous slide. The residuals are 1,-1,2 minutes, with squared residuals 1,1,4. These are the three displayed training examples, not a complete 50-route error estimate. Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from canceling and penalizes large errors more strongly. MSE has squared-output units. Minimizing mean squared error and minimizing the sum of squared residuals have the same minimizers when n is fixed.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Features and the Design Matrix
Features are input numbers. For the distance-only model, use \mathbf x=(1,z)^T and coefficients \boldsymbol\beta=(b,w)^T. There are p=2 features, including the constant 1.
Transpose (T) swaps rows and columns.
\hat y=\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta.
A design matrix stores all inputs. We use features as rows and observations as columns:

X=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{bmatrix}8\\2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\hat{\mathbf y}=X^T\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{bmatrix}10\\12\\14\end{bmatrix}.

This excerpt has n=3 routes. The full training set has n=50. In general, X has shape p\times n.

Each column is one route. Each row is one feature used for every route.


For the example x=(1,z), beta=(b,w), and the three distances are z=1,2,3. The output vector has n entries. The n=3 matrix is only the displayed excerpt, not the full n=50 experiment. Many other libraries store examples in rows, the opposite convention. In the notebook, the candidate features are independent Gaussian inputs and there is no added constant feature. A constant counts as a feature when one is included, as in this illustration. Linear regression is linear in the coefficients; constructed features such as z^2 can represent a curved relationship.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Fitting with a Pseudoinverse
Optimization chooses parameters to minimize a loss. Here we minimize training MSE.
The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse is a matrix operation that provides a least-squares solution even when an ordinary inverse is unavailable:
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^T)^\dagger\mathbf y.

Superscript \dagger denotes the pseudoinverse.
\mathbf y holds the n observed training outputs.
If several fits have the same minimum loss, this chooses the minimum-norm one: the coefficient vector with the smallest Euclidean length.


For the three displayed routes, least squares gives \hat b=23/3\approx7.67 and \hat w=2.5. Their training MSE falls from 2 to 25/18\approx1.39\ \text{min}^2.


For the three displayed routes only, the design has rows (1,1,1) and (1,2,3), with observed outputs (11,11,16). The pseudoinverse gives beta=(23/3,5/2), predictions (61/6,76/6,91/6), and residuals (5/6,-10/6,5/6). Its training MSE is 25/18, below the chosen candidate’s MSE 2. Fitting the observed sample better does not establish better prediction on fresh routes. These values are not claimed estimates from all 50 routes.
The Euclidean length of beta is sqrt(sum_j beta_j^2). For an underdetermined constraint beta_1+beta_2=2, (1,1) has smaller length than (2,0); the minimum-norm solution is (1,1). NumPy’s pinv uses singular value decomposition with a numerical cutoff for very small singular values. Reference: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.pinv.html.
With this feature-row convention, the ordinary unique least-squares formula is (X XT)(-1) X y when X has full row rank p, so p cannot exceed n. Merely having more observations than features does not guarantee this independence condition. The pseudoinverse handles both sides of the interpolation threshold. Gradient descent is a different optimization method that repeatedly adjusts parameters using loss derivatives; stochastic gradient descent uses subsets of examples for its updates. Neither algorithm is required by this notebook.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Underfitting and Overfitting
Underfitting: the model is too rigid to capture the broad pattern.
Overfitting: matching training-specific fluctuations harms prediction on new examples.
For this separate curved-pattern illustration, polynomial degree is the largest power of the input. Degree 2 is quadratic. These models are linear in their coefficients.

Dots are the same seven observations in each panel. The dashed gray curve is the underlying pattern.

A perfect fit to the dots can be a poor fit to the pattern between them.


This constructed example uses the noise-free rule y=z^2 and observed points z=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3 with y=9,5,0,1,0,5,9. The fitted degree-one model is 29/7 with zero slope. The fitted quadratic is 1/21+(43/42)z^2. The interpolating polynomial is 1-(181/90)z2+(79/72)z4-(31/360)z^6. All are linear least-squares models in their chosen polynomial features. Their training MSEs are about 13.265, 0.687, and zero. Degree alone is not a universal diagnosis of underfitting or overfitting.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Prediction Error and Irreducible Noise
Irreducible noise is output variation that the available features cannot predict, even if we know the true mean rule.
Here expected means averaged over fresh training datasets and fresh independent output noise, at a fixed input:

\begin{aligned}
\text{Expected squared error}
&=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}\\
&\quad+\text{noise variance}.
\end{aligned}



The noise standard deviation \sigma is the square root of its variance. In our delivery example, \sigma=2 minutes, so \sigma^2=4\ \text{min}^2.

Even a perfect 15-minute mean prediction cannot foresee this route’s random waiting delay.





Assume observed output Y=f(x)+epsilon with independent zero-mean noise epsilon. Bias is E_D[f_hat_D(x)]-f(x), variance is E_D[(f_hat_D(x)-E_D[f_hat_D(x)])^2], and noise variance is E[epsilon^2]. The identity concerns squared prediction error, not arbitrary losses, and follows by expanding the square. Averaging further over test inputs gives an integrated version. In the delivery illustration, even knowledge of the true mean rule leaves expected squared error 4 min^2 on a fresh noisy route. The separate notebook uses noise standard deviation .2 in its own output units, so its corresponding noise variance is .04. The bias-variance identity remains valid when a model displays double descent.

Model Complexity and Validation
Compare delivery models on the same training routes. Horizontal: increasing p. Vertical: MSE. The curves are schematic, not measured delivery results.


Training error: MSE on the examples used to fit the coefficients.
Validation error: MSE on held-out examples; no refitting on them.


Choose p using the lowest validation MSE. Keep the test set for the final check.


For nested feature sets, fixed training examples, and unregularized least squares solved to the global optimum, the minimum achievable training MSE cannot increase when features are added: setting the new coefficients to zero preserves the old solution. Unseen error has no corresponding monotonicity guarantee. The curves illustrate a possible validation pattern and are not fitted to the notebook results. Reducing complexity, collecting more informative data, and regularization can help; regularization means adding a penalty or constraint to the fitting procedure, such as discouraging large coefficients. A held-out validation estimate itself has sampling uncertainty.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Interpolation: Zero Training Error
Interpolation means matching every observed training output exactly, including its noise:
\hat y_i=y_i\quad\text{for every training observation }i.
Each of the n observations gives one equation to satisfy. We have p fitted coefficients available.

With p<n, we generally cannot satisfy all n noisy equations exactly.
In our independent random-feature example, exact fitting becomes possible at p=n=50: the interpolation threshold.
With p>n, many exact fits exist. The pseudoinverse selects the minimum-norm one.


The earlier degree-6 polynomial also interpolates: its seven coefficients fit all seven dots. Zero training MSE says nothing by itself about new dots.


The selected training design has shape n by p after transposing our feature-row matrix. Independent Gaussian entries give rank min(n,p) with probability one. Thus at p=n it is invertible almost surely and can match any response vector; for p>n it has full row rank and has infinitely many solutions. For p<n, the n noisy constraints are generally inconsistent. The parameter-count argument requires independent constraints and a sufficiently expressive design: repeating one feature many times would not produce this threshold. The earlier seven distinct input locations give an invertible degree-six Vandermonde design. Exact arithmetic is assumed in this explanation; numerical training MSE may be near rather than identically zero.

Linear regression notebook

Each trial generates independent training and test data with the same normalized true coefficient vector. Each fit uses the first p rows of the feature-by-observation matrix and the pseudoinverse of its transpose. Values 49, 50, and 51 are omitted around the singular expected-error threshold. The shaded min-to-max range is neither a confidence interval nor a standard-deviation band. More features alone do not guarantee benign overfitting.

n counts training cases; p fitted terms; s nonzero true terms.
Bias describes systematic offset. Variance describes sensitivity to the training dataset.
Unpredictable output noise remains even with a correct mean model.
Parameter count, interpolation, and harmful overfitting are different concepts.
Evaluate on fresh data. A perfect training fit is not a certificate of generalization.


For delivery models, the final check is accurate timing on new routes, beyond the records used to fit or choose the model.

From the same observation, we can construct several features:
\mathbf x=(1,z,z^2,c,c^2,c^3)^T,\qquad p=6.
These powers allow curves while the model remains linear in its coefficients.

For z=2,c=2, the features are (1,2,4,2,4,8)^T. This is still one observation. Our 50 routes still give n=50.


These are candidate models with different feature sets, not claimed estimates from a real dataset. In the three-feature model, x_1=1, x_2=z, and x_3=c; p counts the intercept as well as slopes. For b=5, w_1=2, w_2=3, a 2 km, two-stop route has predicted duration 5+2(2)+3(2)=15 minutes. The one-stop version of 5+2z+3c is 8+2z, matching the preceding illustration.
Constructed features are numerical functions of the same recorded inputs, not extra observations. The six-feature predictor is b+w_1z+w_2z2+w_3c+w_4c2+w_5*c^3. Its dependence on the fitted coefficients is linear even though it can curve with distance and stop count. For z=2,c=2, its feature vector is (1,2,4,2,4,8). The equal values in this one vector do not mean these features agree across all possible routes. With our feature-row matrix convention, adding three constructed features changes the full matrix from 3 by 50 to 6 by 50. It does not create more training information or guarantee independent feature rows. Under the later assumed true rule 5+2z+3c, the extra power terms have zero true coefficients; increasing p does not automatically increase s. Adding flexibility can reduce bias but also increase sensitivity to training data.

A Separate Controlled Experiment
Each observation now has 250 independent random inputs, x_1,\ldots,x_{250}. Only the first ten affect the output. We include no constant feature:
y=a_1x_1+\cdots+a_{10}x_{10}+\varepsilon.
The a_1,\ldots,a_{10} are fixed, nonzero true coefficients. Independent, zero-mean noise \varepsilon has standard deviation 0.2 in this experiment’s output units.



Symbol
Meaning
Value or choice

The delivery rule had s=3, counting the constant. This separate experiment has s=10 and no constant. The meaning of s is unchanged.


This is a new constructed example with measured random features, rather than polynomial features of one z. In the experiment and its later notebook demonstration, all input coordinates are independent standard normal variables. The ten true coefficients have Euclidean length 1. The remaining 240 true coefficients are zero. Independent zero-mean Gaussian output noise has standard deviation .2. The data-generating coefficients stay fixed across training and test datasets, and no constant feature is added. The noise-free mean output is the sum of the first ten contributions. The word true refers to this constructed rule, not to what a fitted model discovers. Index j identifies a feature. In a real dataset we usually do not know the true rule or which features matter.

Fitted Features and True Features
Recall: n=50 training observations, s=10 truly relevant features. We fit one coefficient for each of the first p inputs:
\hat y=\hat\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\hat\beta_px_p.
The \hat\beta coefficients are estimates fitted from training data.








Choice of p
Comparison
What the model can use




5
p<s

20

All ten relevant features, plus ten irrelevant ones


80

All ten relevant features, plus seventy irrelevant ones



Underparameterized means p<n. Overparameterized means p>n.

s describes the true rule. p describes the model we choose.


The hat on beta indicates coefficients estimated from the training data. In this controlled experiment, the first s features are precisely the relevant ones. Thus p>=s includes all relevant features only because of this specified ordering; an arbitrary selection of p>=s inputs need not do so. Irrelevant means a zero coefficient in the true conditional mean, not necessarily a fitted coefficient of zero. The least-squares fit can assign nonzero coefficients to these inputs by matching chance associations with training noise. Underparameterized is not a synonym for underfitting, and overparameterized is not a synonym for harmful overfitting. The p=5 fit cannot recover the omitted independent inputs from the included ones.

Delivery Data: n, p, and s
To make the unknown true rule visible, suppose our teaching data follow:
y=\underbrace{5+2z+3c}_{\text{mean duration in minutes}}+\varepsilon.
Here \varepsilon is unpredictable variation around the mean, such as random waiting. It has mean zero and standard deviation 2 minutes.

All numerical values and the true rule are explicit teaching assumptions. A feature is relevant here if its coefficient in this specified conditional mean is nonzero. We count the constant as a feature, so s=3 includes the baseline; the number of varying relevant inputs is two. The extra job tags are five numeric random values assigned independently of distance, stops, duration noise, and other routes before departure, with true coefficients zero. Their apparent association with observed delays in a finite training sample is accidental. The full distribution of waiting noise is not important for the definitions; assume independent zero-mean noise with standard deviation 2 minutes. Negative noise means a faster-than-average trip, not a negative duration. Actual delivery data need not follow this simple rule, and a realistic study would investigate the feature set and data distribution rather than claiming s is known.

Useful inputs capture a repeatable pattern. More inputs also create opportunities to fit coincidences.

A Decision Tree
A decision tree predicts by following feature tests.


Root: the first test. Branch: one test outcome.
Leaf: a final prediction, with no further question.


One root-to-leaf path is a rule. For example: Sunny and Normal humidity predicts Yes.


The tree follows the supplied Spring 2025 tennis example. An internal node asks a question; a child is a node reached by a branch from its parent. This tree uses multiway categorical splits, including three Outlook branches. Software such as scikit-learn commonly uses binary splits instead. A prediction is not a guarantee about the next group’s choice. Background: AIMA fourth edition, Section 19.3, and https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html.

New day: Sunny, Mild temperature, Normal humidity, Strong wind. Play = ?

(Intro to) AI
section: Choosing a Split: Pure or Mixed?
text:
Choosing a Split: Pure or Mixed?
A split divides training records according to a feature test.
A group is pure when all its labels agree. Entropy measures how mixed, or uncertain, the labels are.



Example group
Label fractions
Entropy




4 Yes, 0 No
All agree
0 bits


7 Yes, 7 No
Evenly mixed
1 bit


9 Yes, 5 No
Mixed, with more Yes
About 0.940 bits



The unit bit comes from measuring information with base-2 logarithms.

A useful split tends to make its children purer. A pure training group does not guarantee certainty on new data.


Purity describes observed labels, not noise-free truth. For two classes, entropy is largest at equal proportions and zero when all labels agree. Only the 9 Yes, 5 No group is the full tennis set; the other two groups illustrate the endpoints. Other impurity scores exist, but the worked example uses entropy.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Information Gain: Split on Outlook
Information gain (IG) is parent entropy minus the weighted average child entropy. Each child is weighted by its share of the 14 records.


H(\text{after})=\frac{5}{14}(0.971)+\frac{4}{14}(0)+\frac{5}{14}(0.971)\approx0.694.


\operatorname{IG}=H(\text{before})-H(\text{after})\approx0.247 bits, using unrounded values.


Sunny and Rain each have entropy 0.9709505944546686 bits. The weighted child entropy is 0.6935361388961918, and information gain is 0.24674981977443933. Displayed rounded values can differ in the last digit when subtracted; the gain uses unrounded quantities. H(after) is conditional label uncertainty averaged over branches, not the entropy of the Outlook feature.

Numeric Inputs and Regression Trees
A threshold is a numeric cut point, such as distance \leq3 km.
A regression tree predicts a number. For squared-error fitting, each leaf predicts the mean training output in that leaf.


A new 4 km delivery route reaches the right leaf: predict 20 minutes. The output is a duration, not a Yes/No label.


In this invented example, training distances 1,2,3,4,5,6 km have durations 10,12,14,18,20,22 minutes. Thresholds 3 and 3.5 produce the same training partition. Each leaf mean minimizes that child’s squared residual sum. Compare numeric splits using squared errors rather than label entropy. Predictions are constant within a leaf, not sloping fitted lines. Reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#regression.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Overfitting and Pruning
A deep tree can memorize accidental details instead of repeatable patterns.

Depth: the number of questions along a path. Maximum depth limits the longest path.
A minimum leaf size requires enough records to support a prediction.
Pruning: remove branches after growing a tree, replacing them with a simpler prediction.

Splitting on a unique Day identifier (ID) can memorize all 14 labels without providing a useful weather rule for a new day.

Choose tree size using validation data. Pruning can help, but a simpler tree is not automatically more accurate.


Maximum-depth and minimum-leaf-size settings restrict growth; post-pruning simplifies an already-grown tree. A pruned classification subtree can use the majority label reaching it; a regression subtree can use their mean. A weak immediate split can enable a useful later interaction, so early stopping and post-pruning need not give the same result. Day ID is a tempting memorization feature, not one used in the worked tree. Validation comparisons also have sampling uncertainty.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why Combine Several Trees?
An ensemble combines several models’ predictions.


A single learned tree can change substantially when a few training records change. This sensitivity is variance, as in Lecture 25.
Combining useful but different trees can reduce that sensitivity because their errors need not line up.




Would 100 identical copies of one tree give that benefit?


No. Identical trees give identical predictions. The ensemble needs useful differences among its members.


The committee is an analogy, not an implementation. Predictive variability after retraining is estimator variance. Averaging can reduce it when errors are not perfectly correlated, but cannot automatically remove systematic bias or fix bad labels. Breiman’s original random-forest paper relates performance to individual tree strength and dependence between errors: https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Random Forests: Two Sources of Randomness
text:
Random Forests: Two Sources of Randomness
A random forest combines randomized decision trees. Their collection is the forest.

Bootstrap sample: draw 14 times from the 14 training rows, allowing repeats. This is sampling with replacement.
Random feature subset: at each node, select some features and learn the best split among them.



Resample rows for each tree and candidate features for each node.


With replacement means a row can be chosen again after an earlier draw. Bootstrapping adds no new measured information or labels. The diagram’s two-feature examples apply at the first node; repeat feature sampling at every later node, not just once per tree. Implementations can offer settings that use all features or disable bootstrap sampling; we show the standard two-randomization construction. Two is illustrative, not a universal default. Sources: Breiman, https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf, and https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#random-forests.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Combining Forest Predictions
Use the same new day: Sunny, Mild, Normal humidity, Strong wind.
A leaf may remain mixed when growth is limited. Its class fractions estimate probabilities. These are illustrative outputs:

\text{Mean Yes probability}=\frac{0.8+0.6+0.2}{3}\approx0.533.
Predict Yes, the larger average class probability. Some forests instead use majority votes from tree labels.

For regression, average the numbers: trees A, B, and C predicting 18, 20, and 22 minutes for one route give 20 minutes.


The leaf counts are invented, not claimed results from fitting the tennis table. A leaf’s class fraction is its class count divided by all counts in that leaf. Depth or leaf-size constraints can leave mixed labels in a final leaf. Averaging .8,.6,.2 gives 8/15 for Yes and 7/15 for No. This matches scikit-learn’s probability averaging. Breiman’s original classifier uses majority votes; these methods can disagree, though they agree here. The separate regression illustration averages three tree outputs for the same route: (18+20+22)/3=20 minutes. These are predictions from separate trees, not a list of training records. Estimated probabilities need not be perfectly calibrated. References: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#random-forests and https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html#sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.predict_proba.

Using a Random Forest
In tabular data, rows are observations and input columns are features.
Hyperparameters are settings chosen before fitting. Split rules are learned from records.



Setting
What it controls




Number of trees
More averaging, with more computation and memory


Candidate features per node
How much the trees can differ


Depth / minimum leaf size
How detailed individual trees can become




Benefit: can capture nonlinear patterns and feature combinations.
Cost: harder to explain than one small tree. More trees do not fix bad data.


Choose settings with validation data and assess the final forest on separate test records.


The toy tennis set does not establish real-world performance. More trees can stabilize predictions, but accuracy need not improve indefinitely. Candidate-feature and leaf-size choices affect bias and variance. Libraries differ in categorical support: scikit-learn’s tree estimators need numeric representations, so Sunny-like strings need suitable encoding. Fit preprocessing on training data only. Tracing one tree is easier than explaining an entire forest; feature importance is not proof of causation. In a forest, do we choose the final split entirely at random?
Does a pure leaf prove that the next day’s label is certain?


1. No. Follow one path and stop at its leaf.

Entropy measures label mixture. Information gain measures its reduction from a split.
Greedy learning builds locally. Size limits and pruning help control overfitting.
A forest combines trees randomized through training rows and candidate features.
Classification can combine probabilities or votes. Regression averages numeric predictions.


A readable rule and a strong ensemble are both useful. Judge either one on new observations.

Devices and .to(...)
A device is where a tensor is stored and computed on. An accelerator is hardware such as a graphics processing unit (GPU).
if torch.accelerator.is_available():
    device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()
else:
    device = torch.device("cpu")

x_device = x.to(device)
print(x_device.device)

The central processing unit (CPU) is enough for these small examples.

Move a model with model.to(device) before creating its optimizer.

Use Colab or the official stable installer. Check the installed version with torch.__version__.

The modern torch.accelerator interface avoids assuming all students have the same accelerator. Older explicit CUDA/MPS availability checks remain valid. CUDA is NVIDIA’s Compute Unified Device Architecture; MPS is Apple’s Metal Performance Shaders backend. Tensor.to returns a tensor, which may be the same object if no conversion is necessary. Module.to moves its registered parameters/buffers and modifies the module in place; returning the module also allows chaining. A dtype can be changed with a call such as x.to(torch.float64). title:
